2361-2364
Gelli, Llanfrothen
November 3rd 1856
My Dear D.R. Evans
I am taking a few moments to send my best regards to all of you there in the far West.
As I have no better way to pass on information to my brothers D. Robert and John Roberts – if they have been
fortunate enough and had the health, to reach their journey's end as they had hoped. Please make inquiries about
them and pass on this letter or take the opportunity to convey its contents. I want to give them information about
some incidents that have occurred since they set off.
1. David Lloyd (from Tremadog) died on July 6th (6?)
2. Grace Pugh (from Fron Heulog) has died.
3. William Jones (Bryn Golau) has also gone the way of all worldly beings.
4. I go on to outline what happened to our Father. On the 21st of September he began shaking, and this fever
continued - almost every other day. Within two days of his death the fever went on all day and he died on
October 3rd at 4p.m. On the afternoon of the 7th of that month we went on to lay his worldly remains in
Ramoth Cemetery, in the same grave as our dear Mother.
In the short time between your departure and his passing he thought a lot about you and the family and very often
spoke about you to me whilst we were in the workshop. He wondered how things were for you and the children. We,
that is Ellin and myself, have a great feeling of longing after you (he uses the word Hiraeth – a Welsh word which
conveys the feeling of loss/longing and for which there is no real English translation.)
In regards to news about the Erw family (family farm), there have been a few changes since you began your journey.
Rees has married Anne, the youngest daughter of Thomas Roberts (Garreg) and Ellin has gone to America with her
uncle William David, formerly of Cae Glas. He and his wife returned to the Old Country and she went back with them.
They set off on September 1st and arrived safely in America on 2nd of October.
The rest of the family are well as usual. As regards our own situation, we are thinking about returning to live in Gelli.
We would have written to you earlier, but we were expecting to hear from you again – we have received a total of six
letters from you – 3 from Liverpool, and 3 from America.
I thought that you would appreciate hearing about the Creuau family but I do not have much to say other than that
everything is much as it always is. Mary Owens of Tan-y-Dduallt is well.
We would write in more detail if we knew that this letter was actually going to reach you. When we receive a letter
back from you saying that you have safely reached your journey's end and settled into employment, we can go on to
exchange more detailed letters. I will remain concerned about you until I receive a detailed letter from you describing
how you got on. As they say in English "The Truth and Nothing but the Truth!".
We send Gwen our very best regards and want to know how she and her children are getting on. We wish her every
success – both materially and spiritually.
We really look forward to receiving a reply to this letter – either from you {D.R. Evans} or from one of our brothers. If
you cannot find any information about them, please write to let us know that nothing is known about them.
I am your servant
Edward Roberts, Gelli Park, Llanfrothen, Tan y Bwlch, Caernarvonshire
To Mr D.R. Evans, Great Salt Lake
From John Lloyd
Not much has changed since I last wrote on August 1st. We are both in fairly good health and send you our best
regards. We await your reply as soon as possible. If anything unusual happens, I will keep you informed.
John Lloyd

Caernarfon
October 27th, 1856
To the Elder David Roberts
Dear Brother
My heart is thrilled to have the privilege of writing this letter to you in the "Mountain Valley" – that place where you
heart longed to see for such a long period and where my heart also longs to visit. But I have not yet sold my soul to Br.
Despair and I don't intend to do so either. I believe that I may be given the honour to come over there, after I have
finished my work here- but I would love to come even sooner. The word Despair is almost out of use amongst the
Saints these days, replaced by the words Br. Faith in their vocabulary – a much better friend don't you think? I am sure
that you have read much about the strength of Br. Faith but not much is written about Br. Despair - he never did very
much.
Perhaps you will remember reading in the 'Herald Gymraeg' {Welsh newspaper} that the two most hated words in the
Welsh language are "except" and "If only" and these are certainly closely connected.
When I waved you goodbye in Liverpool (I lost sight of you as you boarded the steam tug) I had a strange new feeling
that I find hard to describe. It gave me hiraeth {longing} and certainly made me very uncomfortable. I felt as happy as
I'd ever felt before I left you. a strange feeling suddenly came over me - almost as if I something flashed through my
whole constitution. We people are not accustomed to such feelings, but we control our feelings and passions in
circumstances such as these rather than allow ourselves to be governed by them. These feelings were all the more
intense because I had planned to be there with and made such a commitment to this, and I was deeply disappointed
that these plans could not be realised but had to be cast aside. I have decided not to concentrate so much on but to
await the command "Go! You are now free to go." Then, as you can imagine, it will not be long before I make myself
ready for the journey.
Since I last reported to you up until September 3rd I have been travelling through the Merionethshire Conference. At
that time I received a letter from Machynlleth from Br. Daniels asking me to take on the Conwy Valley & Anglesey
Conference because my precursor Evan S Morgans wanted to be relieved. I decided to agree to this request but not
until I had thought hard about my weaknesses because of my ….???... ???.... the commands and resting that I
undertake them after taking upon myself this work. More than anything, I worry because I am not a very good
preacher – as you well know! But "Strength by the day and assistance will follow the need" as the saying goes.
I came to Eglwysbach on Sunday, September 7th for the Cymanfa {singing festival} that was to be held there and I was
confirmed in the post on that day. I am keen to perform this work diligently and not to bring shame in any way. I know
that I must pray and work hard, and try to keep myself in suitable spirits, lest I allow myself to fall to the evils of pride
and boastfulness, forgetting that I am the servant and not the master. It is quite difficult work to keep to the centre-
path but much is to be gained from keeping to that path and keeping the wheels on track. Our responsibility is to pray
and take care to be the best driver that we can be.
Well, it is good to inform you that I am currently enjoying good health, despite being quite unwell last summer, when I
suffered quite a bit, but I am now improved, so that I look as good as ever and I am feeling good. I am much better
than I would have been had I come there with you – it is important to follow advice and stay put if advised to do so. …
??Staying?? in Hell is what I intend to do now (as Little Jane says).
I hope that you are well and comfortable when you receive this letter, and all the family likewise. We are currently
very far apart but, don’t worry, everything will be fine if we do our duty. That is what will in the end bring us Eternal
Life.
Six of your letters have reached Ffestiniog and they were excellent letters - excelling on ones that I had seen from
other emigrants. Two letters, from … Jones and one from Pastor Parry, were quite good but the others were pretty
poor, to tell the truth. I would advise anybody who intends to write to Wales, to ask somebody who can actually write
well for assistance (unless they write properly themselves) because, when people receive a letter from the Valley, they
expect to learn something about what is going on there, and hope to get something for the shilling which pays for its

receipt. {at the time, recipients probably paid for postage} I will now leave this subject, but I do wish people would do
the best they could.
I replied to all of the letters (except the one that was sent to Owen Prichard – that one didn't turn up) and I read them
to all the Saints from the North. There was great praise from everybody – both from the Saints and the worldly people
(because I read them to tens of people 'of the world'). "That's what a proper letter should be like" said one, "Good on
you, Dafydd" said another "What a fine man Dafydd was" said the others. There was great praise from the quarrymen
in Ffestiniog for the letter that you sent them and they hope that you will write after you reach the Valley. They gave
special praise for the englyn {poems} which you sent - remember to send more the next time. Continue to set a good
example and send as many letters as possible in order to clear the fog that continues to cloud the minds of the people
here about these things.
I now want to say a few words aimed at those brothers who have been over there for a number of years, but have not
sent a letter to their relatives or anybody else since their arrival. Brothers! Wake up, and help us to clear the minds of
these people about the Saints' ways and our beliefs. You know pretty well that there are many of these people, and
tell them the truth and I am sure that the men would believe what they read in a letter from one of you. But alas, it is
not so, and the people just say "They cannot write anything other than what their leaders tell them to. They are
ashamed of the new country, otherwise they would have written something about it. They would say how bad it is but
they are so determined to stay, that the have decided to keep quiet and say nothing."
Brothers, this is what they say, and now in order to help these people to change their tune (and to help us dispel these
bad, unfounded rumours that are told about you over here), write back, every one of you, and seriously, get on with
the task! "Better late than never".
Tell David Evans to write back to his sister and relatives and tell Peter Edwards the same. They complained bitterly that
they had not received letters. There are many brothers who, on leaving, promised faithfully that they would write
once they had settled but they did not do so. In this group we have John Evans Esq. Brothers all, remember to fulfil
your promises immediately, so that people are not greatly disappointed in us. They expect us to be better than we can
ever be, but we should make every effort to be as good as we possibly can. Tell Br. Evans that the people of Waen Hir,
Llandygai, Bangor have long expected a letter from him but have not received a single one. Hence Br. Evans should
write them an excellent letter lest they have reason to tell false rumours about him. I don't think that Br. Evans is
alone in this group. Oh, no! Some dozens are in the same group. Brothers, "If the cap fits", then don't blame me. I have
to tell the truth if I am not to disappoint thousands of people. I don't wish to upset anybody, I always do what is in
your best interests.
To finish, I will always do everything possible to protect your character, one and all but I wish that you would throw
yourself at this task "With both hand and heart" so that you restore your loved ones' faith in you. Because their
allegiance at the moment is wearing pretty thin. Dozens of letters arriving there will give them a refresh and who
knows, that this will not encourage them to spread God's Word more than ever.
The people from Waen Hir's address are as follows: Mr Robert Thomas (or Robert Thomas Roberts), Waen Hir,
Llandygai, Nr Bangor, Caernarfonshire, North Wales. Br. Evans should remember to note Caernarfonshire as there is
another Bangor in Flintshire.
I am sure that you would like some news about what is happening to the Church here in Wales. Dewi Elfed and john
Jones returned to the church. Dewi had been travelling through the south Wales conferences and Br. Jonesis a Pastor
for the north, instead of Parry, but not in the same sense as Parry. Br Jones only travels through the conferences there
is a Council in every Conference every month and Br. Jones attends every one and travles to every branch in all the
Conferences. He is very lively and does great work here in the north. I got a letter from him yesterday . He sends you
all his best regards.
There has ben much public baptisms recently throughout the south. There was a lot of persecution of the Saints in
Mold recently as some old fool came to lecture against them causing a lot of bad feeling amongst people but things
turned out well for us in the end. Seven people were baptised in about two months before then as some people rose
up against this fraud.
This reminds me of something that I heard about the Fench. "If they aren't warring against somebody else, then they
will make war against themselves!" I am sure that these Saints are of the same mind.

Many have been baptised in this Conference recently but you would not know them so I shall not note their names
here.
The Merinethshire Conference is pretty flat still despite the efforts to sell books in every town, village and almost
every house in the Conference. Two were baptised in Machynlleth namely Hugh Edwards (the south Walian that you
have heard me talk about and who was quite drawn to getting drunk) and his son and also Br. Edwards is determined
to make a real effort from now on.
The Kingdom has been put in place in this country at this time and indeed it is flourishing s a result of being well-
received on the whole, but we know that some are opposing this advice but they may as well not bother because I am
certain that it is bound to make its way amongst the Saints in Wales. Every one now pays one tenth of their earnings as
a collection and this Tithe money is split, some towards ….. some towards the Temple and some towards other similar
collections. This is a far better way to share the burden equally between everybody. Br. Pratt has decided to give every
Saint a lot to do. Everybody has to take two essays a week which they will lend to their neighbours informing them
about our principles. Women, children and everyone who is a Saint is to undertake this task. Two essays to every
household and the following week they are to collect them and replace them with two others and taking the old ones
to others. Hence the work will multiply as new people will receive them every week. Br. Pratt is determined that
through this means, with the Saints working faithfully, warn all the British people about this within a year.
The names and prices of our books, where they may be bought, and when and where our meetings are held, is printed
on the covers, for they supply covers for all the essays already published and give details of all the publications. On the
back cover of all of these is written "The reader is asked to keep this essay clean. It will be collected at the end of the
week when it can be bought or returned. Training will be given to any reader who wishes to follow the teaching s of
this church. If they inquire to the President of this Conference".
The essay which was published in "Deserett News" under the heading "Mormon Marriage in Utah" was translated into
Welsh by Dewi Elfed and there is a big effort to spread it throughout Wales. We have almost sold 550 copies of this
essay in this Conference. I read in last edition of The Star about an excellent meeting that the Saints held in Durham,
England about a fortnight ago on …, Sunday in a powerful spirit. Br. Amos Muss… called it a Pentecostal Meeting (it
was he that wrote the article) and that is quite an appropriate name for it. Some other prophesied, some spoke and
some translated and "Angels" were in attendance.Br. Israel Evans and Astyn(?) visited me in the North and honestly,
we learnt a lot from them. Almost everybody in the North has been re-baptised, and all through Wales I believe. We
feel much better because of this.
In many places there are major efforts to learn English. I am sure that you saw the letter in the "Herald Gymraeg" from
Richard M Stevens, complaining that the Saints had stolen his money. He has died and his wife has an interesting letter
in the Herald last week (it would be better for her too to be quiet lest she see what sort of a place there is in the Land
of the Spirits sooner than she may wish). It is a letter that she wrote to her brother in Wrexham and I copy it for you
here.
"Grabbing Coal Diggers" St. Jonis/Louis(?) June 26, 1856
Dear Brother
I take this opportunity to write hoping that you are well. They leave me in quite a poorly state to be honest.
Dear Brother
I am sad to write that Richard Stevens has died. He worried a lot after leaving home. He never enjoyed himself
but always wanted to return home. The doctor says that he killed himself by vexing and having too little food.
He died last Sunday leaving us lonely and poor but, if I trust in my God he will be my good friend.
Dear Brother
It is very bad for us since we came over. I don’t have money to bury Stevens but the neighbours helped out
and I still depend on their charity.
Dear Brother
We have been very unfortunate. We had lost all our boxes (chests) with all our possession except what we had
on our backs. I did not like going to Salt Lake. They stole our clothes and refused to give them back despite my
having repaid our debts. Will you please inform William Williams (Abergele) that you have heard from us and
send all my regards to anyone who asks about me.

every house in the conference. two were baptised in machynlleth namely hugh edwards (the south walian that you
have heard me talk about and who was quite drawn to getting drunk) and his son and also br. edwards is determined
to make a real effort from now on.
the kingdom has been put in place in this country at this time and indeed it is flourishing s a result of being well-
received on the whole, but we know that some are opposing this advice but they may as well not bother because i am
certain that it is bound to make its way amongst the saints in wales. every one now pays one tenth of their earnings as
a collection and this tithe money is split, some towards ….. some towards the temple and some towards other similar
collections. this is a far better way to share the burden equally between everybody. br. pratt has decided to give every
saint a lot to do. everybody has to take two essays a week which they will lend to their neighbours informing them
about our principles. women, children and everyone who is a saint is to undertake this task. two essays to every
household and the following week they are to collect them and replace them with two others and taking the old ones
to others. hence the work will multiply as new people will receive them every week. br. pratt is determined that
through this means, with the saints working faithfully, warn all the british people about this within a year.
the names and prices of our books, where they may be bought, and when and where our meetings are held, is printed
on the covers, for they supply covers for all the essays already published and give details of all the publications. on the
back cover of all of these is written "the reader is asked to keep this essay clean. it will be collected at the end of the
week when it can be bought or returned. training will be given to any reader who wishes to follow the teaching s of
this church. if they inquire to the president of this conference".
the essay which was published in "deserett news" under the heading "mormon marriage in utah" was translated into
welsh by dewi elfed and there is a big effort to spread it throughout wales. we have almost sold 550 copies of this
essay in this conference. i read in last edition of the star about an excellent meeting that the saints held in durham,
england about a fortnight ago on …, sunday in a powerful spirit. br. amos muss… called it a pentecostal meeting (it
was he that wrote the article) and that is quite an appropriate name for it. some other prophesied, some spoke and
some translated and "angels" were in attendance.br. israel evans and astyn(?) visited me in the north and honestly,
we learnt a lot from them. almost everybody in the north has been re-baptised, and all through wales i believe. we
feel much better because of this.
in many places there are major efforts to learn english. i am sure that you saw the letter in the "herald gymraeg" from
richard m stevens, complaining that the saints had stolen his money. he has died and his wife has an interesting letter
in the herald last week (it would be better for her too to be quiet lest she see what sort of a place there is in the land
of the spirits sooner than she may wish). it is a letter that she wrote to her brother in wrexham and i copy it for you
here.
"grabbing coal diggers" st. jonis/louis(?) june 26, 1856
dear brother
i take this opportunity to write hoping that you are well. they leave me in quite a poorly state to be honest.
dear brother
i am sad to write that richard stevens has died. he worried a lot after leaving home. he never enjoyed himself
but always wanted to return home. the doctor says that he killed himself by vexing and having too little food.
he died last sunday leaving us lonely and poor but, if i trust in my god he will be my good friend.
dear brother
it is very bad for us since we came over. i don’t have money to bury stevens but the neighbours helped out
and i still depend on their charity.
dear brother
we have been very unfortunate. we had lost all our boxes (chests) with all our possession except what we had
on our backs. i did not like going to salt lake. they stole our clothes and refused to give them back despite my
having repaid our debts. will you please inform william williams (abergele) that you have heard from us and
send all my regards to anyone who asks about me.

I would be very grateful if you could reply. We will speak again. I would have written but poor Stevens begged
me not to and prevented me from doing so.
I am your heartbroken sister,
Anne Stevens
To: Mr Frederick Roberts"
This is an example of the way that the Devil uses her as a weapon to blaspheme the Hallowed Saints. I explained the
background to this letter yesterday whenever I had the opportunity to do so.
You probably will want some news about home. I have not heard anything from them since six weeks ago, but
everybody was well when I left. I slept at Gelli twice and had the warmest possible welcome by all the family.
Edward ???heard??? the Old New Religion from me (???) and your father was very respectful towards me. He wanted
to talk about you all the time "Dafydd was a great son" he said "I really loved Dafydd".
"He signed up everybody that came to his meetings" he said, "He signed almost 60 of them in the quarry once".
"I won't say anything bad about them because they went away" he said "I did my best to get them to stay but, as they
were intent on going, I wished them every blessings along the way".
Everyone at Gelli was very glad that you sent a letters home. Everybody at Creuau was healthy but everything seemed
to be going too well for them – perhaps they would prefer to hear that Sister Roberts was ill rather than she was doing
as well as you described. I visited Mary Owen (Mary's mother) and read her your letters. She was very welcoming
towards me and wanted me to send Br. Roberts, Mary and the children her best regards. She reports that she is as well
as when they left. A terrible tragedy had just struck the locality at the time. About two months prior a gentleman from
England had visited the Maentwrog Vicar together with his two sons and they went swimming or doing something by
the river, both boys drowned and their father was the one that raised the bodies from the river. I have been with
Margaret Jones (Garreg) many times and always received warm welcome from her and her mother. We were never
allowed to leave without a bellyful of food, Mormon principles still burn in Margaret's breast although some clouds
have been cast over her. She and her mother send you all theior very warmest regards. Rees, your nephew married
the girl from the shop at Gar…. after you had left , he was married when {page ends}
…. that he had received a letter from Robert. Her brother Robert's daughter, has emigrated to America about two
months ago. She married some lad from Traeth Bach recently; his name was Owen Jones. I think that he is the son of
Old Hen Gaeau (as they used to call him) who had a horse and cart and used to ford the estuary. Somehow or other,
he ended up in a whirlpool, and was drowned. The horse came safely to shore but it was a long time before his body
was found.
There was some trouble in Ffestiniog some time back. What happened was that John Jones (Penlan) had an accident at
Llechwedd Quarry (I believe) and broke his ribs and right arm, and only lived for a week after this. He was attended to
by John Roberts {an un-qualified, quarry first-aider, very popular with the workmen, but detested by the professional
doctors (who were much more expensive of course!)}. It was not realised he had broken ribs until after his death - if
they had found this out at the beginning and treated him properly, he would have lived, some alleged. An inquest was
held and a post-mortem undertaken and John Roberts was subsequently accused of Manslaughter. Roberts was
brought before the magistrates at Dolgellau but found to be Not Guilty- much to the acclaim of Ffestiniog quarrymen.
On his return to Congl-y-Wal, they carried him shoulder high through the village, shouting "Hurrah!" and everybody
had a great time. They all agreed that John had had a close shave – the two qualified doctors (the "Red" Doctor and
Vaughan Jones) had tried their best to have John found guilty, but old John won the day.
Jason and his family were well when I last saw them and he sends his best regards. Griffiths (Harlech) did not receive
the clothes that you had left for him, or the sack either. …?... Anne Jones was ….?.... the sack …?... but denies all
responsibility and knowledge …?... for the clothes …?... thus leaving poor Griffith with none of the clothes. Griffith and
family were healthy but Owen Jones (Sister Hughes' brother) had been very ill recently, but he was much better when I
last saw him.
The Cricieth people are well and send their best regards to you and to Pastor Parry. They want Pastor Parry to write
them a letter. It should be addressed to "Capt. Robert Williams, Ty'n y Grisiau Cottage, Cricieth, Caernarfonshire.

I got a letter from Br. Daniels …?... was healthy …?... David Davies (Machynlleth) married a local girl, Mary Wilson , a
small woman but as full of spirit as you have ever seen! They got married about a month after you set off.
As regards the World Situation, the Crimean War has now finished, but some disputes persist.
There is something between the Allies and Naples at the moment and the king refuses to do something that they insist
upon. They are sending their navies there to send him some hot projectiles! The "Herald Gymraeg " {newspaper}
reported that a letter from Marseilles reports "The French fleet is about to set off for Naples and some Sardinians are
to set off from Genoa. They continue to prepare their defences in Naples. A letter from Ajaccio on the 14th says that
the British fleet had set off according to instructions sent from London."
Russia is thought of as being rather like Ismael and ….?... by being up for a fight against anybody. Russia is always at
war with someone as this report from the Herald shows "Journal de Constantinople: A fierce battle has been fought on
the river Taka between the Russians and Turks when the latter won a temporary battle with their foes. The Russians
left 16th….?... and 800 captives in the hands of the Circasians".
It is reported that the Russian army was forced back to the river Ruban with significant loses in men and arms. There
was fierce fighting between the Persians and some of their neighbours recently (the Afghanistans) when the Persians
killed about 800 of them and took their city on the river Herat. It is likely that England saw that the Persians had been
unfair in this. This is what the Herald has to say "Constantinople: The English have sent 16,000 men to the Persian Gulf
to attack that country due to the …?... Herat which was contrary to the Treaty of 1853"
There was an accident in London recently when seven people were killed and 60 injured. It appears that a very
important preacher with the Baptists who goes by the name C.H. Spurgeon used to preach at Exeter Hall. However,
the hall became too small for him and consequently another, larger hall was used and they paid £15 a night in
somewhere called Surrey Gardens. He was to preach there the Sunday before last. The hall was packed with people -
about 10,000 inside and another 8,000 outside, failing to get admittance. When the preacher was half way through his
sermon some idiots shouted from the middle of the balcony (there were three balconies there) "Fire! Fire! The place is
on fire!" there was an indescribable rush and the hall was filled with women and children screaming and people
rushing for exits and jumping through windows. Despite every effort by the preacher to warn them that there was no
danger, the result was that seven were killed and 60 injured with broken legs, arms and horrible wounds.
There was an accident at a coal mine close to my home in Neath two months ago. Fire broke out underground and 114
were killed on one day. The mine was Cymmer, Rhondda.
There was an announcement in the newspapers about a terrible earthquake that happened in …?... Islands when
about 3,000 lost their lives.
Water flooded a coal pit at Brymbo, Denbighshire about three weeks ago and 20 were killed.
I must bring this letter to a close. Tell Br. John Roberts that I send him, Mary and the children my best regards. Tell
them that I visited their debtors three times and I tried my best to get some money from them, but with no success.
Remember me to Parry and William Lewis and Br. Hughes and Sister Hughes (Harlech)and Margaret Jones and
Susannah Roberts and remember me to Robert Roberts (formerly of Llantrisant).
All the Saints of the Conference send you their best regards. John Davies (Bethesda) is working very hard. They all
want to send their best wishes to Abel Evans.
Why don't you write a letter her, you cad! I send you and Sister Roberts my best regards, and to Robert Thomas and
Daniel, and Anne Elizabeth very kindly and especially to Jane. This line from Gwilym Hiraethog's poem describes her
"The fondest mother ever to be born in all of Wales".
I hope that you will reply as soon as possible. Address as follows: William Ajax, c/o Edward Parry, Tanygraig,
Llandudno, Caernarfonshire
Your Brother in the Lord
William Ajax

especially Daniel and little Jane. I appeal to you dear friend, please write me a letter and tell me the truth about things

500041-500044
Date: 1857
12th Carried wood and slate flooring to the ship to finish loading (plenty of flags or slate flooring were to be found
along the lake shore)
13th The anchor was raised and sails extended to the wind for a second time but as we set off there wasn't enough
depth of water for us to sail as there was a wind blowing towards the shore and the water was too shallow. By 4
o'clock in the afternoon they managed to get her to deeper water. We were close to being blown onto Church Island
{today called Antelope Island} but by 4a.m. on the 14th we reached Black Rock with the Timely Gull (that was the ship's
name) carrying its first(??) cargo. They reached Salt Lake City on Saturday 15th. My father heard Arapeen, one of the
Indian chiefs, speaking in the Tabernacl, where there were about 2,00 people present in the audience.
16th Stayed in the City
17th Returned home.
On the 23rd of the above month my father and I set off for Boxelder about 42 miles north of here, where my Aunt
Gwen and family live. We received a very warm welcome. I think that my Uncle David R. Evans is a very good man.
They have enough worldly goods around them. Plenty of wheat GWENITH to feed them and plenty of animals at their
service.
We saw a letter written from Cae'r Llwynog {Gwen's father's home in Croesor} after we had set off from the Old
Country. And from this we understood that you had gotten married, and a few other things. We visited David Peters
and his family, Cadwaladr Owens and his family, Owen Jones (formerly of Tŷ Main). Owen Jones looks particularly well.
He has a machine to help with the work and with this he collected 60 bushels of wheat last year. He is very well-
dressed.
We visited many of the other Welsh people and received every kindness. It really was like being back in the Old
Country. The sound of the Welsh language was to be heard there in both speech and song; very pleasant.
David Peters and Cadwaladr Owens and family are fit and successful. We set back home on the 28th and stayed at
Ogden, with my old Master. They had been …?? The reason why I left was that they were worried that they did not
have much wheat. We arrived home on the 1st of March (a Sunday) {This, together with mention of his father being
alive, confirms that this letter was written in 1857} and found the family comfortable and well. The weather is fine
these days and the people are starting on their chores. There are prospects of plenty of work and a good wage. There
is a need for 300 stone cutters to work on the Temple. The wage will be from $3 to $3-50 a day. Nothing much(??) is to
be had here for free.
I believe that America from the Atlantic to the Pacific is a much better place in which to live. I think that you will have
seen the letters that my father sent. A farm worker earns about $2-50 a month plus his food.
Now I need to draw this letter to a close. {He puts it nicely "I want to put a tail on this letter"}
Remember me and all of us here to your family and my grandfather, the Gelli family, the Creuau family and
Carregalltraeth and all our old neighbours in Llanfrothen. Give our best regards to the Cae'r Llwynog family and my
father and mother send their best regards to Williams Davies of Cae Glas (your uncle) and John Edmunds and the Park
family. Tell everybody that asks about us that we are all well and really like the country. This is an exceptionally
healthy country, there is little talk of any death or illness. Remember us very kindly to our old acquaintances in
Ffestiniog. My father sends his regards to Gwilym Ystradau and Ellis Wyn o Wyrfai. Aunt Mary and children are here
with us. They are well. Elizabeth is still in the same(??) place. Neither she nor ourselves had as much?? bread…. as
before(??).
Robert D. Roberts

robert d. roberts

Caernarfon, January 5th, 1857
Elder John Roberts Dear Brother
I hope that Brother David Roberts has received the letter that I sent him or at least that he has received it well before
you get this letter. I hope that you are all well ….. {unclear}…..
No doubt, you had terrible difficulties to overcome on your journey - as one would expect, because it is not a small
matter to travel seven or eight thousand miles through such places.
I read in The Star and the Udgorn that you were put to quite a testing time and the fire that occurred …. {unclear}....
had to turn back as their constitution ….. {unclear} .... could not suffer such heat.
I have often thought that the migrating Saints are much like potatoes, carried in a truck which has holes in its bottom!
With every yard forward, some of the potatoes fall out, and if the ground is rocky, even more will be lost. It is quite
similar with the emigrating Saints; say seven or eight hundred start off together from Liverpool, perhaps only four or
five hundred will reach journey's end. Because of this we should pray that some of the potatoes are large
(Chr....{unclear}.... Sectarian) so that they will not fall through the holes.
I was pleased to read in Br. David Grant's account that you had a successful journey at least up to Fort Laramie and he
was hopeful that you would complete the rest of your journey even more successfully. I read all your names in Br.
Grant's letter and it brought me great joy to read that you were still alive and had travelled so well. I was especially
glad that you had beaten the "wagon people" and all the Saints in Wales were glad to hear that. To be honest, we did
not wish those who travelled by wagon to succeed (as Brigham had said that it would be better for them to travel
using handcarts) with exceptions of course for those unable to do so.
I saw a letter in The Star about a fortnight ago from Br. Thomas Bullock stating that he had come across a large "Welsh
Camp" about three days out of the Valley and that is the last report that I have received about you. I trust that you
have by now arrived there and are now settled and that you are all healthy and comfortable.
I am pleased to report that I am well and that my health is better than it has been in years. My friendship with "Mr.
Cold Water" is such that I have my Honourable Friends Tea and Coffee and have thrown all of their relatives out of the
house and locked the door behind them! If people made more business with Mr. Cold Water and less with those two
Gentlemen Tea and Coffee then the doctors could hang up their harps as they wished {Psalm 137}, but mankind's
taste for these is almost as if they had sworn allegiance to these habits.
I was in Ffestiniog last week, seeing Jason and family. They were well at the time but Jason had been in having a
problem with his hand - which had turned black preventing him from working for about three weeks. Jason has a Level
{quarrying term} in Hafodty, which he shares with another man. They have enough slate to work until August. They
employ four workers and amongst them is Br. Treharne who has been working with them this past month as the
Conference locally is in a poor state - but they are trying their best. After all, you took many of his group along with
you last time, so there are not many members left now. They will keep Br. Treharne on all winter. He was well and in
excellent spirits and wished to send you his best regards - every one of you. Jason also told me to send his best
regards, especially to Br. David Roberts. Tell him and Sister Roberts that Old Phebe started shaking her head {in
despair?} when I was there. So, you see that times were quite dark in the Ffestiniog district when I was there.
There has been a lot of building from Rhiw to Tanygrisiau and they are building a new road from Blaenau to Llan. It
starts from the old road by the house at the top of the hill above Cae'r Blaidd mill, keeping further east than the old
road and coming out on the crossroad beyond Blaen Ddôl.
Tell Br. D. Roberts, that I visited David and Martha Williams and that they sent you, him and all of his family their best
regards. Martha misses Pierce greatly and she gave me one of his books to remember him by.
Recently, many children have died in Ffestiniog recently as a result of Scarlet Fever - three from a single house (you
would not know them as they are new to the district).
I have called on your debtors four times but to no avail, so I have now given up as I don't think that you will get a single
penny from them. As South Walians used to say "Even the Devil himself could not get it out of them!".

I went from Ffestiniog to Maentwrog to visit your mother-in-law and received a very warm welcome and was told to
call again, whenever I was in the area. I was there on January 2nd. She too wished me to pass on her kindest regards to
you and to Mary and the children. I was to tell you that she was making a very good living and was in good health.
From there, I went on to Margaret Jones' home in Carreg and she gave me the warmest welcome that she could. She
knew that I had ??LOGELL?? {a fund?} and that a little money would be useful for that. To be honest, she has been
very kind to me every time that I have visited, as was her mother before her. She too wished to be remembered to you
and to Mary and the children and to Br. Roberts and his family. Margaret is still a Saint in principle but has not been
baptised yet, but is thinking about having this done.
I went from Garreg to Gelli but there are fewer family members there now compared to my previous visit. Your father
has passed away - he died about three months ago. I think that he died of a fever. He had only been ill about a
fortnight and was still getting out of bed and visiting Edward's workshop occasionally even during that time. Edward
said that the day before he died, he had told him that this would be the last time that he would come into the
workshop - and that's how things turned out: he died the next day. Others have told me that Edward suffered terribly
grief after him and this persisted for a long time afterwards. He was however quite well as was his wife, when I visited
and I received a warm welcome.
I slept there overnight and had plenty to eat and a warm welcome - all free of charge. I have stayed there on previous
occasions and they have never accepted a penny from me, they just say that they are glad to see me and they made
that very clear by their actions. I always judge things according to this saying "Faith without action is dead" {Judge
them by their actions not their words?}. They were both quite well but Edward had been having trouble with his eyes
and had not been able to work for about five weeks, but when I was there, he was better and had been able to resume
work. They sent you their kindest regards.
From there I went on to Creuau, where I of course, had to drop in and have something to eat. Margaret (Catherine's
sister) gave me a sandwich to put in my carpet bag. She too sends her regards - especially to her sister Catherine. They
have a new maid there.
There have been quite a few deaths in the locality, since you left - Daniel Lloyd (Tremadog) who died before your letter
reached his hand. Others have set off on their journey to the Land of Spirits - amongst those who have set off on the
'Long Trail' is old Judge Lloyd and old William Williams (Rhyd). I wonder when they will return?
Cadwaladr Owen (Dolwyddelan) and old John Williams (Llecheiddior) and John Williams (Drenewydd) had gone away
to some far country looking for work I suppose, that is why people usually go there.
I went from Llanfrothen to Caernarfon and there, I visited the home of Sister Lloyd. Who was there but old Robin Ddu
Eryri {a poet - his bardic name} . He was lodging there for two weeks. Before that, his work was going from fair to fair,
visiting the inns and reciting "Adam's Will" {long poem}. He is currently translating "Chambers' People's Education".
The last volume is now in the press and there are two or three volumes already in print, printed by Hugh Humphries
(Caernarfon).
Fair play to him, Robin did not say a word against the Saints although he has left the Church. He recalled that when he
was in an inn in Bethesda once, somebody asked him about the Saints. Parry said that the Saints were the best people
that he had ever met. "Aren't they doing bad things over there in the Valley?" asked one. "How do you know this?"
responded Parry, "It is in all the newspapers" he said. "Do you believe everything that you see in the newspapers?"
asked Parry. "Yes" he replied. "Well" said Parry, "three months back, I read in a newspaper that Robin Ddu had got
drunk, had to sleep out in a ditch and consequently had died. Did I believe that! Another time, I read that Robin Ddu
had married a woman, even giving her name. I did not believe that either, although it appeared in print." The
questioner suddenly became quiet.
Robyn wished to be remembered to you and to Jeremy, Phillips and Davies (the printers) and to Richard Morris and to
Pastor John Parry and all his friends. He said that he would be baptised as soon as Pastor John Jones came by. I asked if
he would like to send you a few englyn {poems} to the Valley as I would be writing shortly. He immediately composed
these five poems for you. {Here is a very poor attempt at translation!}

correspondencePages.suppliedText:
Healthy under Zion's sky
You are, my dear friends
Me, I'm here making a living,
Far across the sea
Jeremy, is still fit and Philips
making a good living
And merry Morris happy
Accomplishing all that he can
Great it is to talk
Once more with Captain Jones daily
And an honour it is for the Saint
Once more to receive praise
Despite foreign difficulties
And a ship in difficulties
The dear Saints after waiting
Praise God in the Temple
Robin Ddu o Eryri
Well done Robin! It is a pity that he does not make better use of his talent.
There has not been much baptising in Merionethshire Conference recently. But one person was baptised in
Machynlleth recently. I hear that the Saints there are doing well. Hugh Edward (Machynlleth) is still doing good work.
In my recent letter, I said that David Davies had got married and that he had at last got somebody who would enable
him to better himself - if the so-and-so wanted to do so; but no good will come of it if he does not follow good advice.
When in Ffestiniog, I heard that James Anwyl was now home.
It is unlikely that anyone from Merionethshire will emigrate this time unless David Roberts (Dinas Mawddwy) decides
to go to the States. It is unlikely that many from Wales even will emigrate this time - probably not more than 150. The
following Presidents have been selected-
President Successor
Israel Evans Mither
Benjamin Ashby Taylor
Thomas Harris John Davies (Merionethshire)
Griffith Roberts (Denbigh) Hugh Evans (Newmarket)
Thomas Jones (Aberystwyth) Joseph Griffiths
William Jones (Carmarthen) Thomas Rees, who had been a Leader at the Flint Conference the previous
year and David John (Formerly of Haverfordwest) is to succeed him in that Conference.
The following are set to emigrate from this Conference. Hugh Davies (Bron yr Haul, Eglwysbach), David Davies (son of
David & Sarah Davies from the same place) and Grace Jones (Bryn Dedwydd, near Conwy).
I give the names of these people so that their relatives know that they are on their way to join them. I do this because
letters so often get lost in the post. If you happen to see the son-in-law and daughter of the said Grace Jones, tell them
that she has sent them several letters and that her husband died some five months ago. She is quite well and has sold
all her furniture and is now ready to emigrate - as soon as the call comes.
This year, Br. Pratt wants the emigrants to reach the Valley by around the start of autumn. To facilitate this, and
ensure that it happens smoothly, everyone must send £3 (apart from the £1 deposit) to the Office so that it can
immediately be sent to the States to get the things needed for the journey across the Plains - rather than having long
delays in the States whilst the necessary provisions for the journey are bought. Nobody is allowed to emigrate from
the British Isles using the Perpetual Fund - not even the ones that put £5 into it last year.

There have not been many baptisms in the North since I posted my last letter but I don't know how it is in other
places. I have not heard of any particular revival anywhere, although baptisms are taking place regularly. We are not
giving up and there again signs of more baptisms in some areas.
Br. Pratt is busy writing a book. He wrote four essays recently under the headings "True Faith", "True Repentance",
"Baptism by water" and "Holy Spirit". These are currently being translated into Welsh by Dewi Elfed. Two have already
been published. Every essay has 28 pages of the same size as the Udgorn and the series has been published in bound
form, with all essays containing listing the names and prices of all the works published by the Saints in Europe. There is
a cover for the essays, similar to that on "The New Old Religion" and the back cover lists all the places in Wales where
the Saints meet, and lists the times of their meetings. These cost two pennies.
Saints borrow these publications every week and take them to show their neighbours. They take "The Real Truth" to a
house this week, then the next week, they take it back, and leave "True Repentance" in its place, and they take "Real
Truth" to another home. This continues until everyone has had the opportunity to see the principles so that they have
no excuse for their disobedience.
Well, the Crimean War has come to a close since you left but Cadwaladr Llwyd was not killed yet as his aunt wished.
He is currently at home, released from the army - not because of injury but because they could do nothing with him
because of his 'inborn perfection'. {???}
There have been quite a few losses at sea recently - or just last week, I should say. Four vessels were lost last Sunday
between Llandudno and Mostyn. As a ship was being rattled by the storm near Prestatyn, a warning was sent for a
lifeboat. They quickly set off lest another lifeboat got there ahead of them. They put up sails, but because the wind
was so strong, the lifeboat overturned and their mast got stuck in the sand with the result was that all hands drowned
- 13 in number.
Floods and strong winds have troubled these regions recently. There has not been such a flood in the Conwy river in
living memory so they say. The lower part of Llanrwst was inundated with floodwater - it was a yard deep in Plas Helyg
Street and the whole valley was under water. It looked as if a new sea inlet had been created rather than a track to
bring the railway there from Llandudno. Talking about railroad, they say that somebody has agreed to dig large tunnel
at Rhosydd {actually, the Crimea Pass tunnel}. £2,800 has to be raised and they will have to work the tunnel from
several places. They will have to dig a vertical shaft down from the centre and then have two gangs working from
there and one from either end.
{letter ends}

between llandudno and mostyn. as a ship was being rattled by the storm near prestatyn, a warning was sent for a
lifeboat. they quickly set off lest another lifeboat got there ahead of them. they put up sails, but because the wind
was so strong, the lifeboat overturned and their mast got stuck in the sand with the result was that all hands drowned
- 13 in number.
floods and strong winds have troubled these regions recently. there has not been such a flood in the conwy river in
living memory so they say. the lower part of llanrwst was inundated with floodwater - it was a yard deep in plas helyg
street and the whole valley was under water. it looked as if a new sea inlet had been created rather than a track to
bring the railway there from llandudno. talking about railroad, they say that somebody has agreed to dig large tunnel
at rhosydd {actually, the crimea pass tunnel}. £2,800 has to be raised and they will have to work the tunnel from
several places. they will have to dig a vertical shaft down from the centre and then have two gangs working from
there and one from either end.
{letter ends}

3671-3678
Tanygraig, Llandudno
April 10th, 1857
Dear Brother Roberts
I start this, my second letter to you. I have also written to Br. John Roberts but I don't know if either letter was
received. I understand that it is difficult for letters from this country to reach the Saints once they have set off.
I am glad to report that I am fairly well and comfortable and I hope that you and all your family and all the brothers
and sisters who accompanied, you are blessed when this letter reaches you. I am sure that you will have been tested
along the way and suffered many difficulties as you went to the Kingdom of God.
We were glad to hear that you had arrived without having suffered half as much as the company that followed you
did. The newspapers reported that the "Mormons" starved in their hundreds, but we did not believe this at all,
although we were sure that there would have been testing times for you. But as the old saying goes "Empty vessels
make the most noise" - the newspapers always make terrible sounds – like ghosts haunting a house. After hearing the
noise, one goes to look to see what has happened and one always finds nothing amiss.
I have really looked forward to receiving a letter from you, but in vain (unless a letter has arrived in Llanfrothen). I
have not received a letter from anyone from north Wales except one from somebody called John Parry, from
Newmarket.
I am rather worried (although I do not believe this yet) that you intend to make yourself famous by learning the "Art of
Silence" by not writing letters to us, but I think that you will be too set in your ways to learn this new 'art form' and will
want to let me know that you are still alive.
I have not heard anything from Llanfrothen recently but I intend to visit in the near future – perhaps before I post this
letter.
It is an important time for me in the British Isles at the moment as a Religious Revival is beginning. It started a month
or two back and I can assure you that the Church in Wales or in England has never seen anything like it. There will be a
proper pruning of the Orchard - and the trees within the Orchard really needed this done. The Orchard had become
full of weeds and it was impossible for the trees to bear fruit whilst there was so much dead-wood on the trees. It will
now be a time of much-needed pruning. Axes are aimed at the the boughs of every tree and ones that bear no fruit
are to be cut down.
The CYNYDDAROTS (??rules??) that who were once respected by some are once again being practised more than ever
and there is talk about those who had upheld such things (when they were here) with respect for their efforts in
upholding "God's Words" whilst being ignored for that (alas) by many of Israel's Elders. But things have changed since
then and a Revival has made this the 'Major Subject of the Day' amongst the Saints in these countries now after
receiving President Brigham Young's letter calling on all the Saints on these islands to change/revise.
A meeting was held in Liverpool for that purpose and also Apostle Ezra Benson recently visited Swansea. He was
starting a new Revival in Wales and re-baptising everyone who wishes to be a Saint. From now, on everybody who has
not been re-baptised will not considered as being in the Church, and everybody who has been re-baptised will have
their names recorded in a new place in the books. We will not see the Church start anew unless this happens. Also, the
only ones to be re-baptised are those who pledge to pay the Tithe and to follow the Word of Truth - young and old
must pledge, if they are to remain within the Church. You can argue that some will think this harsh, and already some
complain that it is a Hard Master that we follow. Indeed, there is reason to think that this will cause many to turn to
become followers of Demas. "Let them do so!" say I, for we need Doors to work in a way that people can enter to
participate in the feast rather than their being like "…." {unclear} scaring away everybody who comes looking for
somewhere to eat.
But all these rules will do is uphold True Mormonism; this has affected some more than anything that they learnt
before, because some have decided to obey the Word of Truth more than they had ever done. I am glad to say that I
have been keeping to this for more than a year and I was re-baptised last week, and I am now doing my utmost to re-
baptise all of those who pledge to keep to the rules.

14th April
After writing the above, I came to Ffestiniog, a bit sooner than I was expecting when I started writing this letter. I had
expected to receive a letter from you by now, but that was not to be. I was in Llanfrothen yesterday and met your
brother Edward and his wife and they were both well. This time, I spent the night with them once again as I have done
on numerous occasions and he and his wife were very kind to me. He too was really looking forward to receiving a
letter from you. He and his wife send you their best regards. John Llwyd of Garth Llwynog and his wife are healthy and
send you their regards. I also called at Garreg and saw Margaret Jones and she and her mother were both healthy and
send you their regards. They are always kind towards me.
I also heard that the Creuau family were well but I didn't see any of them this time. The man at Parc had recently been
buried when I visited. Owen Jones (Ty'n Ddôl) and the man from Morfa Du have also left for The Land of the Spirits a
while back.
I will tell you about Ffestiniog now. Br. Jason Thomas and family are well and he is working in a level in …. Hafodty and
it is turning out to be a very good site. Br Trehearne is working with him since the start of winter but will be stopping in
about a month's time in order to go preaching.
Several have been involved in bad accidents in the quarries recently as a result of blast holes blowing back on them
{this happened to 'blind' John Roberts, DRR's brother} Owen Cadwaladr (Jason's co-worker) was killed about a week
ago and David jones (Tanygrisiau or "Big" David Jones) and Sion the servant were lost due to the same horror. Evan
Williams (Emah Williams – Dolgarregddu's husband) almost lost his eye, when a blast hole blew back on him before
Christmas. He has not worked since. He is currently emigrating to Utica in the USA.
Everything is going on much the same over here - everything is quite expensive. Butter is one shilling and fourpence a
pound here but 2d more expensive in the Bethesda area. Other things are pretty similar.
William Roberts the shoe-maker and his family are well and send their regards. He is currently moving to Congl-y-Wal.
There isn't much more success in making Mormons of Ffestiniog residents than there was when you were here, but we
are not giving up, because some of our seeds may have hidden away in unexpected places. A fair wind may cause
these to grow and became an adornment for some corner of the Orchard once again.
I heard that the Saints at Harlech were well when last seen by Br. Trehearne about a month back, and the Cricieth
Saints the same as are all the Saints of this Conference.
I received a letter from Br. Edward Roberts (Dinas Mawddwy) about a week ago informing me that he had received a
letter from his siter Susannah informing him of the death of Owen Jones (Tywyn). This reminded me of the spirit that
he received in the Cymanfa in Towyn, Merionethshire when you were there. It was said at the time that there were
some present that would not see one another after that, but would see one another in the Land of the Spirits.
Br. Roberts said that they were all well there and that they intended to write directly to Susannah. David, his brother
has emigrated to the States.
I was in Liverpool a while back, delivering other migrants. They were setting off on March 27th on board the excellent
ship George Washington (1649 tons). On board were 817 Saints, mostly going to The Valley . There were about 60
from Wales, 48 Swiss, about 20 from the Isle of Man, some Scots and the rest were English. I cannot list all of those
from Wales, but these are the few that I did know.
Name Home address County Aiming for
Griffith Robert & wife Abergele Denbigh The Valley
Anne E Roberts Abergele Flint The Valley
Elizabeth Jones Rhuddlan Flint The Valley
Owen Williams, & wife & 2 children Abergele Flint States
Evan Read & family Nant-y-Glo Glamorgan? Not known
John Lewis & family Penycae Flint Not known
Evan S Morgans Pontardawe Glamorgan States
David Roberts Dinas Mawddwy Merionethshire States
{end of letter}

3611-3616
Pen-y-Cae, Monmouthshire
1858
To the Elder D.R. Roberts
Dear Brother
Today is probably the designated day for me to reply to your letter, which I received about eleven weeks ago.
It is not a lack of affection towards you, or a lack of time that caused this long delay; I thought that it would be futile to
send a letter whilst there were still hostilities between the States and Utah. We heard three weeks ago that this
difficulty had been settled, but it was not possible for me to write until now.
I am sure that Br. John E. Jones will have told you all the news about the North, from the time that you left up until the
time that he himself left. I have not had much contact with Merionethshire recently. I got a letter from Br. Treharne
about six weeks ago reporting that he was well as were Jason and family (as Br. Treharne has been working with them
for about a year). I don't know how things are with Jason but I think that things are not going too well in the Church as
I heard. Br. J.R. Jones that things were 'as dry as a bone'.
Phebe has been suffering from dropsy in her limbs once again. David was buried about a year or more ago.
Griffith (Harlech) is as thirsty as a bone and I don’t really know if he remains in the Church or not. I heard that James
Anwyl pays his Tithe and Br. Edward Roberts (Dinas Mawddwy) is still the same – trying his best, and he is certainly a
good man.
There is nobody of any substance in Machynlleth, apart from Sister Griffiths and her parents, because only elderly
people live there now. The Ellis Sisters are surely …?... them and Sister Davies (Towyn) is working hard, all on her own,
there.
I think that David Vaughan and his wife are out of the Church, but I am not certain about this. I have not heard
anything about David Davies (Machynlleth) for about a year. He is still out of the Church and no good has come of him
since he left Ffestiniog. It is a shame that a young man, in the prime of life, wastes his time at such an important
time!!!
Br. Meredith (Llanidloes) remains a good man and pays his Tithe. Isaac Jones (formerly of Machynlleth) now resides
about two miles away from me, in a place called Nant-y-Glo along with his family. I have visited him several times but
he is too conceited/selfish to allow anybody to help him, and to be honest, I did not even try! I went to see him
because he was family and because of old friendship. He is full of feelings of withdrawal so what I did with him was not
to talk about Church principles, just let everything pass, as we do with other secular people.
I would like to give you news about your relatives but I am afraid that I can't at the moment.
Saints are few and far apart in the North at the moment - just a handful remain. Br. John Daniels (Bethesda) is working
here at the moment. He was in hospital for nine months and there are only three months since he was released. His
wife was like the devil to him, but he is now out of her grasps at last. He wishes to be remembered fondly to you.
Well, Br. Roberts, almost three years have passed since we parted on the river in Liverpool. If anyone had told me at
the time that three years would have passed before I saw you again, I would have felt really feel sad, but the time has
flown; the likelihood of this happening now is not much better than it was then. It is good that our future is hidden
from us because faith and hope reign and we have can have some enjoyment.
I understand that you formed an excellent procession when setting off for the South. If only I was there with you! But
perhaps there was some bitterness about this, yet again I think that every one of the Faith has some means/medicine
in their possession, which will turn the bitter into sweet and turn everything to the service of those that believe in the
Lord. People here wished to have the honour of experiencing the bitterness and sweetness that you experienced.
It is true that some became followers of Demas but they were of no value and we are better off without them.
In the South, everything is going well at the moment. The Saints are working particularly hard and a big effort is being
made to repay the Debts Book. As proof of this, the Millennial Star received £566 this week. Truly, the Saints are
making a very special effort. The people of this Conference are as good as any that have come down from Heaven. It is

a pleasure to be working with them. I am delighted to be with them. All of the officials and many of the sisters keep to
the Word of Wisdom. Through this, I can say that I too have kept to this for two years now, and am determined to
continue doing so.
I cannot yet say who will be emigrating next spring - this secret has not yet been disclosed to me.
The "Udgorn" is now published weekly and costs a penny ha'penny. Wales currently has many newspapers – here are
their names: Y Cymro, Yr Herald Gymraeg, Baner Cymru, Yr Arweinydd, Y Gwladgarwr, Udgorn y Bobl, Yr Amserau, Y
Gwron Cymreig, Y Gweithiwr, Seren Cymru and Punch Cymraeg. This last one is published in Holyhead and is in the
same format as the English Punch. All the above are weekly publications apart from Gwron Cymreig and Punch, which
are bi-weekly.
A large regional eisteddfod is to be held on 21-4th of this month in Llangollen, with prizes totalling £500. I am afraid
that I don't know the subject of the competitions - I am sure that you would like to know what they are.
Employment is going well here but wages are not good, however food is more affordable – I think that …?... is the
most expensive, butter is one shilling and three pence and cheese costs the same.
On the whole, we had a very dry summer and we had good harvests – better than ever I believe. Crops of grass and
wheat, apples and all sorts of fruit were plentiful. This reminds me of what you said in your letters about the
prophesies of Br. Brigham about Three Years of Plenitude.
General news is in rather short supply for me at the moment so you will have to wait to hear very much, but I am sure
that you get a lot of news in your newspapers and so there is no point in my repeating these.
Oh! I forgot to tell you about Br. John Davies (formerly of Merionethshire). He is now in Merthyr. I heard from him last
week and both he and Sister Davies were well.
I would like to hear from you as soon as you possibly can. I will reply sooner next time than I did this time (as I have
noted earlier).
I would like to know how Thomas, Robert, Daniel, Anne, Elizabeth and Jane are getting on.
Please address your letter to: William Ajax, 100 Newtown, Ebbw Vale, Newport, Monmouthshire.
Please show this letter to Br. J.E. Jones and anyone else that I know and remember me to Br. Jones and all my
acquaintances. Remember me to Sister Roberts and all the children and to Mary the widow of Br. Roberts and to
Elizabeth, her daughter.
If you see Br. Daniels remember me to him and to Br. William Lewis (previously from Caernarfon) and to John Lewis
(Llanrwst). If you see anybody from Ben-y-Cae or Victoria tell them that everyone here is well. Remember me to Br.
James Taylor and Michael Vaughan (Lehi City) and tell them that they will soon get a letter.
I am currently well and comfortable and well. Please be so kind as to write as soon as possible.
With best regards to you and all faithful Saints.
Your brother in the Gospel
William Ajax

the "udgorn" is now published weekly and costs a penny ha'penny. wales currently has many newspapers – here are
their names: y cymro, yr herald gymraeg, baner cymru, yr arweinydd, y gwladgarwr, udgorn y bobl, yr amserau, y
gwron cymreig, y gweithiwr, seren cymru and punch cymraeg. this last one is published in holyhead and is in the
same format as the english punch. all the above are weekly publications apart from gwron cymreig and punch, which
are bi-weekly.
a large regional eisteddfod is to be held on 21-4th of this month in llangollen, with prizes totalling £500. i am afraid
that i don't know the subject of the competitions - i am sure that you would like to know what they are.
employment is going well here but wages are not good, however food is more affordable – i think that …?... is the
most expensive, butter is one shilling and three pence and cheese costs the same.
on the whole, we had a very dry summer and we had good harvests – better than ever i believe. crops of grass and
wheat, apples and all sorts of fruit were plentiful. this reminds me of what you said in your letters about the
prophesies of br. brigham about three years of plenitude.
general news is in rather short supply for me at the moment so you will have to wait to hear very much, but i am sure
that you get a lot of news in your newspapers and so there is no point in my repeating these.
oh! i forgot to tell you about br. john davies (formerly of merionethshire). he is now in merthyr. i heard from him last
week and both he and sister davies were well.
i would like to hear from you as soon as you possibly can. i will reply sooner next time than i did this time (as i have
noted earlier).
i would like to know how thomas, robert, daniel, anne, elizabeth and jane are getting on.
please address your letter to: william ajax, 100 newtown, ebbw vale, newport, monmouthshire.
please show this letter to br. j.e. jones and anyone else that i know and remember me to br. jones and all my
acquaintances. remember me to sister roberts and all the children and to mary the widow of br. roberts and to
elizabeth, her daughter.
if you see br. daniels remember me to him and to br. william lewis (previously from caernarfon) and to john lewis
(llanrwst). if you see anybody from ben-y-cae or victoria tell them that everyone here is well. remember me to br.
james taylor and michael vaughan (lehi city) and tell them that they will soon get a letter.
i am currently well and comfortable and well. please be so kind as to write as soon as possible.
with best regards to you and all faithful saints.
your brother in the gospel
william ajax

Creuau
February 5th, 1859
Our dearest sister
A long time has passed since we have seen one another - or even received a word from you. But two letters
have reached this area - one from Mary Roberts, addressed to Edward Roberts at Gelli and another, from
Gwen and her family to John Lloyd of Garth Llwynog. Through these two letters, we have gleamed a little of
your story. The few facts that we gathered have had quite an effect upon us. Firstly, our minds are a bit more
at ease because we now know something of your circumstances – something about which we had absolutely
no knowledge. But there is a second way in which it has affected us and caused great sorrow in our minds;
we understand that your husband David Roberts has passed away, leaving you and the children in a strange
and distant land.
As you can imagine, since hearing this we have only had a few moments of peace when we don't dwell on
thinking about your circumstances. How are you getting on now? We are really surprised that you have not
written before now. We impeach you to send us details of your circumstances. How is it for you these days?
We gathered from the letters that David Roberts had been ill and that you, as a family, had also suffered from
this illness, but the letter sent to Garth Llwynog {John Lloyd} said that you had made a good recovery. This
change to your circumstances has been a real cause of worry to us. How on earth will you and the children
be able to get the essentials needed to sustain you?
We understand that you now have got two cows and a few smaller cattle, also a yoke and oxen and also
wagon – at least when David was alive, but by now quite naturally, we are sure that things will have become
tighter because of your new circumstances.
We do not think that employment opportunities for yourself and the children are as good over there as they
are here. If you were in Ffestiniog, the boys would have a choice of good jobs, and they would make good
money and thus be able to help you. And it's also certain that there is no social assistance over there to help
widows and poor orphans as there is over here.
If these few lines actually reach you, we really wish that you would send us an acknowledgement that you
have received it and also give us details about your situation. Tell us about the children - where are they
now? Are they still at home with you or have they gone their own way and left home?
Also, I want to know how you and the children feel about staying over there or do you want to return home? If
you want to return home, then it is up to you. We want a definite answer to this question.
Gwen's husband wrote in his letter about the Market over there. Apparently, wheat prices are high at the
moment - I hope that you get some benefit from this and that you are able to keep some for your own use.
We really want to know if the soldiers are still there. Is everything quiet and peaceful between you and the
United States?
You probably want to know a bit about our situation just as we want to know about yours. I, your brother
Richard, generally enjoy good health and I send you and every one of the children my very best regards.
Your sister Jane is fairly well, but suffers badly from pain in her leg – it is not much better than when you last
saw her. At times, waves of cramp go through her whole body and these cause her great pain. But Jane
sends her best regards to her dearest sister, in true friendship, and also to the children one and all.
Morris Isaac is fit and well and sends his best regards to you and the children. Your Aunt Catherine gets up
every day but is bent over with pain, she too sends you her best regards. Edward Roberts and Ellen are both
well. Robert Roberts of Erw Fawr is also well as are his family.
Economically, things over here are generally quite good at the moment; animal prices are good, there is
plenty of work and food prices are low. A 240lb sack of seed varies between £1-14-0 and £1-3-0 (from best
to worst). Ordinary butter costs 1/6 and cheese, 4½ d. There is a plenitude of potatoes this year - to be
honest, we have more than enough. A sack of oats is £1-4-0.
With this I bring things to a close in the hope that you will do me the favour of sending me a reply.

Yours
R. Thomas and Jane Thomas
Post Script:
I, your brother Richard, have decided and made my mind up that I want to help you and the children
to return home – that is of course, if you are thinking about returning home and if you are willing to
accept my help.
I want you to write to me, telling me exactly how I can send you something that will be of assistance.
What I mean is that you should make an audit of what money you have to set off on your journey,
and then I will send assistance to meet your needs.
But, perhaps you can make up a better plan. I await your reply.
Your brother
Richard Thomas

3461-3463
Creuau,
July 1st, 1859
My Dearest Sister,
I am delighted to send you acknowledgement of receiving your letter dated May 2 nd , 1859. It was a huge relief for
myself and your sister Jane (as much relief as one could get from reading lines in black and white), but despite that, we
remain very concerned about you and the children- over there, in a strange land, lest unpleasant things affect you with
us being so far away and unable to help. We try to calm ourselves by remembering that you say in your letter that
neither you nor the children have gone hungry since you arrived. Despite that, circumstances can change so quickly
between nations causing all sorts of bad things to happen in a short time.
In our old Welsh homeland there is almost no conflict or major change except that food prices go up and down – for
man and beast. Circumstances have been good here for a long time now. We get good money for our animals and our
food prices are low, despite there being some increases a short time ago – that coming about as a result of war
between, Austria, France and Sardinia.
As regards ourselves and this community, things are as follows: I and your brother (R. Thomas) are fairly well, despite
being rather ill in the spring with some sort of pox affecting my skin, but I have got over it quite well by now. I cannot
say the same about your sister Jane though, the wound on her leg remains sore and painful and some muscle swelling
also gives her a lot of pain. Your Aunt Catherine is also fairly well but is her life is coming to a close {put poetically in
Welsh "bending like a sickle towards the grave"}. Morris Isaac is also fairly well. Edward and Ellin Roberts (Gelli) and
family are well. Robert Roberts (Erw) and family are well but Rees is now a widower some months since. Peter is alive
and sometimes comes to visit us at Creuau. The girls are fine. Not much has changed for our neighbours. John Lloyd
and Catherine (Garth Llwynog) are well and receive the occasional letter from Gwen.
It was a very wet winter but recently it is has been dry and a drought is causing a problem with a lack of water for the
animals, but we still have healthy crops of wheat, barley and oats, but the potatoes are not looking too good. There is
not much grass for the animals to graze.
The news that most people are talking about these days is the war between France and Austria.
By now, I think that I have given you all the information that you asked for - if you want to know about anything else,
ask in your next letter. I am replying quickly in order to give you time to reply. We hope that you will give us a more
detailed letter the next time. We are pleased that you have two cows – but do you have rent and taxes to pay for your
home and land and also expenses towards feeding yourselves and your cattle? I hope that Robert's new adventure
works out and that he will have good health so that he can return with his ox and wagon.
I am including all of those friends whom you mentioned together with myself, your sister, Morris Isaac and your Aunt
Catherine as I pass on our best wishes and deepest love towards you and the children. We wish you the season's
blessings and also spiritual blessings. I hope that this letter you will make you think of the Old Country and that those
memories will cause you to start a new adventure that will see you set off on a path that will bring you back, so that
we can see one another's faces once more, before we all go the way of all worldly beings. These are your brother and
sister's the true wishes. Amen.
You said in your last letter that you could not give a definite answer to my question about how I could help you and
the children to return home. We expect that in your next letter you will be able to give us a definite answer. I remain
committed to wanting to be of assistance.
Your dearest brother
Richard Thomas
