Name Address County Going to
Hugh Davies Eglwysbach Denbigh The Valley
Grace Jones Bryndedwydd nr. Conwy The Valley
**Anne C Roberts Mochdre Denbigh The Valley
Thomas Stevens Merthyr Glamorgan Not known
Israel Evans + Benjamin Ashby The Valley
There were a few others going from Wales but I did not know them.
** This Anne Roberts was baptised in Liverpool a day or two before leaving. She is a niece of the above Grace Jones
and she (Grace Jones) has a daughter living in Wilson Creek, Weber County. If at all possible, can you inform her
daughter that her mother, niece and brother-in-law, are on their way. (The address is: Mr William Davies Mason,
Willow Creek, Weber County). I am sure that she will be very appreciative. These Saints were very kind to me so I
would be very glad if you could do this favour for them.
It was not possible for anybody to be more faithful than these Saints were. All the Saints from the North promised to
keep the Word of Truth onboard the ship. They had been re-baptised a few days before leaving and had committed to
the Tithe and to keeping the Word of Truth (but they all did Tithe even before this).
There has not been a lot of baptising in Wales recently but there has been quite a lot in various parts of England.
About 200 were baptised in Scandinavia in about four months. It is quite likely that the sound of scythes will be heard
drowning all other sounds in Wales and England for quite some time, because undoubtedly, many are keener to feed
their greed rather than to leave their wordly pleasures behind - despite knowing that they will be thrown out of God's
Kingdom.
It is quite a difficult time at the present; it is more difficult to stand up for the Church than it has ever been because of
the slippery pavement of the Word of Truth and the Tithe. We have to have members who are flexible - but many
have been busy anointing their joints so that they can run on our behalf, and they thank God that they have such
embrocation to help them so that they do not have to walk the same path as other people - and in consequence, end
up in the same mire as the others. "All strength to the Mormons!"
Despite having to cut out perhaps half of the Church members in Wales, that will clear the way for good men to come
in – ones that will help a hand to push the wheel forward rather than to be, as many are, putting in every effort to stop
the wheel going forward.
A series of Essays has been written recently by Apostle Orson Pratt and four of these have been published in Welsh,
having been translated by Dewi Elfed. Four more are soon to follow – making a total of eight. Every one costs two
pence and there are covers to fit over them – similar to the covers for "Old New Religion". On the back covers, there is
a list of all places that Saints worship and times of worship. The essays are:
1. True Faith
2. True Repentance
3. Baptism by Water
4. The Holy Spirit
5. Spiritual Talents
6. The need for miracles
7. General recantation in the 17th century
8. The kingdom of the Latter Days
There is no need for me to say that these are good essays - you know the author.
Currently peace reigns between the countries of Europe and the war between Persia and England has come to an end.
But there persists some quarrel between Britain and China. This is what "Herald Gymraeg" says about these
"Here is a letter from Hong Kong, 15th February.

Ten thousand homes have been destroyed in Canton. The British persisted firing on the city and 1,000 Chinese junks
attacked the British. The Chinese were overcome."

and another chosen to replace him. The American government has had to send a regiment of soldiers to the place in
order to preserve life and property."
Isn't it amazing how easily the Devil can persuade his friends to believe his lies?
There will be a General Election in this country shortly.
We had a very wet winter here this year – much more so than any that we have had in years. There was not much
frost, but today, it is Easter Sunday and all the ground is covered with snow.
Well, it is time to bid you farewell.
Remember me kindly to John your brother, and to Mary and the children and to Margaret Jones. All her family are well
and John, her brother, is working with Jason. I send my best regards to Parry (Newmarket), William Lewis (Anglesey)
Susannah Roberts (Dinas) and of course, to you and Sister Roberts and to Robert, Thomas, Daniel, Anne, Elizabeth and
Jane especially.
Remember to send letters as often as you can because I can assure you that they are welcomed with shouts of joy by
all the Saints back here. Br. Thomas sends you all his fond regards and Sister Thomas and Br. Treharne.
Hurry up to send a reply and address it thus: William Ajax, c/o Mr Edward Parry, Tanygraig, Llandudno.
Your humble
Friend in Truth
William Ajax

Gelli, Llanfrothen
February 21st,1860
To Mrs. Catherine Roberts Salt Lake
My Dearest Sister
After quite a wait, I am finally writing to confirm that I received your letter dated November 17th, 1859
on (or close to) the 25th of January – so it must have taken close to ten weeks to complete its
journey.
We were overjoyed to hear that you are all well and comfortable and that the children have been
able to settle into good worldly employment.
In my opinion, you made a gamble in your big adventure considering that you had made quite a
good home and had ownership of the property. But, of course, you know best what to do.
I was very pleased to hear that Robert had returned successfully from his adventures. I hope that he
will again be successful in his second adventure to your new settlement.
I gather from your behaviour that you don't really want to return to the Old Country.
I will now go on to say something about ourselves - Ellen and myself. We are quite well and we live
in the same place, in Gelli. What concerns us, and everyone that keeps animals, especially in these
winter months, is the shortage of hay. It's almost impossible to buy any. They say that it is about 8/-
a hundredweight.
We would have written to you earlier but Jason had promised to come down from Ffestiniog with
some news about your old friends in Ffestiniog but he never turned up.
One or two interesting things have happened to people whom you used to know. Pierce Owen (Tyn-
y-Cefn) was killed in the mine, after being hit in the eye. Tom Evans (Ceunant) died in Rhosydd
barracks after being unable to get home. I don't know much about anything of note that has
happened in Ffestiniog recently.
Now on to news about our neighbours here and in this neighbourhood; again, there is not much to
note (Peter Roberts is still living) and nobody that you would know has got married, apart from
Margaret from the Smithy who has married her cousin Robert Griffith. The family at Erw Fawr are all
well, without much change to their family.
John Lloyd (Garth Llwynog) is grateful for the tit-bit of information about his daughter,
Gwen, which he gathered from your letter and he is really hoping that he gets a letter from her. He
asks you let Gwen know that he and her mother are fairly well and in a better place materially. As
regards her sister Mary, please pass on our regards to her and her husband and children. Her
mother, Mary Owen, is pretty poorly suffering from breast cancer.
As you did not say anything about spiritual matters in your letter, I wonder if your religious fervour
has cooled? That certainly is not how things are over here - all the denominations are experiencing
Religious Revivals. In Llanfrothen these days there are only about a couple of dozen people that are
not regular churchgoers.
So as I come to an end, I hope that these few words actually reach your hand, over there in the new
land. We dearly wish to hear from you again in your new place. We wish you every success this
season.
I gather that the death of my brother, David, has affected you greatly just as it has affected us.

Be Great
Edward Roberts
About the people at Creuau, your sister, Jane Thomas, is quite poorly these last few weeks.
Something like palsy has affected her. In Creuau, they are awaiting a letter from ……
….. fairly fit but Jane is lonely and send you best regards, in the expectation of hearing word back
from you.
E.R.

2481-2483
Gelli, Llanfrothen
May 28, 1861
My Dear Nephew
I have your letter here in my hand and I was very pleased to receive it - although there was nothing special in it, but it
at least gave me the assurance that you were, at that time at least, alive and well - however you may be by now.
I understand that the farm did not produce much for you last year. You were under quite a disadvantage, having only
recently arrived there, it was difficult to improve the land - hopefully, you will be able to do better this year, now that
things have settled.
I am sure that you are feeling a great loss after the death of your father - but there is nothing that can be done except
try to make the best of your situation, and you, as children, should look after one another, and especially look after
your mother.
It is quite difficult for me to know what to say as regards your well-being. Over here, businesses are flourishing with a
shortage of workers so that wages are high. Nobody in Ffestiniog recalls having to advertise in the newspaper for
workers before. Unless something major happens, many new workers will need to be found to satisfy industry’s needs.
Now is the time for you to weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of the two countries and make up your own
mind as to where it would be best for you to make your living.
We have plenty of food here and it is not too expensive – a sack of 240 or 280lb of seed is about £2-7-0 to £2-15-0,
butter was quite stable in price this last winter and costs about 1/4 a pound, but it has recently started to fall in price.
A sack of Tremadog oats costs £1-12-0 to £1-14-0. As regards cheese and various meats they are as follows - a live pig
makes about 4d a pound or, having been killed, from 5½d to 8 ½d a pound and all other meats are similar in price.
Potatoes are scarce as many crops failed this last season. I have talked here about prices that the farmer receives, but
shop prices are also quite stable. If you were in Ffestiniog, you could easily make £1-0-0 to £1-10-0 a week. This should
give you enough to make up your mind as to where is the best place for you to live - Ffestiniog or Salt Lake.
As regards religion, I can tell you that for certain, since God is omni-present, there is no place better than any other in
which to worship Him. The only difference is that in some countries, the government oppresses people’s freedom to
worship as they please. But you know about England’s religious freedom.
I will now go on to address other matters, your family and relatives. Your Uncle Robert and his family are fairly well, I
will only say one thing about Rees as I understand that he is writing to you himself, he has stopped keeping house.
Your cousin Mary, who used to live at Tŷ Newydd Cae Glas is now a widow with three children as her husband died
suddenly at Rhosydd quarry and was unable to get home alive. I haven’t got much to say about your Ffestiniog cousins.
I and your Aunt Ellin enjoy quite good health. We would dearly love to see any of you again if you decided to come
over to the Old Country to visit.
You ask about finding somewhere for Robert Evans to preach, well, there is nowhere convenient, but we would be
pleased to welcome him and be of assistance.
Please accept our dearest regards.
In the hope of hearing from you or better still, seeing you…
I remain your dear uncle
Edward E Roberts

Dolgarregddu, Blaenau Ffestiniog
August 16th, 1862
Dear Friend
A long time has passed since I last wrote to you or heard from you. Good Friend, perhaps you think that we have
forgotten all about you on this side of the world. Be that as it may, but it is certainly not the case. I have been thinking
about writing to you for many months but something has always come in the way, anyway, now I am fulfilling my
promise. I hope that you and the rest of the family are in good health.
Many things have happened since you left Ffestiniog – far too much to list but here are a few.
Margaret Roberts, wife of John Roberts (Y Mynydd – Dolgarregddu) along with William their son. Robert, son of John
Jones (carpenter – Llwyn-y-Gell), Ricahrd Morris (Jr.) of Tŷ Crwn, Lewis Thomas (Maenofferen shop) along with many
others. But I should also mention Thomas, son of Elen Thomas (Uncorn) who was killed in Rhiw Quarry.
Ffestiniog is growing yearly with huge growth in population. There are a lot more strangers here now than 'original'
Ffestiniog people. Also, there are dozens if not hundreds of new houses that have been built in the last few years. I
don't think that it is possible for you to imagine all the changes that have taken place here since you left. Many new
quarries have been opened, with dozens of people working at Maenofferen (near the old Lord Quarry) and other new
quarries here and there. Ffestiniog is more prosperous than ever.
I would be very pleased to hear that you are planning to visit the old hills of Ffestiniog so that you can chat with your
old friends. I do hope that you can spend some time here in the future.,
I saw Robert your cousin last night (Friday August 13th) and he told me that, last Thursday, he'd received the letter
that you sent him when he {???should that be from ???} was in America. From this, I learnt a lot about what has
happened to you recently. I am glad that you are flourishing there and I hope that you are happy there as well - I am
glad to hear that gold has been discovered there recently. More than anything, I hope that you will prosper there.
I understand that you have become a Real Saint - that came as quite a surprise to me! My belief though is that being a
Methodist or a Church-goer or anything else will result in your being Saved – nor will moving to a new country bring
you happiness/blessedness. Oh no! Being in Christ Jesus is the only to be Saved - whatever country you are in,
whatever denomination you profess. I hope that you have reached the said Salvation by being a good Christian.

Dated: c.1862
Perhaps what you would like to hear next is some local news, although it is difficult to report all of the changes that
have taken place here recently.
Regarding the quarries, nobody can recall it being as good as it is here at the moment. They cannot get anything like
the amount of slate that there is a call for, despite working all sorts of rock; some rock being far too poor for anybody
to even consider working a few years ago.
There is a lot of work going on in the old Lord Quarry and it looks better than ever. They discovered a new vein of slate
which is 60 yards thick. There are dozens of men working there now. They built a huge new mill to saw and dress the
slates. It has never been as busy there. They are moving all the old Diffwys tips and tipping them over the rock outcrop
that was below, and burying the houses at Tan-y-Graig and Tan-Pistyll.
Diffwys now looks as flourishing as ever. They have built a very large mill above all the working and it is visible from
everywhere - bigger than any in Ffestiniog. The quarries have never been as busy as they are these days.
There appears to be the making of a big new quarry at the Maen-y-Fferam ffridd. There are dozens of men working
ther – from almost all nationalities!
They have driven a rail track from the town to Rhiw Bach. It starts at Dolgarregddu, with an incline up to the Lord
quarry and then another one up to the level of Llyn Bowydd. It passes the lake on the Graig Ddu side and carries on
until it ends above Rhiw Bach. From there, there is an incline down to the quarry (but this is unfinished at the
moment).
{This rail track was begun in 1861 and they started using it in 1862 and it was finished in 1863, so that dates this letter
to 1862}
That is quite a lot for you about your old working haunts. This side of town too is full of life.
Llechwedd is much the same as it was.
In Rhiw, they have dug a round shaft near Llyn Iwerddon. It is ten yards square and goes down to the lowest level in
the quarry. They intend to have a water ballast there to lift slate and rubble up to the mill. They intend to remove all
the rock below the old water ballast. This will be a 'job for life' for somebody!
There is talk about building another large mill at Gloddfa Ganol, in the boggy land behind the Bôn and then work that
through into the other part of the quarry. You see that there is no shortage of work here!
You will have heard a lot of talk about Twm Evan James's quarry above Craig Glan-y-Pwll. Speculators have invested
£30,000 towards developing this quarry, and they are now working hard – but it is more of a 'rubble sink' than
anything else I would say! Be that as it may, what is needed here is employment.
They have started building a flagstone saw mill near the "Mathew" houses. They have also started building an incline
up the mountain, but I understand that this must be done in two parts. They are blasting these old rocks until the
whole place is shaking!
Cwmorthin is a hive of activity and is looking good. They built a lot of houses there but despite that, they cannot
attract enough workers.
They are digging into the Moelwyn in all directions near Drws Ellan – it is like a rabbit warren there.
There are also hopes for a good a quarry in Croesor. There are between 120 and 140 working there. They are talking
about building a rail track from Porthmadog, through Llanfrothen, to Croesor. This will pass by Erw Fawr and across
the Morfa, according to the plans that I have seen. It looks as if Llanfrothen is going to be an important place quite
soon. Many who used to live there are planning to move back with the prospects of good employment there.
In this district there are now hundreds of strangers – only about one-in-three is an original inhabitant; the district has
changed dramatically. There is a huge boom in building in such a remote place. Dozens of new houses have been built
near Congl-y-Wal, Penygroes and Fodlas – and especially around here. There are also many new houses stretching
down from Rhiw to Tanygrisiau and a new road has been built down there.

Glan-y-Pwll, Blaenau Ffestiniog
July 9th, 1862
Mr Robert D. Roberts along with my dearest relatives living in the Salt Lake Valley,
Here I am, trying to compose a few lines from my dear mother's home once more. Fortunately, I am enjoying the
benefits of good health - as other members of the family (but these are no longer as numerous as they once were).
I wish to inform you that I received your kind and sincere letter although it had taken a few months to reach me, but it
eventually did, perhaps more successfully than other letters. It came via Vermont, where some of my kind friends
forwarded it to me. I can assure you that reading that you had arrived safe and well was one of the best things that I
have ever read in a letter! I cannot tell you how much I have waited to hear from you. I had sent two letters and
another two after going to America, and indeed I was by now not expecting to hear from you ever again as so much
time had passed.
I will start with a bit about me; I was very self-confident and enough of a 'lad' (as you know) that I decided to leave my
mother's home and head for America. With this youthful determination and commitment, I crossed the wild Atlantic in

a month back. But it is likely that your old friend David Roberts will have told you about some of these already, so I
won't tire you by listing more of those that have left this Worldly Realm.
Such a long time has passed without my hearing from you that I find it difficult to know what to write about. I ask your
forgiveness but I have written to you four times (at least) and I have only received this letter from you. Believe me that
I have been longing to hear if you were still alive.
I understand that you are now a farmer – but, no doubt you would be happier working slates if this was an option foer
you. One day, I dreamt that I could see Thomas carrying a load of mortar up to the top of the Temple for the stone
masons. I laughed out loud. Oh! That I could see you in the Salt Lake Valley!
I often think about Aunt Mary and her dear young children and I wish from the bottom of my heart that they do well
there, and also, Uncle Daniel's family. I heard that Catherine had recently married – I am surprised, as she is so young.
Send them, one and all, my best wishes. A word from one of Uncle Daniel's or Uncle Sion's {John's} children would be
very welcome.
I have to remind Thomas that he promised to write to me from wherever he ended up and promises must be fulfilled. I
hope that he writes very regularly from now on.
I hear a lot about the booming gold mines of British Columbia and Vancouver. It is not far from where you are - if you
know anything about this, please let me know as I have been thinking a lot about going there. Talking about gold
mining, there is quite a boom in the Merionethshire goldfield. They are mining in a place close to Dolgellau, called
Clogau. They extracted £10,000 worth of gold from there last year. Pretty good – eh?
Robin Owen (Bethesda) and William (Plas Isaf) have returned from Australia having made very good money there.
John (Fourcrosses) and Owen Price (Ty'n y Cefn) have gone to New Zealand to prospect for gold. You see that
Ffestiniog boys have gone all over the world seeking their Fortune.
Boys, before I go on to ask you a few questions, take care not to get married whilst you are over there. I do not think
that I will be changing my situation in life for quite some time.
First Question: Are you free to leave the Salt Lake as you see fit or are you bound to stay there for life?
Question 2: Do you tolerate other denominations/religions in your midst or others whose beliefs are different from
yours, but do not make a point of displaying that to the Mormon World?
Q3: Do you have to be a Saint before you can live there?
Q4: Who is Brigham Young – your governor or your prophet?
Q5: Do you prefer to live in the Land of the Mormons or in Britain?
Q6: How do you live in a Territory before it becomes a State? Do you have laws or is it every man for himself?
I await and expect your full answers to the above questions in your next letter.
I impeach your forgiveness for my untidiness and for going on at such lengths. As I draw to a close, I send you all my
warmest regards and also those of my mother, Eliza and Evan.
Your faithful cousin
Robert W. Roberts, Glan-y-Pwll, Blaenau Ffestiniog

Creuau, Llanfrothen
August 17th, 1865
My Dear Sister
There is something warm and familiar about that word 'sister'. Despite Devine Providence having thrown us far apart,
separated by deep oceans, high mountains and vast plains, we are still able to communicate by means of letters such
as this, even if we are prevented from meeting face to face. Nor can we be prevented from flying on the wings of
imagination, to distant America, crossing lands and seas and not resting until we arrive in Logan City where we can
chat to our hearts content about our relatives.
I understand that you had plentiful crops this year and that you get good prices for all types of agricultural produce in
your province, and so I gather that you are comfortable. My solemn prayer now is that you get the health and long life
to make the most of your blessings and that, at the end of your worldly life, you will be welcomed with open arms by
your Good Lord to life everlasting.
There is an unusual vibrancy in this country these days, there is a high demand for slates and consequently, thousands
are employed in the slate mines and they are well-paid for their labour.
Railways are being extended in all directions. The railway is being built to connect Aberystwyth with Porthmadog and
then on to Porthdinllaen. Another branch goes through Llanllyfni to Caernarfon, and another branch is being
constructed from Porthmadog to Beddgelert. These employ lots of men and they pay good wages, consequently, we
now find it difficult to find farm workers to help with the hay, despite paying 15 shillings a week and free food.
Our animals are selling well – sheep make good money and cattle as well. These days, you need to pay about £10 to
£15 for a cow in calf. Prices of meat and butter are quite high - you cannot buy a pound of fresh butter below 15d or
1/6 a pound. Flour costs are as follows – a sack of best seed £2 to 2 guineas for 280lbs. Wheat 13/- to 14/- a hob. Oat
flour £1-8-0 to £1-10-0 a sack (220lb).
From this you can see that it is quite a good life for workers in Wales these days - yes, much easier than it is in England
for our English brothers.
I understand that you know that my circumstances have changed. My wife's name is Margaret, she is the daughter of
Evan Owen (Glanyrafon, Beddgelert). I can honestly say that I am feeling very happy with married life. It is much better
than just living with preachers, like a sparrow sitting on a rooftop with nobody to hear my confessions. {??? that is
definitely what he wrote }. When our baby was born at the end of last year, my wife was very ill. Indeed, she was so ill
that I feared that she was not going to pull through, but the Almighty saw well to save her life, as only He could. The
baby however was lost.
Morris Isaac and his wife have two children.
I finish by sending you my best regards to you and all the children. I hope that these few words reach you well and
comfortable just as I and all the family are as I write this letter.
I am your dear brother
Richard Thomas

Gelli, Llanfrothen
August 28th, 1865
My Dear Nephew
I have hesitated longer than I should have before acknowledging the receipt of your letter dated June 11th 1865. In
your letter, you mentioned that you had sent me numerous letters, but had not received a reply. I can assure you that
I have not received any letter which went un-answered - I cannot however vouch for the way others to whom you may
have written may have responded. I have long awaited a letter from you and I am very grateful for the gift of this letter
and so I wish to return your kindness with a courteous reply.
I was very pleased with the contents of your letter as I learnt that you are alive and well and in quite comfortable
circumstances as regards making a living in this life. I would like to go on to summarise my own circumstances.
I am enjoying good health and therefore can carry on with my usual employment. I assume that you know that my
wife Ellin died almost 21 months ago, consequently, I only have a maid to supervise my material well-being. As you can
imagine, however honest and caring a maid is, I am not as comfortable as I was when Ellin and I lived together and saw
eye-to-eye on everything. But, however things are, there is nothing to do but to bend to Providence and try one's best
to be satisfied with the situation. Providence has been so generous towards me in my present circumstances - I get
enough to satisfy my needs - in this world and in the next.
I will now go on to tell you something about your Uncle Robert and his family. He is rapidly deteriorating physically and
has almost given up his job in the slate mine. Rhys remains unmarried thus far; he is some sort of supervisor in Mr
Holland's quarry {in Blaenau Ffestiniog} and the young son is at Erw with his grandparents. Your cousin Mary lives in
Tŷ Newydd Cae Glas with her second husband. Eliza lives in Glan-y-Wern. Meurig remains single. He spent some time
in Dublin whilst at school.
As regards your cousin R.W.R, I have just received a letter from him asking me to send you his best regards. I
understand that your Uncle Richard Thomas has written to you himself, so I cannot add anything about him. Perhaps
he did not say anything about Morris Isaac though - he is living at Carreg Alldrem with his second wife (the daughter of
W. Hughes, Bryn Celynen) and they have two children.
I think that I have now given you enough detail about your family and what has been going on locally.
But let me finally take you to Ffestiniog. If your mother, or someone who used to be familiar with Ffestiniog, was to
return on a visit, they would be very surprised seeing all the new houses that have recently been built there. From
Congl-y-Wal to Rhiwbryfdir there are terraces of houses, all facing the main street. They have opened many new slate
mines in the area.
There is another major development; you will recall the railway that was built from Ffestiniog down to Porthmadog - it
used to be serviced by horses pulling the wagons – but now they have 'iron horses'. They wind their way, steaming
through Tanygrisiau down to Porthmadog.
Let us look at Llanfrothen- from the top of the valley (Bwlch Cwmorthin) down to the sea at Porthmadog. A new
railway carries the slates down from Rhosydd and Croesor quarries down to Porthmadog. The Croesor valley is dotted
with new houses and there is also a brand new chapel there.
We go down a bit now to the shoreline at Traeth Bach and Traeth Mawr, and here we see dozens of men constructing
a new railroad to connect Caernarfon with Aberystwyth and necessitating the building of two major new bridges.
The market: a 280lb bag of seed is normally £2-2-0 to £2-5-0 but poorer quality ones may be had for £1-16-0. Oat flour
is £1-10-0. Meat of all legally edible animals is between 6d and 9d a pound and butter 1/3 to 1/5 a pound. Animals of
all sorts are making good prices.
I have now more or less summarised how things are over here. Religious-wise, things have cooled down quite a bit and
things are pretty stagnant these days.
I can now only draw this letter to a close. If it reaches you, then I really hope that you will remember me fondly and

families that left Llanfrothen along with you – Wm. Owen's family, Nathan, Ioan Owen (their children), Uncle Daniel's
family (that is, his children).
Thus, I close my letter by sending my fondest regards to your mother and all the children. Before I finish and put away
my pen, I would like to ask you one final question – does any one of you have even the slightest wish to return to the
Old Country – either for a visit or to come back to end your days here?
I am your Uncle
Edward Roberts
A word from the writer to your mother.
It is strange how time slips by and friendships cool with absence. There was great friendship between myself and D.
Roberts but to this day, it pains me to think how such a good and sensible man came to be possessed with a fanatical
spirit as to lead you as a family to a distant nation rather than stay in your own land, amongst your own people.
I cannot understand that there is any advantage whatsoever to you in this. If you thought that it was a better place to
practise your religion, then, as I have heard from one source, you may have been deeply disappointed; surely
corruption of the flesh does not glorify religion? A better place to live? It must indeed be a very good place if it better
than over here. I am sure that you will have seen the error of your ways.
I have had the opportunity to talk to someone whom I once knew very well, and who has been over there for some
time. He gave me a good picture of what goes on with religion – almost too repulsive for me to waste my ink and
paper to repeat.
If I am mistaken in what I have said, I ask your forgiveness.
It is likely that there is not one of the saints that can rest comfortably unless they gain forgiveness in this life.
So rests your old friend
No matter who
P.S.
I forgot to say that W. Davies, your Aunt Margaret's husband - that is the wife of your Uncle William has died as a
result of an injury in the slate mine. {make of this what you can – that's what it says!}
E.R.

Glan-y-Pwll, Rhiwbryfdir, Blaenau Ffestiniog
June 20th 1865(?)
Next time I am going to send you my Carte de visite.
First of all, I have to tell you that I recently saw Abel Evans {Mormon missionary} and another, quite short man who
visited this area. I chatted with them and I heard a little about you – mostly good news from when they had last seen
you, namely leaving Logan City in a wagon.
Secondly, I have also seen your photographs. You've changed more than I have! But my heart was warmed to see you
looking so good and I hope that you remain in good health.
Thirdly, my sister buried her husband, a fortnight before Whitsun. She is now staying here once again and is not as well
as she usually is.
We are hoping to send you photographs of ourselves with our next letter- after we hear from you.
I was down in Llanfrothen last week placing a memorial stone on my father's grave. There had been nothing there to
mark his burial place, and by now, some twenty years have passed. The Llanfrothen family are all well - in Gelli, Creuau
and Erw. I recently received a letter from America from John (?surname?). He is now married and has a son by the
name of Daniel Abiah Humphrey (what a mouthful of a name – enough to put your mouth out of place trying to get it
all out!).
My dear cousin, I feel really bad that I have been so remiss and unmindful not to have written sooner. If you wish to
know anything in particular, just ask and I will try to find answers. So many of your old friends have passed away that I
could not name them all even if I was able to chat to you for a whole week. The same is true of those who have got
married. I am coming to the end of my bachelor days but I would be pleased to hear that you are sticking to your state
of bachelorhood rather than getting betrothed to someone from a foreign land.
I must finish by hoping that I receive a letter with lots and lots of your news. I just want to tell you that all of us as a
family send you our kindest regards – to you all, from your mother down to Jane and that also extends to the other
two families of course, they are too numerous to name individually.
Your friend and fellow traveller/associate D. Roberts sends you his best wishes and promises to write. Many others
have said the same but my pen and paper won't allow me to list them all. In the next fortnight, I will write to you
again.
I remain your faithful cousin
Robert W Roberts
{New sheet}
Six sheets of paper would not be enough to list everything that has gone on in this area in the last two years, so I will
excuse myself and just list those things that I think will be of greatest interest. Trying to describe the recent
developments in Ffestiniog would be nigh impossible, but in case any of you ever decides to make it over for an
unplanned visit anytime I will list a few changes.
A new chapel has been built in Bethania almost adjoining the other one. A large new road has been built from Dafydd
Rowlands' smithy way up towards Maenofferen fields and another from Fourcrosses up towards the Uncorn bridge.
The fields near Tyddyn Gwyn are dotted with new houses and David (Bron Manod) has built a new inn at the junction
with the new road.
You would be amazed at the changes that have taken place.
The Wesleyans have built a new chapel opposite the old Maenofferen store and a Baptist chapel has been built on
Uncorn Street and a Methodist chapel in the field below Fuches Wen – the largest and finest chapel in the county and
quite an embellishment for the town. It will seat about 800 comfortably.

2332-2333
Erw Fawr
Llanfrothen
There have been many changes since you set off; there have been many accidents making things quite uncomfortable,
especially in the Middle Mill. I will name a few of your acquaintances who were killed and call them by the name that
you would recognise. Richard William (Pen-yr-Orsedd) was hit in head by crane handle, David Jones fawr (Tanygrisiau)
had a hole blast back on him and Jack (the servant) had a large slate slab slide onto him, hurting him badly. Many
whom you would not know have also been killed or badly hurt.
Many have emigrated from here this last summer- young men going to Australia and old Edward Jones (Penrhos)
followed them there.
Employment in the quarries was slack this last winter and wages were poor. It was not easy to find work at that time
but it has improved lately. There is a good demand for slates - selling better than ever. Despite this, the drop in salaries
that happened last winter was not restored and it is unlikely that it will happen at least until the end of the year.
It has been an excellent summer for us thus far. The grass and wheats have been harvested neatly everywhere and
there has been an excellent yield. But we have never seen potatoes as bad as this year. Everywhere, throughout the
country, they began to show well and flowers appeared, but then a plague hit them.
The prices of everything remain high. All grain and animal flour is about 52 shillings for 280lb, oat flour in a Tremadog
sack is 30 shillings. Animal prices, especially horses and cattle, are good.
I sent my cousin's regards on to William Williams the poet and to Ellis Roberts. They asked me not to write back to you
without letting them know - but I have waited a long time already but I fear that the Muse must have left them or they
would have composed a pile of bungling words by the thousand by now. I hope that they will be ready by next Monday
or else I will send my poor letter to swim the sea without them.
I think that you will have heard about recent troubles and disasters. If I knew that you were not seeing the newspapers
then I would send a few on to you. We hope that the insurrection will soon be over as many British soldiers have gone
over to settle things.
I hope my dear cousin that you will write as soon as you can and that your letter will be full of news.
My dear uncle, how are you there by now? I often imagine seeing you and I would love to have the opportunity to sit
and talk to you - but as that is impossible, we will have to do that using paper and ink. We can use this as a means to
communicate despite the thousands of miles that separate us. Let us make a habit of this.
I finish by wishing you all, as families, the very best - one and all.
I am yours in the most sincere way
Rees Roberts

2391-2393
Creuau
July 27, 1866
My Dearest Sister,
Your letter dated March 26th arrived safely. It feels very special, here in my hands, as I look at it and read its contents.
You have expressed your emotions and feelings of longing for the Old Country and those times that we played
together as children, with bat and ball. Such thoughts and memories go around and around in my head as well. The
warmth of the love that I feel means that I can my almost see you there, in person, in front of me. We will have to
share such feelings of emotion until we can fall into one another's arms once again - despite all the vast lands and seas
that today separate us. Perhaps there will come a day when we can again shake one another's hands and chat face-to-
face about everything and 'put the world to rights'.
You mentioned old friends and who have passed away. I am afraid that I have to tell you that more have left this
Worldly Realm since I last wrote. Namely, Evan Jones (Garthfoel) and his oldest son John Samuel (Cefn Cyffin) and
Henry Jones (Tyddyn Gwyn). There are no major outbreaks of disease here apart from the measles and scarlet fever.
This has struck several children in the Beddgelert and Porthmadog areas but we have been quite fortunate around
here.
You were very keen to hear about Thomas Jones and Robert Jones. Thomas moved away some four or five years ago.
Bachelorhood had such a hold on his constitution that he was not able to get on with the maids {young girls?} in
Hendre Sela. He has taken up home with his sister and is now working somewhere. As for Robert, he has gone to work
in the working horses' stable. He has a wife and one child and they live in a small cottage; he works hard. You would be
surprised to see how old they both look. Robert lives close to Garn Dolbenmaen.
I heard suggestions from someone that your daughter Anne had married, but I cannot figure out from your letter
whom she might have married. I would very much like you to tell me in your next letter – is this is true or not?
I sort of gathered from your letter that you would like to return to the Old Country. If you were to do so, I would be
happy to give you every assistance that I {emphasised} could possibly offer and there would be a warm welcome
awaiting you when you got back. People make a good living here, there is plenty of work and a good wage. The old
Gerrynt slate quarry is again working and there is further construction work going on there. They are planning to build
a railroad down through Cae Dafydd, Hafod Garregog, Creuau, Carreg Alldrem and Erw Fawr where it would join the
line coming from Croesor and Rhosydd quarries, thereby allowing the slates to be transported to Porthmadog.
However, I personally doubt that this plan will ever be realised.
In your last letter, you sent me the costs of various things over there, but I don't see much purpose in doing the same,
as there has been little change from my last letter – apart from the cost of sheep. These are some five shillings a head
more valuable these days. There is a disease amongst cattle which has meant that thousands have had to be culled
since I last wrote. In this neck of the woods, we have been fortunate that the disease has not appeared – but we are
not allowed to move cattle from one county to another without a licence signed by a Justice of the Peace.
As you can see from the enclosed, we agree with you that it would be good to exchange photographs. I hope that you
can reciprocate with your next letter.
I now bring things to a close and there is no better way to do so than to send you our best regards and good wishes –
to both yourself and the children. My sincerest prayer is that these few lines find you all fit and well, just as we
ourselves are, and that, when we leave this Worldly Realm, we are deemed worthy of Everlasting Life. Amen.
The following people wish me to convey their best regards: Morris Isaac, Ellin Jones (Turnpike), Catherine Parry
(Hendre Sela) and also many more old friends.
Your most faithful brother
Richard Thomas
Mrs Catherine Roberts, Logan City

2651-2654
Logan City
May 20th, 1866
Dear Uncle Edward Roberts
Perhaps you feel disgruntled, waiting for a letter from me, but I will try to make good if I can. I was really grateful for
your kind letter giving a short, concise rundown of family matters and what's being going on locally, where we were all
born and raised, where we spoke our first words and took our first steps, where our relatives and old friends – whom
we used to love, and to be happy with, but whose company we no longer have after we moved to a distant land. The
reason for this separation we will get to later in this letter.
Now we come to your letter. Firstly, I was sorry to understand that Aunt Ellen had died, but there is nothing that can
be done when the Call comes to leave loved ones. We are glad that God has blessed you with health and strength. If
you have found yourself a good maid then I will be glad to hear that you have made her your wife. If I come on a visit
to the Old Country, I will be pleased to meet with any new cousins through my Uncle Edward.
Secondly, I regret that my Uncle Robert is in failing health - this is the situation that my father could foresee happening
to himself - it was certain to come. "Whilst I am able to work", he used to say, "I will get a wage, but when I get old and
unable to work, I will be thrown aside as an old man, and I will only get whatever they see fit to give me. Something
which would not be half enough to keep me I'm sure. That will be my situation before long, so I think that I should get
a parcel of land for myself where I could build a cottage that I could call my own. I'd have no rent to pay and would not
be left with a month's notice to quit. I could build a palace if I wished and live there, plant fruit trees, work the land

landowners who just sit on their backsides, feasting and making a living on the backs of me and my sort. If I was half an
hour late, or if I left early, I would be fined sixpence or a shilling but if I was on my own land then I could work when I
wanted and rest when I wished. I would eat the fruits of my own labour, from land which I could call my own and
thereby prepare for my old age".

somebody by the name of Amos Wright, an American, and has three or four children, and lives in Bear Lake Valley, 40
miles to the north of here. Elizabeth has married somebody with the name Collap {?} Jones, a Welshman. Aunt Mary

somewhere near Council Bluff but I don't know much about him. David Peters is alive and well, unless something has

rain. The season is a month earlier than last year.

forty families living in the whole valley then. Now, there are twenty towns and villages. In Logan, there are some

Now, since the writer took the opportunity to address my mother in his letter, I take this opportunity to respond.
Firstly, she is amazed that a man of wholesome spirit such as my father, David Roberts, is said to have become
possessed and fanatical causing him to lead his children to a foreign land.
My uncle Richard Thomas, in a letter addressed to my mother, stated that it was Divine Providence that had separated
us and that is the truth; but what is the reason for this? I said at the start of my letter that I would try to explain this.
If you believe that we have been pure these past days, then I refer you to Daniel 244 and this verse will show you that
our Heavenly Father does not have a realm or kingdom on earth during these days – these Latter Days. If so, what
have you to say against Joseph Smith? He says that God appeared before him during these days and that he went on
to accept the holy priesthood, and God gave him the right to preach that everyone had the right to hear the gospel
and to become priests in order to realise God's Kingdom on earth during these Latter Days. He saw evidence himself of
the truth of the Gospel, that no individual should miss out on the evidence.
However, some who attended the church and saw the evidence that this was indeed God's Church but despite this,
turned their backs, saying that this was all a falsehood - but this does not prove that the Gospel and the principles
have changed. God remains the same, but man changes and forgets the evidence. This is natural for man – read about
the Children of Israel when Moses led them and you will see how they celebrated and praised God after crossing the
Red Sea, but soon afterwards, began to complain bitterly.

Gwyndy, Rhiwbryfdir, Blaenau Ffestiniog
{Letter mentions Gwen being about 14 years old.
She is recorded as being 18 on the 1871 Census,
hence this letter must be dated around 1867}
Dear Cousin and Family
Here I am after years of delay, sitting down to write a few lines to you. I hope that you are all experiencing good health
as we are (perhaps better than we deserve).
I have written you several letters, but I now know that you have not received a single one of them or you would have
mentioned it in …?...
I have seen several from you …?... and heard that some have reached …?... Robert … and Uncle Edward and R.W.
Roberts, our cousin.
I don't really know how to start, so I will just start as things come to mind.
We will start off in the slate quarries. From Talywaenydd right up almost to the top of Allt Fawr has now become what
a stranger would think of as one huge quarry because the three existing quarries have grown so much. It would be
difficult for a stranger to know which is which.
There have been many changes here as regards births, marriages and deaths but it would not be useful for me to
name more than a few whom I think that you would know.
Deaths: Owen Thomas (watchmaker), Owen Thomas and his wife (Bethesda), Price Jones (shop), Dr Vaughan Jones.
Smallpox affected the town two years ago and many died – far too many to name.
Marriages: A week ago R.W. Roberts (our cousin) was married to a daughter of Owen Jones (Llenyrch Moch). All that I
know is that she is a beautiful young woman. (Owen Jones is dead.)
Robert Owen (Bethania) with the daughter of William Jones (The Flour {merchant} – that’s how I knew him!).
Robert Thomas (Fuches Wen) with some woman from Capel Curig.
Robert Williams (Congl y Wal) but I don't know details.
And lastly, and most unexpectedly, Thomas (Creuau) has married some woman from Beddgelert!!!
And Morris Isaac has re-married – with some young girl, and he's had three children from her!
I too have got married as I told you that I intended to when you were setting off on your journey. But within three
years, I lost her – she went the way of all wordly beings, aged just 23 years. I have a son, who will be ten years old next
May 1st and I think the world of him. He lost his mother at a very young age but is a good lad and easy to care for and
has been thus these past eight years. I don't yet know if there is anybody else for me - up until now, none has
appeared.
Mr Holland's Quarry has grown more than any other around here and there is enough work for two stewards there -
and this is how I have been employed these past three years. I am the deputy or foreman to Robert Owen – Mr
Holland's Manager. It is quite difficult although …?... In such a big place, with close to 500 employed, I do a lot of the
accounts, although there is a clerk who works full-time in the office and two slate inspectors.
I am lodging close to Dinas in a new house between Dinas and Llwyn-y-Gell. I have two rooms and the family do my
chores. That is a bit of information for you about my situation in life.
My mother and father are making a very comfortable living as farmers and quite well although my father suffered
from Se?fs Fever a while back and was quite ill - we feared if he was going to make it. His health has not been good
ever since. They make a very comfortable living – better off than they have ever been. They have more than doubled
their land holding.
My sister married but become widowed as her husband died at Rhosydd Quarry. She remarried in two years with the
half-brother of her first husband. You see that she must have been attracted to the breed! They are now living
comfortably and between them they have five children.
Elin is married and lives in Wisconsin – that is all that I know.
Elizabeth has married a man from near Pwllheli and lives close to Garreg with three children. She has room for 3 or 4

Ellis is still farming at home and is as fat as ever!

Now a note about prices over here. Everything is quite expensive these days, but women still cost the same.
Wheat flour 55/- for 280lb Oat flour 35/- 240lb Beef meat 7d to 8d a pound, Mutton 10d, Hams 10-11d, Butter 1/5,

that is probably unlikely. I would however like to receive a letter from you, full of news about you all, as soon as you
possibly can get around to writing.

– especially my two aunts and their children.
I am including my Card in this letter. If convenient I would be glad to receive your card.
My kindest regards to you all – a thousand-fold. I finish by wishing you as a family every success.
Your faithful cousin
Rees Roberts

Glan-y-Pwll, Blaenau Ffestiniog
Thursday 2nd January, 1867(9)?)
Dear Cousin
I received your letter the day before yesterday (23rd January). My heart never felt as joyous as when I saw the
photographs that you sent and I was so glad to read that you are all well as a family, out there in the far West. I am
pleased to be able to say that we, as a family, are also as well as normal. I cannot put down in words or express how
pleased we all were to see your photographs. Previously, my mother and the others had very different ideas as to how
things might be over there. The photograph of my aunt kept us smiling for a whole month! She is there, just as natural
as if she was alive. "Oh, look! She's laughing" they said "I think that she has lost her teeth" said others. But the story
always ended with "If only we could see her…". The photograph of yourself reminded me of your dear father – I think
that you bear a great resemblance to him both in your gestures and around your mouth. It is much more of a likeness
than the other photograph that you sent. I will treasure them forever.
I think that if your Janie was here, she would get a husband in no time - she is such a pretty girl. Everybody that has
seen her picture says that there is something very likeable in her appearance. They are great photographs – very
natural and we are so grateful to have received them. When all hope of seeing you has been lost, I will still have these
images to hang on to. But where are the photographs of Thomas, Daniel, Anne and Elizabeth? Pardon me for being so
bold "This Welshman is always requesting…".
I include my own photograph for you with this letter and am determined to send photos of the rest of the family as
soon as we have them taken. But perhaps we will await hearing that you have received this one before we send more.
I must get this chapter finished and look for something to say.
Firstly, I would like to acknowledge receipt of three newspapers from you. I enjoyed looking through them although
my English is not great. I will try to send you some copies of 'Baner ac Amserau Cymru' {Welsh newspaper}
occasionally.
You had a lot of questions about the Reading Room {library in Blaenau}, asking for as many details as possible. The
main sponsors for the building were local nobility and quarry-owners. After this, a local committee of the Great and
the Good was elected to draw up rules and to select the newspapers that would be available. Nine different
newspapers are provided – in both English and Welsh, along with monthly periodicals published by all the religious
denominations. Books have not been yet been obtained but local quarrying companies intend to supply books of all
sorts.
By paying a penny, and giving one's address to the supervisor, it will be possible to borrow one of these books for a
week or longer. The usual cost for a worker to join this system is a shilling per quarter, or a penny each time that a
book is borrowed (note that payment is per quarter). For this we can call in any time from 10a.m. until 9p.m. I can
assure you that this has already been of immeasurable benefit to the town but much remains to be done.
In my clumsy way, that is about as much as I can say about the arrangements.
I must now change my tune and turn to the minor key to raise a complaint her about the severity of this winter. I
cannot remember seeing such a season – snow drifts, ice and bitter cold (at least in this area). The haggard, dark rocks
that surround the town were covered in white and looked pure and smooth. Only a few men have been able to work
this month and I am afraid that many have suffered as a result of a shortage of fuel at this, the coldest of times. It is
however good to report that the Giver of All Gifts has now seen fit to take away the snow, for a while at least, by
pouring rain like waterfalls from the skies. It rained as if it were never going to stop.
I think that I gave you a glimpse of the changes that there have been in the district in my last letter but as time and
years pass, generation follows generation and so I do not think that I can list all who died, got married and so on unless
I think that you would know them well.
Married:
Joseph Griffith (Dolgarregddu) with the daughter of Will Robert (shoemaker)
Lewis, son of Jack bach (formerly of Tanrallt) with some girl from Beddgelert

cannot remember seeing such a season – snow drifts, ice and bitter cold (at least in this area). the haggard, dark rocks
that surround the town were covered in white and looked pure and smooth. only a few men have been able to work
this month and i am afraid that many have suffered as a result of a shortage of fuel at this, the coldest of times. it is
however good to report that the giver of all gifts has now seen fit to take away the snow, for a while at least, by
pouring rain like waterfalls from the skies. it rained as if it were never going to stop.
i think that i gave you a glimpse of the changes that there have been in the district in my last letter but as time and
years pass, generation follows generation and so i do not think that i can list all who died, got married and so on unless
i think that you would know them well.
married:
joseph griffith (dolgarregddu) with the daughter of will robert (shoemaker)
lewis, son of jack bach (formerly of tanrallt) with some girl from beddgelert

From the Erw, my Uncle Eban (Glan-y-Pwll) and his cousin from Llanberis. I went to Liverpool at Christmas to tie
together these last two and I had a great time.
Dic Joseph (shoemaker) as well
Will Robin Sion with Lisa (Trefeini)
John Holland with the sister of Stuart Holland
Hugh Griffith (Penygroes) – since dead and buried
Hugh Pengwern and Will Hughes (Fourcrosses) and also his brother (also Ellen, daughter of Griffith Jones (R'uncorn))
with some boy from Llanllyfni.)
But I think that it will be better for me to bring this list to a close although there could me much more that I could add.
I am afraid that I cannot remember all the wives' names.
Before finishing, excuse me for saying so, but David Roberts is a 'proper fully-fledged bachelor'. He promises to write
to you soon. Don't be frightened if you hear that I have got married by the next letter! What about your branch of the
family? You are almost at the stage of life where you will enter the cold world of bachelorhood - take care that you
never fall into that category. But I must leave this, and tell you some more about our family.
My mother is fit and well and gets enough for her keep and honestly, I think that she is happier than she has ever
been. Betsan has been here with us since she buried her husband. She too is healthy and happy and sends you all her
best wishes. At home, there remains just one boy – David, the youngest of the lot, who is 13 years old and is working
with us in the quarry and earns from £3 to £4 per month. Despite everything that life throws at us we are living quite
well. Oh, yes, my cousin Meurig is now lodging with us here. He has just as large a beard as I have. You will notice from
my photograph that I am much hairier than you!
{An englyn – special form of poetry that he wrote. It is impossible to translate. It goes something like this}
Curly rings encircle my mouth
Smooth my chin with sharp implements
Shaving around the mouth never makes you look good
The employment situation around here is pretty much unchanged but things are quite bad in London, Liverpool,
Merthyr and many other places and there are fears that this will happen. We hear good news from America though -
on the same day that I got your letter, I also received another, saying that there was plenty work over there in the
slate quarries and that they were paying $2-75 this winter- it was $3½ in the summer. I sometimes have the yearning
to return to America but I probably will stay here a while longer.
'Well House bach' has recently come home to visit from over there. He is setting off back home in February. I heard
that my Aunt Ellen and family over there were fit and well.
Another thing – have you heard that Wales has been given Patagonia to make a homeland? A group of 150 settlers
went over eighteen months ago and they are beginning to make a success of it. Another group are setting off next
April. A plan is afoot in the land to raise £50,000 to facilitate commerce. Some of the major players in Wales are
working hard for the emigration movement and I am sure that it will succeed if the Welsh populous support it.
That is the end of my news, you will get a lot more the next time, but I have written quite a lot more than I normally
do since I had to answer your questions.
Now you remember to keep to your promise and reply as soon as possible! I cannot stress how glad I am to hear from
you.
I studied the photograph of Brigham - does he consider himself your regional governor as well as the spiritual leader
for you Mormons?
Is there any chance of our getting photographs of Uncle Daniels' wife and family?
Accept my kindest regards, from the bottom of my heart
Your dear cousin
Robert W. Roberts

Penbrynllwyd, Glan-y-Pwll, Blaenau Ffestiniog
21st September 1868
To. Mr Robert D Roberts, Logan City
Dear Friend
Week after week, and year after year, I have delayed writing to you despite having intended to do so. Now I have no
recourse other than to seek your pardon and accept that I was at fault.
I hope that this letter finds you in good health as I and my family are.
About seven years have passed since I last received a letter from you, but I understand that you have sent me your
regards in your letters to other family members, and that you bear no grudge against me for being so remiss. Believe it
or not, but I did write a very long letter to you about a year after you had left this country (after I had received a letter
from you) but it was too heavy when I took it to the Post Office, so I took it back and decided that I should re-write it in
a more condensed form by cutting out things not directly relevant, but I waited too long and consequently it never did
get re-written.
With that background, I will now go ahead and tell you a bit about what has been happening here and with me these
past seven years.
About eight years ago I joined with four others to take over a slate quarry near Machynlleth. The others were Uncle
Edward, John Evans, (Tanyclogwyn), William George (Tanygrisiau) and my father. We went there to work and initially
we thought that we could work it on our own, but it needed further investment which we could not afford, and so we
decided to sell it. We did quite well with it and got £40 to £50 profit each (after paying salaries and costs). After having
finished there, I returned to work in the Lord Quarry in Blaenau and found that wages there had improved quite a lot
in the 18 months that I had spent in Machynlleth.
I decided to buy six houses that my father owned in Tanygrisiau for £120, and I now rent these out for £20 per annum.
After that, I decided to go to school in Liverpool and I spent 15 months there. That was expensive and time-consuming
and I didn't actually learn as much as I had hoped that I would; I don't regret going there though.
I returned home about two and a half years ago – returning somewhat before the end of my course, to attend the
funeral of my cousin and fond business partner, William George (Tanygrisiau) who died suddenly.
The first thing that I did after that was to get married (March 1st, 1867) but I am sure that you will have heard about
that. My wife is the daughter of Owen Mathew (Talywaenydd) and we live in one of William Foulkes houses near the
crossroads at Glan-y-Pwll. We have a nine-month-old son.
I moved from Lord Quarry to Rhiw Quarry some 18 months ago. And am doing well there.
I don't know who exactly I should write about – but it would take too long, so I will only mention a few. If any old
friend comes to your mind, ask, and I will tell what they have been up to.
Perhaps you did not hear about the deaths in Australia of Edward Jones (Penrhos), William Davies (shop) and Robert
Parry bach. William (Plas Isaf ) returned from Australia but was killed on the railway coming up from Porthmadog.
Robert (Bronmanod) also died after returning from the same place. As you can see, several of my close friends and
contemporaries have passed on recently, others have got married or moved away to foreign lands. You could say that
only my cousin Robert and myself are left here.
Much has been happening in Blaenau these past few years. Steam trains now run along the railroad to Porthmadog
and there is another railroad that goes from Dolgarregddu to Llan. The slate quarries are flourishing. You probably
know that Robert Owen (Bethania) is now a steward at the quarry.
I was able to read the letter that you had sent your cousin Rees and I am very pleased to hear that you are alive and in
good health and are doing well over there. I learnt that, as a family, you have lost a dear husband and father who was
a good man. I was glad to learn from your letter that the country is now doing better and that transport, produce and
commerce are all improving.

Don't you sometimes fancy coming back home to work? Now that the railroad has been completed it would not take
you very long to get back here.
I was glad to hear that Elizabeth had got married to somebody from Wales.
I finish by asking you to pass on to your mother my warmest and sincerest regards, also of course to everybody else –

Your old friend
David Roberts

Llanfairfechan Post Office
5th August 1869
Our Dearest Mother and Father
We received your kind letter some time ago. We are very sorry to have taken so long to reply. We are quite busy here
now with visitors – there are hundreds of them!
We hope that you are all as a family healthy and comfortable, just as we are when these lines leave us.
Elisabeth, Mary Jane and I were over in Harlech for Whitsun. They were all well there and had received a letter from
you; they had answered it before we arrived. We visited places like Abermaw. Robert has become a strong young man
and resembles his Uncle John; I really missed you {hiraeth} since Robert reminded me so much of John. Jane and I
chatted and chatted about you all. She is going to come here quite soon.
On the front of this letter, you will see a picture of this village. It does not show our new house because it is lower
down, opposite the school. We are expecting that this row of houses will be photographed(?) soon.
We have all sorts of sweets, biscuits, toys, shoes and clogs on sale here and they are selling quite well. Mary Jane and
Lizzie attend school daily. They have a Tea Party tomorrow, arranged by William Platt in the hall.
Our sister Jane saw that Mary Jane bore a huge resemblance to her grandmother. She is really sharp too just like her
grandmother.
We have a very nice, large parlour here. We got a carpet recently and the room is now full of furniture. Our front
garden is very pretty – full of flowers at the moment. We have the nicest front garden in this row of houses - and this
is just our first year here.
We hope that you will write to us soon and tell us all the news. We will reply sooner the next time.
My mother sends you all her kindest regards.
Margaret has moved to live in Penmaenmawr. Hugh Davies has found a good place.
The two of us and Mary Jane and Lizzie and Maggie all send you our kindest regards
Remember us to anyone there who mentions us.
We are your son and daughter
Robert E. Roberts

Harlech
26th October, 1869
Dear Dad and Mam
I am sending you these few lines hoping that you are all well, as we are when these lines leave us.
We received your letter last week. We were so happy to receive it and to understand that you are all healthy and
comfortable in your new country. We have often thought about writing to you, but have delayed thus far. After
waiting so long though, we don't have much news for you.
My father went to Llanrwst recently. He met Aunt Mary and our Aunt Margaret and found them both well. The
Llanfairfechan family were well and very comfortable too.
Aunt Elisabeth intends to visit us at Whitsun. We got a letter from them yesterday.
Aunt Margaret was here last week. They live in a mill in Dyffryn. She took the letter with her so that all her family
could read it. She has one daughter and four sons. The youngest is 13. The eldest daughter married a sailor four years
ago and they live close by with their three children.
The eldest son is a blacksmith, the second son is a joiner and the other two are still at home. They are all well and send
you their regards. They are delighted to hear that you are all well and comfortable.
My Uncle Griffith (my father's brother) sends you his regards. He and his family are well. His eldest son got married a
year ago and has a young son. They live in Liverpool. The other son married five years ago and lives in Ffestiniog. He
has three children. His daughter is in service in Porthmadog.
My Uncle Hugh lives within a mile of us. He has seven living children and one dead. Two of them are in service.
My Aunt Jane (my father's sister) is in service.
Little Hannah is still pretty small. She has not grown very much - she was one year old last February.
Jane Elisabeth is a lovely three-year-old.
Humphrey is eight and attends school.
We have made a garden outside the front door this year and we carried flowers to plant there.
I, your grand-son Robert, have the honour of writing to you so that you can see my handwriting. I would much prefer
to see you face-to-face.
I was pleased to read the letter that you sent here.
I started to work with my father nine months ago.
I hope that these lines find you well as they leave us.
Our kindest regards
Edward J Humphreys and Robert your grand-son.
Dear Taid and Nain {grandmother and grandfather} and family
I too am being given the honour of writing to you so that you can see my writing work.
I am at home nursing Hannah - she is a bit of a handful. I also crochet netting headwear.
My father showed me pictures of Llanfairfechan, Aunt Catherine and Mary and Margaret and Hannah.
I would like to see you - everybody says that I resemble the picture of Hannah.
I send you all my kindest regards
Your grand-daughter
Mary Humphreys (aged 13)

Llanfairfechan Post Office
28th January, 1870
Our Dear Dad and Mam
We hope that you are all as a family healthy and well as we all are here.
We are feeling very concerned as we have heard from you – even a brief word would be acceptable. I hope that you
will agree not to let a single post to pass without replying – even half a dozen words would suffice.
We sent you a letter quite a long time ago, along with several newspapers and an Almanac.
We got a letter from Harlech saying that a baby boy arrived on the 24th of this month. They were doing well at the
time.
Mary Jane, Lizzie and Maggie send you kind regards. Jane now writes and she can sew – you would be surprised to see
the quality of her work. She runs errands.
Her Eglwysbach grandmother ..?... Owen Jones (Nant) spent the weekend with us recently.
We finish by sending you our kindest regards
We are your son and daughter
Robert and Elisabeth Roberts
P.S.
My mother sends you her best regards
P.P.S.
Remember to write soon. To put us at ease.

Creuau, Llanfrothen
February 7th, 1870
Dear Sister and Nephews
I am very sorry that I have not written to you earlier after receiving your letter dated 4th of January, 1867, but there is
an old Welsh saying 'Better late than never' so we ask your forgiveness this time and we will try to do better from now
on.
We wish you to pass on our warmest thanks to Thomas, Robert and Jane for their photographs. Although we don't
have the pleasure of seeing them face-to-face, the photographs create a picture of how they look now, how they have
grown and how they are clothed. My, how they have grown since we saw them back here in 'Quiet Wales' when they
were children and used to play around the fire here in Creuau. But there is an old saying 'As the child, so will be the
man'.
I can't but remember the old times when Daniel (or Little Daniel as he then was) ran away from Ffestiniog one day to
come here to Creuau and I had to bring him back up. On the way, I gave him a half-crown coin as a present and he said
that he would drill a hole in it to remind him of me. But by now Little Daniel is a man – how strange is that! But things
change, generation follows generation, boys become men... and the young become the elderly. I really would like to
get a photograph of Daniel, and in return, I will send him a photograph of Catherine Ann - my own daughter
We are really grateful for your photographs and are happy to see that you are looking so good in your new land. We
heard a rumour that you had married - we would like to know whether that is true or false. If true, what nationality is
your new husband?
Now on to some news about this country. Everything is going on quite well and market prices are good. Cattle in calf
make £10 to £16, horses are exceptionally scarce and expensive, fat pigs (living) make five pence a pound, butter is
one shilling and sixpence to one and eight a pound, bacon is ten pennies a pound and salted butter 1/2 a pound. The
flour market is poor, best seed is £2 for a 224lb sack, and oat flour is £1-9-0 a sack.
Many things have changed in the Old Country since you left; a large railway has been built between Porthmadog and
Caernarfon and down to Aberystwyth. It is a great convenience as we can now send anything by rail to anywhere in
the country. This has resulted in a significant increase in prosperity and commerce. Especially so for the slate industry,
as thousands of tons of slates are now being sent all across the country by rail. There are good employment
opportunities in the area and good wages to be made.
We would like to know about America when you next write, and especially about the development of the railway. How
has this affected your country? Good or bad?
Since the country is booming, land owners are cashing in and realising the value of their land. Rents are rising
everywhere – ours, here at Creuau has risen from 18 guineas to £30.
We hope that this letter finds you well – as we are well here. We send you all our very warmest regards. Give us all
your news in your next letter – and be totally honest.
Your dear brother and sister
Richard & Margaret Thomas
To: Robert David Roberts
Dear Nephew
Since I get this opportunity, I too will write to you. I wish to inform you that I am alive and well and still living in Gelli.
I would be pleased to get a letter from you telling me what you have been doing and how things are going in your new
country. I send you all our best regards as a family and hope that you are enjoying good health.
I remain your dear uncle
Edward Roberts
Gelli

Logan City
March 8th, 1870
Dear Uncles Edward Roberts (Gelli) and Richard Thomas (Creuau)
If there is cooperation between my hand, my eye, my mind and my heart then I intend to present you with the story of
this land, as correctly as I can. But I am not sure how to start as the American continent is so huge and Wales is only a
tiny drop in the ocean by comparison. There are thousands of acres of land here, many expansive valleys with wild
rivers running through them, all filled with fish and all uninhabited, apart from a few Indians here and there, hunting
and fishing and just living on these.
The railroad is bringing great improvements from coast to coast – I think that it is now 3,000 miles long and about
1,500 of these miles is through uninhabited lands. Hundreds of farms and townships have been built along the track,
bringing homes and employment to thousands of settlers. Utah has been transformed by the Saints who have built
about 300 miles of railroads, but despite the help and hard work of the Saints, the railroad owners have kept back
some thousands of dollars from their wages. The Company was in debt to the Saints to the sum of $1,500,000 some
while back, but I think that they have by now repaid at least some of this.
Here are some of the prices that we pay over here, so that you can see how things compare - sugar 60c to $1 a pound,
yellow calico o 60c-$1¼ a yard, tea $4-$5 a pound, but you can buy sugar for 20c-25c and the calico for 20-25c a yard
and tea from $2-$3 a pound. Flour is 3c a pound but it used to be 6c a pound and sometimes even 10c. Barley, oats
and corn for animals have kept their prices well.
Things are very dead around Utah these days but I believe things will improve when the railroad company repay their
debts to the poor workers.
Logan City is the main settlement in Utah and here both companies have decided to build a station. One track comes
from California and the other from New York. The Saints have built a road from here to Salt Lake City - some 40 miles
thus far, where three branches of the railway come together and are likely to make Ogden a very large town.
Minerals:
There aren't many mines or quarries here. Four or five coal mines and an ironworks have been opened, but they aren't
too busy so far. I think that there is a silver mine in the area, but I am not sure. I believe that Utah Mountain is as
valuable as any mountain in the world for any type of mineral. It only needs hard work and a bit of time to bring these
into being.
Farming:
You can raise all sorts of wheat, corn, oats, barley, ??phug?? and every type of root vegetable – potatoes, carrots,
rutabaga, ??mangls?? and they also grow cotton, silk, fruits, apples, plums, figs and raisins. I think that you can grow
almost any sort of fruit or raise any animal if you choose the right season.
In the north, summers are quite hot but the winters cold. There is not much rain apart from the spring and at the end
of the year and summer. There is usually quite a thickness of snow and ice on the ground. The west is quite different -
no snow or ice and their summers are very hot and their winters quite mild. You can see that in Utah there are
significant differences in the seasons in various parts - in the north gets about six months of really cold weather but
not in the south.
The inhabitants:
Most of the inhabitants are Saints, but there are a few who live in the territory that are not Saints. Some 6 miles from
Box Elder and again, some 6 miles from Salt Lake City there are settlements of soldiers. There is one other town at the
mouth of Weber Canyon and perhaps a few other places, but I cannot recall.
The difference between the ways of the Saints and the others that come to Utah: In Salt Lake City, there are about
twenty five thousand inhabitants. In the whole of the City there is no house of ill-repute to attract women nor an inn
to attract drunks. Liquor is available from drug stores and similar places and perhaps there are a few that manage to
get hold of too much at times, but that does not happen often.
I do not know the population figure for Logan, but I think that there are about 3,000 people here. I cannot recall when
I last saw a drunk or heard that anybody else had seen one here.

In the city of the Saints there isn't much quarrelling or fighting. They are friendly towards strangers but these people
often make up stories and lie about them after being shown great the kindness whilst in this territory. Some are
grateful for the kindness but many aren't.
Every good man has the freedom to have two or three 3 wives if he has the means to keep, feed and clothe them
comfortably. Perhaps that you think that it is impossible to keep two or more wives peacefully? The man whom I lived
with when I first arrived in this country two wives and it was a long time before I figured out if they were wife and
daughter or just two sisters (I could not judge their ages to allow me to figure that out). But everything was just as
peaceful as if there was just the one wife.
Cities of those that aren't Saints:
One of the first things they establish are houses to sell alcoholic drinks and houses for bad women - and these are the
very people who say they come here to put the Saints to rights, to bring them chastity and to save the Saints from
their barbaric situation! So, here I have given you both sides of the story. Would you rather live with the Saints, in their
sober and peaceful cities where love and unity are on the increase or would you prefer to live in a city where perhaps
half of them are drunks who go around swearing, blaspheming, fighting, prostituting and sinking ever-deeper into evil
deeds of all sorts year after year?
