letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
3320-3321
Harlech
26th October, 1869
Dear Dad and Mam
I am sending you these few lines hoping that you are all well, as we are when these lines leave us.
We received your letter last week. We were so happy to receive it and to understand that you are all healthy and
comfortable in your new country. We have often thought about writing to you, but have delayed thus far. After
waiting so long though, we don't have much news for you.
My father went to Llanrwst recently. He met Aunt Mary and our Aunt Margaret and found them both well. The
Llanfairfechan family were well and very comfortable too.
Aunt Elisabeth intends to visit us at Whitsun. We got a letter from them yesterday.
Aunt Margaret was here last week. They live in a mill in Dyffryn. She took the letter with her so that all her family
could read it. She has one daughter and four sons. The youngest is 13. The eldest daughter married a sailor four years
ago and they live close by with their three children.
The eldest son is a blacksmith, the second son is a joiner and the other two are still at home. They are all well and send
you their regards. They are delighted to hear that you are all well and comfortable.
My Uncle Griffith (my father's brother) sends you his regards. He and his family are well. His eldest son got married a
year ago and has a young son. They live in Liverpool. The other son married five years ago and lives in Ffestiniog. He
has three children. His daughter is in service in Porthmadog.
My Uncle Hugh lives within a mile of us. He has seven living children and one dead. Two of them are in service.
My Aunt Jane (my father's sister) is in service.
Little Hannah is still pretty small. She has not grown very much - she was one year old last February.
Jane Elisabeth is a lovely three-year-old.
Humphrey is eight and attends school.
We have made a garden outside the front door this year and we carried flowers to plant there.
I, your grand-son Robert, have the honour of writing to you so that you can see my handwriting. I would much prefer
to see you face-to-face.
I was pleased to read the letter that you sent here.
I started to work with my father nine months ago.
I hope that these lines find you well as they leave us.
Our kindest regards
Edward J Humphreys and Robert your grand-son.
Dear Taid and Nain {grandmother and grandfather} and family
I too am being given the honour of writing to you so that you can see my writing work.
I am at home nursing Hannah - she is a bit of a handful. I also crochet netting headwear.
My father showed me pictures of Llanfairfechan, Aunt Catherine and Mary and Margaret and Hannah.
I would like to see you - everybody says that I resemble the picture of Hannah.
I send you all my kindest regards
Your grand-daughter
Mary Humphreys (aged 13)

Dear Taid and Nain {grandmother and grandfather} and family
I am writing a few lines so that you can see my handwriting.
Robert is helping me with my spelling. I am at school.
Mother says that I grow to resemble Aunt Mary more and more every day.
I would like to see her and the other aunts who live there.
I send you all my kindest regards
Your grand-child

Llanfairfechan Post Office
28th January, 1870
Our Dear Dad and Mam
We hope that you are all as a family healthy and well as we all are here.
We are feeling very concerned as we have heard from you – even a brief word would be acceptable. I hope that you
will agree not to let a single post to pass without replying – even half a dozen words would suffice.
We sent you a letter quite a long time ago, along with several newspapers and an Almanac.
We got a letter from Harlech saying that a baby boy arrived on the 24th of this month. They were doing well at the
time.
Mary Jane, Lizzie and Maggie send you kind regards. Jane now writes and she can sew – you would be surprised to see
the quality of her work. She runs errands.
Her Eglwysbach grandmother ..?... Owen Jones (Nant) spent the weekend with us recently.
We finish by sending you our kindest regards
We are your son and daughter
Robert and Elisabeth Roberts
P.S.
My mother sends you her best regards
P.P.S.
Remember to write soon. To put us at ease.

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.notes: First of two distinct correspondence items printed on PDF page 52.
letters.suppliedText:
Creuau, Llanfrothen
February 7th, 1870
Dear Sister and Nephews
I am very sorry that I have not written to you earlier after receiving your letter dated 4th of January, 1867, but there is
an old Welsh saying 'Better late than never' so we ask your forgiveness this time and we will try to do better from now
on.
We wish you to pass on our warmest thanks to Thomas, Robert and Jane for their photographs. Although we don't
have the pleasure of seeing them face-to-face, the photographs create a picture of how they look now, how they have
grown and how they are clothed. My, how they have grown since we saw them back here in 'Quiet Wales' when they
were children and used to play around the fire here in Creuau. But there is an old saying 'As the child, so will be the
man'.
I can't but remember the old times when Daniel (or Little Daniel as he then was) ran away from Ffestiniog one day to
come here to Creuau and I had to bring him back up. On the way, I gave him a half-crown coin as a present and he said
that he would drill a hole in it to remind him of me. But by now Little Daniel is a man – how strange is that! But things
change, generation follows generation, boys become men... and the young become the elderly. I really would like to
get a photograph of Daniel, and in return, I will send him a photograph of Catherine Ann - my own daughter
We are really grateful for your photographs and are happy to see that you are looking so good in your new land. We
heard a rumour that you had married - we would like to know whether that is true or false. If true, what nationality is
your new husband?
Now on to some news about this country. Everything is going on quite well and market prices are good. Cattle in calf
make £10 to £16, horses are exceptionally scarce and expensive, fat pigs (living) make five pence a pound, butter is
one shilling and sixpence to one and eight a pound, bacon is ten pennies a pound and salted butter 1/2 a pound. The
flour market is poor, best seed is £2 for a 224lb sack, and oat flour is £1-9-0 a sack.
Many things have changed in the Old Country since you left; a large railway has been built between Porthmadog and
Caernarfon and down to Aberystwyth. It is a great convenience as we can now send anything by rail to anywhere in
the country. This has resulted in a significant increase in prosperity and commerce. Especially so for the slate industry,
as thousands of tons of slates are now being sent all across the country by rail. There are good employment
opportunities in the area and good wages to be made.
We would like to know about America when you next write, and especially about the development of the railway. How
has this affected your country? Good or bad?
Since the country is booming, land owners are cashing in and realising the value of their land. Rents are rising
everywhere – ours, here at Creuau has risen from 18 guineas to £30.
We hope that this letter finds you well – as we are well here. We send you all our very warmest regards. Give us all
your news in your next letter – and be totally honest.
Your dear brother and sister
Richard & Margaret Thomas

Logan City
March 8th, 1870
Dear Uncles Edward Roberts (Gelli) and Richard Thomas (Creuau)
If there is cooperation between my hand, my eye, my mind and my heart then I intend to present you with the story of
this land, as correctly as I can. But I am not sure how to start as the American continent is so huge and Wales is only a
tiny drop in the ocean by comparison. There are thousands of acres of land here, many expansive valleys with wild
rivers running through them, all filled with fish and all uninhabited, apart from a few Indians here and there, hunting
and fishing and just living on these.
The railroad is bringing great improvements from coast to coast – I think that it is now 3,000 miles long and about
1,500 of these miles is through uninhabited lands. Hundreds of farms and townships have been built along the track,
bringing homes and employment to thousands of settlers. Utah has been transformed by the Saints who have built
about 300 miles of railroads, but despite the help and hard work of the Saints, the railroad owners have kept back
some thousands of dollars from their wages. The Company was in debt to the Saints to the sum of $1,500,000 some
while back, but I think that they have by now repaid at least some of this.
Here are some of the prices that we pay over here, so that you can see how things compare - sugar 60c to $1 a pound,
yellow calico o 60c-$1¼ a yard, tea $4-$5 a pound, but you can buy sugar for 20c-25c and the calico for 20-25c a yard
and tea from $2-$3 a pound. Flour is 3c a pound but it used to be 6c a pound and sometimes even 10c. Barley, oats
and corn for animals have kept their prices well.
Things are very dead around Utah these days but I believe things will improve when the railroad company repay their
debts to the poor workers.
Logan City is the main settlement in Utah and here both companies have decided to build a station. One track comes
from California and the other from New York. The Saints have built a road from here to Salt Lake City - some 40 miles
thus far, where three branches of the railway come together and are likely to make Ogden a very large town.
Minerals:
There aren't many mines or quarries here. Four or five coal mines and an ironworks have been opened, but they aren't
too busy so far. I think that there is a silver mine in the area, but I am not sure. I believe that Utah Mountain is as
valuable as any mountain in the world for any type of mineral. It only needs hard work and a bit of time to bring these
into being.
Farming:
You can raise all sorts of wheat, corn, oats, barley, ??phug?? and every type of root vegetable – potatoes, carrots,
rutabaga, ??mangls?? and they also grow cotton, silk, fruits, apples, plums, figs and raisins. I think that you can grow
almost any sort of fruit or raise any animal if you choose the right season.
In the north, summers are quite hot but the winters cold. There is not much rain apart from the spring and at the end
of the year and summer. There is usually quite a thickness of snow and ice on the ground. The west is quite different -
no snow or ice and their summers are very hot and their winters quite mild. You can see that in Utah there are
significant differences in the seasons in various parts - in the north gets about six months of really cold weather but
not in the south.
The inhabitants:
Most of the inhabitants are Saints, but there are a few who live in the territory that are not Saints. Some 6 miles from
Box Elder and again, some 6 miles from Salt Lake City there are settlements of soldiers. There is one other town at the
mouth of Weber Canyon and perhaps a few other places, but I cannot recall.
The difference between the ways of the Saints and the others that come to Utah: In Salt Lake City, there are about
twenty five thousand inhabitants. In the whole of the City there is no house of ill-repute to attract women nor an inn
to attract drunks. Liquor is available from drug stores and similar places and perhaps there are a few that manage to
get hold of too much at times, but that does not happen often.
I do not know the population figure for Logan, but I think that there are about 3,000 people here. I cannot recall when
I last saw a drunk or heard that anybody else had seen one here.

In the city of the Saints there isn't much quarrelling or fighting. They are friendly towards strangers but these people
often make up stories and lie about them after being shown great the kindness whilst in this territory. Some are
grateful for the kindness but many aren't.
Every good man has the freedom to have two or three 3 wives if he has the means to keep, feed and clothe them
comfortably. Perhaps that you think that it is impossible to keep two or more wives peacefully? The man whom I lived
with when I first arrived in this country two wives and it was a long time before I figured out if they were wife and
daughter or just two sisters (I could not judge their ages to allow me to figure that out). But everything was just as
peaceful as if there was just the one wife.
Cities of those that aren't Saints:
One of the first things they establish are houses to sell alcoholic drinks and houses for bad women - and these are the
very people who say they come here to put the Saints to rights, to bring them chastity and to save the Saints from
their barbaric situation! So, here I have given you both sides of the story. Would you rather live with the Saints, in their
sober and peaceful cities where love and unity are on the increase or would you prefer to live in a city where perhaps
half of them are drunks who go around swearing, blaspheming, fighting, prostituting and sinking ever-deeper into evil
deeds of all sorts year after year?

letters.title: Catherine Roberts to Richard Thomas and Margaret Thomas - 18 March 1870
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2600
Logan City
March 18th, 1870
Richard and Margaret Thomas
Dear brother and sister
I was delighted to receive your kind letter - I was starting to think that you had forgotten about me or had died. A
letter from my old home warms my heart.
Ann has written a few lines to you but I do not think that she has told you that Elizabeth has given birth to twins – a
boy and a girl, but they did not live very long. You ask if I had married, well, I can answer that I have not married a
living soul being except David Roberts and it is not at all likely that I will ever marry anyone else whilst I live on this
earth.
We went to Salt Lake City January 19th, 1865 when Robert and Thomas were washed and anointed and I was sealed
with David Roberts for Eternity in God's House. Perhaps somebody took this as the basis for their rumour but I can tell
you it would be unreasonable for me to marry anyone else after my having been sealed forever with David.
If it were ever possible, I would be pleased to see you but we must accept things as they are. I would like to hear news
about my old neighbours at Fedw, Hafod, Carreghylltrem, and of Morris Isaac (Parc) and Thomas (Cwm Trwsgwl). I was
glad to hear that things are going so well in Wales and that you were well and comfortable. Things are pretty dead
over here these days but I am quite well and am happy with my lot. I have plenty to eat and clothes to wear. The boys
and Jane are home with me and the other two girls are both happy and well. However, Elizabeth has not been at all
well these past couple of years.
I will await your letter if you feel inclined to write to me.
I remain your dearest sister
Catherine Roberts
P.S. Send my warmest regards to all my old neighbours.

letters.title: Robert Roberts and Elisabeth Roberts to Their sister - April 1870

3291-3293
Llanfairfechan Post Office
April 1870
Our Dear Sister
As soon as we had written to our parents a while back, the storm hit and little Hannah arrived. I am glad to inform you
that both I and the little girl are coming along well. Robert was a bit disappointed as he had hoped for a little Hugh this
time. Whatever, we are so glad of Hannah. The children are very happy with their little sister and always call her by her
full name Hannah Roberts.
I enclose half a dozen newspapers in two bundles – I hope that they arrive safely.
I would love it if you could see our new house. The front garden is lovely and we also have a kitchen garden where
everything grows really well – as they used to do in your old garden. The gardens are hugely important to Robert. Last
year, Catherine Davies sent us a lot of apples that had grown on the apple tree in your old home - big green apples.
We don't have any interesting news for you.
Mother, Mary Jane, Lizzie and Maggie and also Hannah send you best regards and also to their grandparents and also
to Uncle John.
Accept our warmest wishes. I hope that we will get a letter from you soon.
Your brother and sister
Robert and Elisabeth Roberts

full name hannah roberts.
i enclose half a dozen newspapers in two bundles – i hope that they arrive safely.
i would love it if you could see our new house. the front garden is lovely and we also have a kitchen garden where
everything grows really well – as they used to do in your old garden. the gardens are hugely important to robert. last
year, catherine davies sent us a lot of apples that had grown on the apple tree in your old home - big green apples.
we don't have any interesting news for you.
mother, mary jane, lizzie and maggie and also hannah send you best regards and also to their grandparents and also
to uncle john.
accept our warmest wishes. i hope that we will get a letter from you soon.
your brother and sister
robert and elisabeth roberts

letters.title: Robert Roberts and Elisabeth Roberts to Their parents - 4 April 1870
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
991-994
Llanfairfechan Post Office
4th April, 1870
Dear Dad and Mam
How happy we were to receive your letter and photographs! We were just so happy! Seeing you all look so well! We
received your letter on 27th of March and despite it being a Sunday {the Welsh were very strict about "keeping the
Sabbath"} we had a birthday celebration for Hannah and all the children were joyous.
Mary Jane, Lizzie and Maggie look at your photographs all the time.
We were glad to see little Huwcyn's {Hugh's} handwriting as we had heard that he had died around Christmas –
although we did not believe it to be true.
That is why were implored you to write the last time.
It was Thomas Edward the joiner who brought us that rumour, but when he told us, Robert said that we would have
definitely heard from you if that had happened. Thomas Edwards went away with his tail between his legs.
Robert was delighted to get the letters and went straight to Eglwysbach the next day to show them to everybody.
Everybody who saw them could just about eat the photographs!
Catherine Williams (Cefn-y-Coed) is still alive but I did not see her. Owen Williams (shoe maker) buried his wife but has
now married the daughter of William Thomas (formerly of Ty'n-y-Pistyll). Ann Davies (Tŷ Canol) was widowed a year
ago. She stayed in Graig for three hours so that she would see the photos. We intend to send the photos to London to
have other prints made from them, so that we can give copies to your old friends in Eglwysbach.
Jenny Evans still has had a pair of shoes that you made for her seven years ago. She keeps them in a cupboard. Betsan
Wynne also has a pair of "best shoes" that you made for her. She is worried that she will have to keep them another
seven years if it is not possible to persuade you to come over to make her another pair.
Owen Evans(?) and Mary Jones (Nant) and Ellin Davies and Catherine Davies and the Chwta(?) family, everybody we
saw, send you their kind regards. Aunt ?? has been bed-bound for six months after having had a stroke. She does
retain her senses fully however.
Mary Jane is sewing aprons at school. You would be surprised to see her sewing ability. She will be 7 years-old on 9th of
June and Lizzie was 5 since 20th of February. Maggie will be 3 on the 9th of May.
If I could, I would get a step-ladder to reach up to John and kiss him on the cheek for the photos.
Not one of you looks much older than when you left. We will send you our photos as soon as we have the opportunity
to have them taken. We will have to go to Bangor or Conwy for this as there is nobody locally that can do this.
This is Mary Jane's handwriting.
We do not have anything else to add, other than to send you our kindest regards.
We will expect a letter from you soon. We too will write soon. Tell our brothers and sisters, especially the brother and
sister who have not left home that we send our best regards.
Your children.
From your children
Robert and Elisabeth Roberts
{in different handwriting} Mary Jane Roberts Post Office

letters.title: Jane Humphreys and Edward Humphreys to Their parents - 11 April 1870
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1061-1063
Harlech
11th April, 1870
Dear Dad and Mam
We had awaited eagerly for your letter; we were delighted when it finally arrived and enjoyed seeing the photograph
of the four of you. We too will do the same as soon as it is possible to have a photo taken and I will send it back to you.
I (Jane) am now much-recovered and Edward Humphreys is coming along well. He is quite tall 22" and Hannah is 23".
She is two-years-old since the 1st of February and is now walking un-aided.
We can't recall if I have told you that I have been employed as a tax-collector by the parish for a year now. I am paid
£15 a year for doing this. We have taken land to keep a cow for the summer. Economically, things are doing pretty well
at the moment, but flour is cheap. Butter is 1/6 a pound and mutton 10d a pound and beef 8d a pound. Tea is quite
cheap, costing between sixpence to a shilling a quarter – I expect that you are enjoying many a cup of tea over there.
We would like to hear more about our sisters who are there with you. It pains us to read what the newspapers say
about you – that one man can take several wives.
Robert is at home, working with me; he will be 16 next June. May has been in school in Talsarnau these past 6 months;
she will be 14 next Friday. Margaret is at home nursing Edward and little Hannah. She is 11 since December.
Humphrey attends school here but has learnt nothing in three years! He is 9 since last January. Jane Eliza is four since
the 2nd of this month.
Our family in Dyffryn are healthy. We saw your sister Margaret last week and she said that her daughter Mary's
husband was drowned last winter. She also buried a child last week. She still has three children.
We hope that you will not take so long in replying next time.
We send you our kindest regards
Jane and Edward Humphreys
P.S.
Here is a piece of satin which Mary sends to her grandmother.

letters.title: Robert Roberts and Elisabeth Roberts to Their parents - 21 September 1871
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
3341-3343
Llanfairfechan Post Office
21st September, 1871
Our dearest Dad and Mam
By now I am sure that you had thought that we were not going to write to you. I would have written earlier but we had
waited for an opportunity to take the children to have their photographs taken.
Little Hannah, myself and Elisabeth will be going next week and we will post them to you when we get them. There are
another four that we are waiting for. Can you just send us a word to say that they reached you safely?
We hope that you are all well – as we are at the moment.
Peter(?) was very ill for four months last winter with rheumatism and was in great pain for weeks. He also had an
inflammation of his eye and was not seeing well at all; his eyes are still very weak and he has to wear dark glasses –
coloured blue. He was so ill that we had begun to think that he was not going to improve but the Almighty saw fit to
make him better and spare him for at least some time. He looks much older after this. He lost all his hair and the wig
which he now wears, cost £3-10-0.
In the photo, it is Mary Jane, the eldest, that is sitting and Lizzie is standing on the right. Maggie is in the middle. We
will send you a photo of Mary Jane standing and Lizzie sitting in the next photo.
Owen Jones (Nant, Eglwysbach) was here on a visit recently. Also, Ellis Davies (Hendy) brought a whole basketful of
apples and plums. We see one of them quite often. We will go there to see them shortly to see how everyone is.
We have taken 12 photos from the card which you sent and shared them with everybody at Eglwysbach. They all send
you their best regards.
Edward (husband of our sister Jane) and little Robert were here for a week. He is quite a lad.
The telegraph reached here four months ago but we are having a lot of trouble with it. We would love to be able to
send you a note every day using this.
There have been lots of visitors around this summer.
Send us a few words when you receive this letter. My mother and everybody send you kindest regards.
Your son and daughter
Robert and Elisabeth Roberts

letters.title: Robert W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 4 June 1872
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
3161-3165
London House, Glan-y-Pwll, Blaenau Ffestiniog
4th June, 1872
Dear Cousin
I received your letter two months ago and was glad to hear that you and family are well. I see that the branches of the
family in Utah are fruitful and multiplying - and filling the place. (Some more so than others.) You are far busier than
those of us who stayed on this side of the Atlantic. Some of us too have given birth to twins namely Eliza' of Erw Fawr.
Rhys had a son and daughter after re-marrying and Meurig also has had two sons. Mary has six or seven children and
has just buried her second husband. Ellis and Gwen are unmarried.
I am sure that you have not heard that Ellen has been buried is Wisconsin, America. Her husband sent her Box (?) and
clothes back home to the Erw. Despite being glad to receive them, this did add a lot to their grief. I recently heard from
some of Aunt Ellen's family in America - all were quite well. Robert has married some Yank and has eight children. Kate
has married and keeps a drug store and she has two daughters. John has married but he buried his wife and his only
child, just a week apart. David keeps a saddlery shop and makes good business, staying at his parents'. Ebenezer the
youngest was apprenticed as a Tinman and keeps his own shop about four miles from his parents' home. He was here
on a visit about five years ago, for about a month. My uncle and aunt have buried William, Daniel and James Henry in
America. The last was born after arriving in America. If you feel in your heart to write them a letter, I can assure you
that they would be delighted to receive it.
We have had very mild winter but a cold spring; I can't recall such a spring and early summer when things were
growing so slowly. The harvest will be very late this year and I'm afraid and it probably won't be a very good harvest.
Things remain flat here in the slate quarries. Wages are low but the market for slate is huge. There is a surplus of
workers here, so we will not see much better times. We have though had the honour of having our weekly working
hours cut – we now start at 6:00 on Saturdays and 7:30 on Mondays. This was given without anybody having to
demand it. The general rule for workers in this country is to work nine hours a day, but amongst us quarrymen, there
is no initiative, we just keep our heads down, work like fools and are just grateful for what we are given and there no
protestations.
I would like to know about business matters in your country (not women's matters). Our mountains here are full of
good slates – wouldn't you be better off here, rather than farming? Are wages in Utah good? Is there steady
employment, or do people just go from job to job and just and live hand-to-mouth? I want you to know that I don't
disbelieve anything that you said about Utah and the Mormons. You did tell me quite a lot in your last letter – tell me
more.
I hope that you will excuse me for taking so long to answer your letter. I hope to hear from you soon. I have received
several copies of Deseret News from you and have responded by sending you copies of Welsh newspapers – I don't
know if you received them.
My family are all well and quite comfortable. I hope to return to America before I die, I hope that have enough years
left.
My wife and I send you our kindest regards. You will get our family photos as soon as I have been able to have them
taken.
I am writing this in a bit of a hurry on a day when we were turned back from the quarry because of unusually bad
weather.
Give my best regards to your mother, your two brothers and three sisters. If you see my other cousins, give them our
regards as well.
Your cousin
Robert W. Roberts

letters.title: Robert W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 20 March 1877
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
3260-3262
Market Place, Blaenau Ffestiniog
20th March, 1877
Give my best regards to all my relatives. Write soon.
Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin
I have the following note in my diary " letter to R.D. Roberts June 4th 1872" but I have not heard a word from you
since.
I received word from old Uncle Edward (formerly of Gelli) on October 8th saying that he would like to see me and our
cousin Rees Roberts. He had left Gelli and gone to live in Penrhyn. We had not seen him in years but we went down
two days later to see him (the 10th).
I was very surprised to see that he was in a very bad way- so ill, that really, I did not get more than a few words from
him. He did recognise me though, and asked me a few things – that's all. Amongst the questions that he asked, one
was, would I answer the letter which he had received from you, sometime at the start of February. He seemed to be
very anxious to say something if he could, but only managed to grip my hand very tightly. I really felt bad.
He had been sent to such a poor and ignoble corner to die – but, this was all of his making. He had failed to pay his
rent for quite some time and so, you see, he had to leave. My Uncle Robert Roberts (Erw Fawr) offered to make him a
home at the Erw, but he refused flatly. Hence there was nothing to do but plan to move to the Pant in Penrhyn where
he would be solely dependent on the charity of the parish. {Pant was a very poor area in Penrhyn. A neighbour of ours
is from the town and remembers the area as "slum housing" – for the lowest of the low.} But his time there was not to
be long.
The spinster who was his house-keeper thinks that he died from heartbreak after leaving the Gelli, but the doctor put
down 'inflammation of the lungs' on his certificate.
Be that as it may, we played our part in making his funeral as respectable as possible. Between myself, my cousin and
Uncle Robert, we paid for his coffin, the preparation of the grave and all funeral expenses. As I understand it, the
spinster got all his belongings in lieu of wages for the time that she had been serving on him. She had been with him
for years and I don't think that that she was paid more than a pittance for her efforts. This did not amount to very
much.
{end of page – it seems that he delayed completing the letter}
My dearest cousin, I was very pleased to understand that you are all alive there, but I am sorry to hear that you
yourself have been ill. Wouldn't it be better for you to come back to Wales for a while to see if that would do you any
good? Improved travelling facilities are enough to tempt one, but it is true that the cost is too much for many.
My family are all well. Oh! How good it would be to see you again - Thomas, Daniel, Anne, Jane Eliza and my dear
Aunt, yes, and the other two aunts, and their children as well (I have almost lost all recollection of them), the children
of Uncle John, Eliza and William D. Roberts – I can only remember the name of one of Uncle Daniel's children,
Catherine and her curly head! Tell Thomas that I have your family photographs – but not one of him.
Would it be possible to receive photographs of the other cousins?
You will get a good long letter from me if you reply to this one. My warmest regards to you and your wife, your
brothers and sisters.
Your Cousin
Robert W. Roberts

Middle Granville
July 12th, 1883
Robert D. Roberts
Dear, Kind Nephew and relatives
I received your kind letter on the 10th of this month. It brought me great happiness and pleasure to read a little about
my dear relatives and to understand that you were comfortable and well.
I too am being allowed to stay alive and being given enough mercy to carry me to my journey's end – which in the
order of things, will not be too far off. "Oh! to inherit a Better World!" I have been able to outlive most of my relatives,
but this causes much sorrow and feelings of loss.
It is likely that I have told you before how many of us remain alive – namely my children, Robert E Humphreys, (his
address is Poultney, Vt.) He is five miles north of me here. He too lost his first wife – the mother of 8 or 10 children but
he has now remarried. There are no children from this marriage.
My oldest son is married and lives in the western part of this state. He is a printer. Robert owns the weekly newspaper
Poultney Journal and has a printing office and employs 4 or 5 men. His second son is the supervisor there. They make a
good living. The second of my children and my only daughter, is Kattie. She lives close to me and I eat my meals with
her although I live in my own house. In my house, two rooms are my own, and I rent the rest out to Kattie's married
daughter (her youngest daughter). The eldest daughter is also married; her husband is an American, but the other's
husband is Welsh.
The eldest daughter lives in Rutland, Vt about 25 miles north of here. Her husband is a storekeeper and does good
business. Kattie's husband is also a storekeeper and runs a post office in this town. He too is doing well.
Well, I just have one more child to tell you about – Daniel J. Humphrey, Hoosick Falls, NY is his address. He lives about
45 miles south of here. He is married to an American girl. They have one five-year-old daughter but have buried a four-
year-old son. He is a heumis(??) maker and has his own store.
That is all of the children that are still alive – just 3 living out of 9. I really feel the loss when I look back at the large
family that I once had. But one must bend to the will of the One who is too wise not to do everything in the best way
possible. It is our duty to obey Him and to worship Him. There is no situation that we shall ever face where it could not
be very much worse for us. We have the honour and duty to live according to His Word and leave it up to His honour
to do as He sees fit. He never does an injustice to any man.
With regards to you and all my relatives, I would be pleased to learn about what has been going on. Where are you all
now? How many of your father's family are still living? What is their occupation? Also the families of Daniel and John?
I heard from John's wife a while back and I replied, but I have since lost her address. If you know anything about them,
I would be pleased to hear it. Daniel's family in the same. Who is still alive, where do they live and how are they?
A word from my dear relatives would be very warmly received as I am lonely here in my old age. News from afar is like
cool water to a thirsty soul.
I have seen that your cousin Rees Roberts lost his wife (around last March). I have not heard from him in a long while.
We used to write to one another regularly. You may still hear from some of our relatives.
As regards the picture of the Temple that you sent, it is excellent. We are proud and thankful for it and hope that the
Holy Presence will fill it as in Solomon's Temple long ago.
To finish this short letter, I send my kindest regards to you all. Firstly, to you my nephew but also to all my dear
relatives. If dear Sister Catherine Thomas of Creuau is still alive, I send her all my love.
I would be delighted to be able to speak to you all. Can you still speak the old Welsh language I wonder? All of my
children speak it as if they had just arrived from Wales.
I must finish, but look forward to hearing from you soon.
John W. Humphrey

letters.title: Robert D. Roberts to Unnamed nephew - 16 December 1884
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
851-852
Logan City
16th December, 1884
Dear Nephew
After a three-month delay, I am now taking this opportunity to write to you from the country of the Far west as we
used to say in the Old Country years ago. So much has changed since then, as travelling is now so much easier, more
comfortable and faster and one can chat to one another whilst travelling. This brings more places within reach.
Now for a few excuses. When I received your letter, rather than reply immediately, I decided to wait a while, but then,
before I could start writing, I went to work to Beaver Canyon on the section which is 260 miles away from here – on
the branch of railroad that is going to Idaho and Montana – "The Utah & Northern Railroad". I was working on the first
section and making $1-70 a day and paying $5.00 a week for food. So, you see that I did not have much left over.
It has been very poor here for quite some time now – no work of any sort to be had anywhere. Farming the land does
not bring much profit to the worker – only enough to live on. There is no value to anything that the land produces at
the moment.
My dear nephew, I am very thankful to you for your generosity in writing to me. Since I said in my last letter what I
thought was best for you to do I won't add that it would great to see you and all the family, brothers and sisters but I
do think that this is the best place, especially if you want to serve God. This is my opinion. I will not add to this at the
moment but I will turn to Evan.
In the kindest way
I remain your uncle
R.D. Roberts

East Bangor, Northampton County, Pennsylvania
29th April(??) 1885
Dear Cousin and Family
I was delighted to hear from you. I am very grateful to you for noting everything in such detail.
As I read your letter Robert, I could see that times have changed for you and that you have suffered bitter experiences.
I was very sad to hear that you had lost your dear wife; from your letter I gather that things are much the same there
as they are here with death roaming through the family and taking our loved ones away. I have buried two of my
children – Robert Wilfred(?) Roberts and Elizabeth Ann Roberts.
I have four remaining children - Jane M. Roberts, William J. Roberts , Martha Samantha(?) Roberts, Laura E. Roberts.
My home(?) is a poor place as I write this letter but the family have been fairly healthy this winter. But I should not
complain as we have plenty for our needs and I trust that we are making good preparations for the Life Hereafter
which we will spend in Heaven.
In Bangor (America) there are two Welsh chapels- one Calvinistic Methodist and the other Independent and they are
both flourishing. I and my family have been (not the best) members of the Methodist chapel since it was established.
So you can imagine, there is quite a gap between our beliefs and those of the Mormons. I can tell you from the bottom
of my heart that I do not feel any animosity towards Mormons as individuals, definitely not, and I respect the fact that
there are in their midst very wise men, but about your ideas and principles, I believe that they are things to put aside.
In a time when the practice of having multiple wives exists in your area, I am disgusted at them in light of my Bible's
teachings. It is a shame that educated men lower themselves to such depths.
It was very good to read in your letter that after your wife's death left your children orphans that you remain a
widower with your old mother looking after you. I feel very grateful that you are so kind and tender towards my old
Aunt Catherine of Llwyn-y-Gell (as I used to know her).
Tell her that Gwen Lewis died last March. Her daughter Catherine lives here. Her son Lewis is in Vermont and his sister
Ellen. You will well-remember them I am sure.
Oh, yes, I left the subject of having multiple wives. Your letter left me with a good impression that my old family was
once again pure and free from the idea of having more than one wife at a time. That is how God taught us and how He
set out His laws. The best advice that I can give, is to keep clear of any false prophets and trust in Jesus Christ as Lord
and Saviour, with no need for anyone else as a go between. There is only one God and He gave us Jesus Christ, put
between man and God, and everyone who believes in Him will have Eternal Life.
Several of my wife's family, her uncle's name is Hugh ?T. Roberts, I believe came there at the same time as you did. He
is from Harlech and his daughter still lives there. The daughter of William Griffiths (printer in Dolgellau) is my …?.... Her
mother was the sister of Hugh Roberts who is over there. Her parents and all her family are dead; she is the only one
of the family still living.
Well Robert, what next? Don't you fancy going over to Wales? If you do decide to travel, it would be good to have you
come visit us whilst passing; we are not 80 miles from New York. It would be great to see some of you.
I hope that you will not feel bad towards me for taking the liberty of stating my opinion about Mormonism.
I hope to hear from you soon – and from Thomas and Daniel (they can write in Welsh or in English).
If health-permits and I have the opportunity I will send you a family photograph soon.
Best regards
Your cousin
Evan W. Roberts

letters.title: Rees Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 13 February 1885
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1931-1934
Glan-y-Pwll Cottage, Rhiwbryfdir, Blaenau Ffestiniog
13th February, 1885
Dear Cousin
I was delighted to receive your letter as so many years had passed without my hearing from you. I was glad to learn
that you and all your family are well. Since you have so many questions for me to answer, I should get on with it
straight away with little more formalities - or the paper will run out!
My son, Robert, emigrated to America almost a year ago. He is a doctor - quite talented but he was also somewhat
lazy and thoughtless and considered that I should 'keep' him. So I decided that the best thing to do was to allow him to
do as he wished and leave, so that he could fight his way through life, as I did – and he is getting on well and has been
very lucky.
I now have three sons and one daughter at home with me. The eldest is 14 years old and the youngest 8. They are all
excellent learners but I have no mother for them and this makes life difficult. But fortunately, Providence has been
kind to me and given me everything that I need made sure that I will never be in need of anything.
I have been employed by the Oakeley Quarry Co. since Mr Holland's lease came to an end seven years ago; I was with
him for the previous 15 years. Things are not good in the quarry these days though, and there are no real signs that
commerce is going to improve.
If you were to come to Blaenau now I am sure that you would think that you had come to some foreign land – such are
the changes here. No fewer than three railways operate from here now. A tunnel under the mountain to Dolwyddelan
brings one track in, another track comes over the Migneint from Bala and the third track comes from Porthmadog. The
old Glan-y-Pwll yard is now a station.
The son and daughter of my sister Mary have gone to America and the daughter has got married. The old Llety
building is now just a ruin. My mother is quite well but old and frail. She was really pleased to hear that your mother
inquired about her, and wishes to be remembered to her and all the rest of you.
William Williams Creuau ), Charles(?) Roberts (Carreg Alldrem), Ellen Jones (wife of Richard Jones the blacksmith),
Mary Griffith (Bwlch Llindir), Dafydd Williams (Cwm Bowydd) all died some twenty years ago. As did Thomas Jones
(Rhosydd), old Williams and Chesel (?) Welsh Slate, Mr Greaves and many more.
Richard Jones the blacksmith still looks much the same. Robert Roberts is a fellow-official with me under the trading
name Dafydd Roberts & Co. working here and looking good. He has one son.
Aunt Margaret is well but very frail but she does manage go out. She now lives in Glan-y-Pwll Bach.
Our cousin Robert lives in New Market Square, Blaenau.
In Blaenau, the area from Rhiw all the way down to Congl-y-Wal is now built up – one long as a long street. Every
building and street have been given a new name - I find it difficult to find my way around (but I am not one that gets
around much anyway).
Jason Thomas died about two years ago and Robert Rhys died quite a while back.
There are still old family members living in Fedw - that is the daughter of one of the old ladies who lived there. She
married somebody that I would describe as a cross between a man and a devil!
The old family left Hafod many years ago, but John Roberts is alive and has built a new home close to Garreg. He too
has grown old and frail.
The same family live at Ynysfawr – namely the eldest son. His sister lives close to Pwllheli. The other brother and sister
died a while back along with their father.
The Park family have all passed away, the only living daughter lives in Cwm Bowydd, having married Lewis Thomas's
son.
Nelly Robert died years ago. Her sister Laura lives in the Gatehouse leading to Ynysfawr. That place has been turned
into something of a palace by Mr Jones. He is the chairman of the Penrhyn Magistrates.
Mr Holland is still alive and well and living near Barmouth, aged 83.
Meurig has been managing a quarry near Towyn for quite a few years. He has a wife and, I think, eight children.

Ellis is a bachelor and lives here with me. He fractured his arm three weeks ago. He refused to take up farming after
my father died although I offered to take on the farm so that my mother would have a home. But I had to find her a
home with my brother William. He offered her rooms in his house.
William lives in Penrhyn and works in the quarry. He is married and has lots of children.
Elizabeth lives in Glan-y-Wern, close to Garreg, in a small farm. Her husband is from Caernarfonshire. There are loads
of children there.
My sister Gwen, the youngest of us all, died, leaving three children, three years ago.
Thirty years have brought major changes – far too many for you to comprehend from reading a letter. Young children
at that time are now middle-aged and the elderly have moved on to the cemetery. This area has seen more change
than any I can tell you.
Welsh Slate, Gloddfa Ganol and Holland quarries have all merged in to one huge quarry - from Talywaenydd to the top
of Allt Fawr. But a few years back there was a major 'fall' in the quarry which fractured the mountain causing untold
damage and huge expense.
The buildings in town are so numerous that it is impossible for me to begin to name them all. There are six schools in
Blaenau and every one accepts from 400 to 600 children. There are 20 to 30 chapels belonging to the various
denominations. The population of the parish is about twelve thousand. The Valuation for the Poor Rate is £70,000
with the Poor Rate set at 2/4 in the £ and the Local Board charging 9d at the moment.
There is a Market Hall by the new church with an Assembly Room above it and this can accommodate 1,500 to 2,000
and is often crowded when meetings are held there.
There are lots of shops and hotels – far too numerous to list.
The town is a nice place to live in and has all the facilities that one would need. Alcohol is not a problem here and the
townspeople are pretty law-abiding and honest people. It is a very Radical town - nobody apart from a Liberal would
dare to turn up here! The people remain religious and always speak out when there is any wrong-doing.
Well, I am coming to the end of my paper, so I must finish by wishing you all well. My mother, my brothers and all my
friends wish you every success. We look forward to hearing from you again soon. Perhaps I can compose a better
letter the next time.
Best regards
Your cousin,
Rees Roberts

mr holland is still alive and well and living near barmouth, aged 83.
meurig has been managing a quarry near towyn for quite a few years. he has a wife and, i think, eight children.

ellis is a bachelor and lives here with me. he fractured his arm three weeks ago. he refused to take up farming after
my father died although i offered to take on the farm so that my mother would have a home. but i had to find her a
home with my brother william. he offered her rooms in his house.
william lives in penrhyn and works in the quarry. he is married and has lots of children.
elizabeth lives in glan-y-wern, close to garreg, in a small farm. her husband is from caernarfonshire. there are loads
of children there.
my sister gwen, the youngest of us all, died, leaving three children, three years ago.
thirty years have brought major changes – far too many for you to comprehend from reading a letter. young children
at that time are now middle-aged and the elderly have moved on to the cemetery. this area has seen more change
than any i can tell you.
welsh slate, gloddfa ganol and holland quarries have all merged in to one huge quarry - from talywaenydd to the top
of allt fawr. but a few years back there was a major 'fall' in the quarry which fractured the mountain causing untold
damage and huge expense.
the buildings in town are so numerous that it is impossible for me to begin to name them all. there are six schools in
blaenau and every one accepts from 400 to 600 children. there are 20 to 30 chapels belonging to the various
denominations. the population of the parish is about twelve thousand. the valuation for the poor rate is £70,000
with the poor rate set at 2/4 in the £ and the local board charging 9d at the moment.
there is a market hall by the new church with an assembly room above it and this can accommodate 1,500 to 2,000
and is often crowded when meetings are held there.
there are lots of shops and hotels – far too numerous to list.
the town is a nice place to live in and has all the facilities that one would need. alcohol is not a problem here and the
townspeople are pretty law-abiding and honest people. it is a very radical town - nobody apart from a liberal would
dare to turn up here! the people remain religious and always speak out when there is any wrong-doing.
well, i am coming to the end of my paper, so i must finish by wishing you all well. my mother, my brothers and all my
friends wish you every success. we look forward to hearing from you again soon. perhaps i can compose a better
letter the next time.
best regards
your cousin,
rees roberts

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:

Bangor, Pa.
22nd May, 1885
Dear Uncle
After a long delay I take the greatest pleasure in sending you a bit of news about me in reply to the letter which I
received several months ago.
The first thing that I am going to do is seek your forgiveness for taking so long to reply. But the blame is not solely
mine, as I waited because you had written to both myself and to my Uncle Evan and he wanted to reply to you and
wanted me to wait until after he had written before I replied. April came and went but eventually he did write, but
even then he forgot to bring the letter down to me to post. He lives in …?...Tavern(?) namely (?)Great East(?) and I don
not live there with him. Eventually I went up to collect the letter and visit my aunt.
Evan got a son after he wrote and the baby is doing well. Aunt is getting better. Things here in our community are
pretty flat, wages are very low and there is much unemployment.
Few came over from the Old Country this spring and they are wise not to do so. Evan, myself and two others have
taken the lease of a quarry but thus far have not profited at al from it but we hope to make a little money this month.
I got a letter from the Old Country the other week and they are all well. Things are pretty flat there as well, with the
wheels of commerce turning very slowly, and if the war between England and Russia goes on things will be terrible
over there.
That is all that I have to say so I will now finish by asking you to write as soon as you can and not repay me by doing as
I did, although I well deserve it.
I am
Your Nephew
R.M. Parry

letters.title: Rees Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 10 March 1886
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2233-2234
Glan-y-Pwll Cottage, Rhiwbryfdir, Blaenau Ffestiniog
10th March, 1886
Dear Cousin and Family
Thank you for kind letter. I had intended to write much sooner, but had hoped to gather some information about the
family of David Eames for you. I gave your letter to the son of Gwen (his sister) who works with me, to see if he could
give you any information. However, very few members of the family remain around here now as far as we can surmise
– perhaps two sisters and their children. I attach a little that Ephraim Jones wrote (Gwen's son) and he promises to
find out more for me.
I knew David Eames well and I am sorry to hear that he is no longer in this world. He was always courteous, kind and
friendly. Did he leave family members behind?
I don’t have much interesting news for you, commerce remains pretty flat in all areas and we have had a very hard
winter - snow and ice these past three months. It is said that about 20,000 sheep have been lost as a result of this, at a
huge cost to farmers. The price of animals is very low and rents and taxes high.
The slate market is very slow and many are out of work, although salaries are not so bad that one could complain too
much. Quarry men earn, on average, five shillings a day and the surprising thing is that the quarry owners are so
tolerant of this situation.
There have been more changes than you could ever imagine in the quarries and in the town itself. It seems that there
is just one big quarry from Talywaenydd to the top of Allt Fawr. It has been worked to such an extent that, in several
places now, you can walk through the mountain into Cwmorthin. The slate though is of much poorer quality than in
your day, with faults ruining many rocks. If we did not have powered engines, the produce would not be worth very
much.
The town has improved a lot - you would be amazed to see the boggy ground at Glan-y-Pwll now covered in railway
carriages and trucks. Go on a bit to Dolgarregddu and you would see the same again there. The London & North
Western Railway is in Glan-y-Pwll and the Great Western and Ffestiniog Railways are in Dolgarregddu. Houses have
been built in every nook and cranny as well as shops, hotels and chapels. Somebody coming back after having been
away for years would be lost. Despite the growth in the town, the behaviour of the population remains good and they
are to be praised. There is not much drinking or such like here.
I can't think of any interesting news about anybody that you would have known I'm afraid.
There are only about eight or ten people in old Holland's Quarry who were there when I started working there, over 40
years ago. Similarly, here in Gloddfa Ganol quarry. I don't think that you would even know six people if you came back
here now - "One generation leaves, another comes along".
David Roberts works here and is looking good. He has a boy working with him. The Llanfrothen family are much the
same. You would be surprised to see Creuau with none of the old family there now. So too Carreg Alldrem and Erw
Fawr and many other places.
My mother is still alive, but is getting on in years; she still remains fairly healthy. Also, Margaret Roberts (Glanypwll
bach) but she is becoming very frail these past couple of years.
R.W. Roberts and family are well.
Evan is in America and Betsan is long-buried.
My sister Mary is a widow, but not doing too badly. Her youngest son is about 18 years old and works in the quarry.
She has two daughters at home and a son and daughter, both in America.
Elizabeth and family are well and living in Llanfrothen.
Ellis lives here with me – a perfect bachelor!
William and family live in Penrhyn and are quite well and living comfortably.
My son is very clever and working in America as a doctor – in ??Rutland?? County. I also have three sons at home and
also a daughter who still at school and doing really well. Despite having four children at home I often feel quite lonely,
although my situation is comfortable - but I should not complain about God's Providence – I always say that
complaining without good reason is a sin.

I had thought about sending you a photograph of myself and the children but unfortunately, I have not had the
opportunity to have a group photo taken. I will do so soon.
In finishing, I can only send my regards to you and your family also to the family of my uncles Daniel and John. Are they
well? I have not heard about them in years.
I remain your faithful cousin
Rees Roberts

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.notes: Date reading is uncertain in the supplied text.
letters.suppliedText:
1483-1485
Box #132, Bangor, Northampton, Pa.
2nd November, 1887{?}
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
Several months have passed since I last wrote – not for any lack of thinking about you or any carelessness, but I have
been very busy all summer. I often feel that there should be two or three of me not just one so that I can manage to
do everything at the same time. I am not trying to do everything just to make money, just that I feel that I cannot
cope. You know as well as I do how much work is needed to raise children and how expensive it is. But our children are
beginning to reach the age when they can help out. The eldest daughter stays in New York with a well-off family. She is
in a good place. My son worked all summer and now attends school. The other children are coming along well.
Oh, Yes! Whilst I remember, Mr. Willi Williams (of the mail stable) sends you his best regards. He used to work with
you in Gloddfa Ganol quarry {in Blaenau} – he comes from Harlech.
The slate quarries here are working well but wages are low.
Hywel, the son of blacksmith Dafydd Roland often inquires about you as a family. Edward Foulkes (son of Wil Foulkes
formerly of Rhiw, Blaenau) also wishes to be remembered to you. Joseph Jones lives close to us. "Joe bach del" and his
brother John, are the sons of William Richard (Dolgarregddu). Many, many people inquire about you – far too many to
list or to recall names.
I am sure that you hear from my brother and my cousin Rees in Wales. Last week, Robert M. Parry said that he had
received word that Ellis Roberts of Erw Fawr had set off from Wales for Washington Territory – I don’t know if he has
arrived there yet. He is accompanied by Lewis Roberts, the son of Evan Roberts (Llwyn-y-Gell) and some family from
Glan-y-Pwll.
As you can see, I am including a newspaper cutting in this envelope at the request of R.M. Parry. I forward it to you -
you can see what they are after, funds for a new organ for the chapel. They are writing to Welshmen all over the world
asking for financial contributions to reach their goal. They hope that you will not think this presumptuous.
I remain and send you best wishes
Evan W. Roberts

Logan, presumably (Scrap of paper - no date/address)
Again it is likely that he will get real dd… ? next spring. The committee have met with me and asked how much I was
willing to donate towards building the house. I said $50. Well, that will do pretty well to begin with. From the way they
were speaking, I could guess that they expected to get another $50 or more before the end.
There are a lot of collections going on here at the moment and of late, in order to defend themselves in the Congress
and the various courts in this territory. This is how I understand that there is enough room for me to support the cause
that is under such oppression and under so many disadvantages. I have contributed some hundreds, if not thousands
of dollars since I was in Utah towards one cause or another. It would be a huge pleasure to assist you too but at the
moment I don't have much money. And I see that many are asking for contributions from me. I have lost my good
health these past 20 years. I am not very strong due to rheumatism which is a big worry and means that I am not
always able to work. But I have been a bit better these past three years.
{continues on back of this sheet}
Friendly towards Robert M. Parry. I am pleased to understand that you are attempting to serve God. There is nothing
better for a man than to receive personal evidence that he has understood the plan and order that God laid down for
man's salvation. If man does not get evidence of the reality of the order then he will be in doubt and ignorance and
there will be no certainty. But if he receives from the sacred priesthood and the Holy Spirit comes to rest upon him
and light up his mind and open his eyes and understanding get full happiness this is how I hope that you are as you
read this letter.
It made me think like this.
Has God changed or not in the time of Jesus Christ? There was only one way to serve him. Are there more ways by
now or not? There are many differences between my cousin and myself in the way in which we try to serve. I know
what I know and he knows what he knows. Everybody is responsible for their own actions. For that reason, be quiet
and go away.
In the kindest way, your cousin
Robert D. Roberts
P.S.
I sent my wife's note to you. Hugh Roberts

Logan County
29th December, 1889
Dear Cousin Evan Roberts and Family
I got your letter around the start of this month. Thank you, I had not heard from Wales in about two years.
We are all well here and nothing much has changed since I last wrote to you. Therefore, I do not have anything much
to tell you in terms of family news.
I am enclosing a photo of Hugh and Mary Roberts - but I expect you to return this to me. This was taken about
eighteen years ago. I encouraged them to have their photo taken before they moved to Bear Lake Valley but they did
not want to do so. They are now old and frail. I thought that you would be glad to see the photograph and so I am
posting this to you. This photograph belongs to one of the children so I hope that you will return it after having a good
look at it. I believe that they are fit and well at the moment.
About the assistance that you wanted in order to ?????
I was called one …???... collecting money to get a new organ for this Ward. This City is being split into seven districts or
seven bishoprics. I lived in the Third District when we came here to establish this place, 28 years ago. There were no
houses or anything here then, but from around 1862 we built a schoolhouse and we used to worship there, up until
now. But this place is going out …???

letters.title: David Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 5 December 1891
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
620-622
2 Dorfil Street, Blaenau Ffestiniog
December 5th, 1891
David Roberts – to - Robert D. Roberts
Dear Friend,
It was a huge surprise to see your brother, Thomas D. Roberts turn up here a month back. But it was tears of joy and
not surprise. It's certain that there is no other person from that side of the ocean that I would be so pleased to see -
that is of course, unless I saw you. I have a child-like longing {hiraeth} for you still - although I have not written to you
in years.
Thomas recognized me straight away - from my voice apparently. I only had about three hours' time with him whilst
he was here for a few days, but I hope to have much more time with him before he returns. I look forward to taking
him to those places where we used to play and work back in the day; places where we had so much fun as children.
It was good to hear about Daniel and your two sisters, and of course, about your dear old elderly mother and yourself.
Although you are now well, you have suffered great loss and have been in pits of despair, but you are still alive and
prospering. Give everybody my very best regards- especially your highly-respected mother. I cannot go into detail
about everything that goes through my mind – a wealth of fond memories, but I do not have the words to describe
them.
If I have not misunderstood what Tom said, I understand that Dafydd Peters and his wife Lowry (of the watermill at
Rhydsarn) are still alive. If so, please convey my sincerest good wishes to the elderly couple. I have enjoyed many of
Lowry's tasty honey-and-treacle sandwiches as a reward for carrying milk down from Llechddu farm to the factory in
order to feed their daughter, Sarah. Tell them that 'Dafydd Llechdu' sends his regards – the grandson of old Lowri
Lewis (Llechddu). If you have their address please send it on to me before they pass away – they were a very kind-
hearted family.
And Robert, wouldn't it be great if you could come over to the Old Country once more? I really think that you should;
as I understand it, you are now a widower.
I have a wife and four children, the oldest is 24 years old and the youngest 13 - two girls and two boys.
I will not write more this time, but wait until I get a letter back from you.
With my sincerest good wishes,
Your faithful friend
David Roberts
P.S.
My father died ten years ago

december 5th, 1891
david roberts – to - robert d. roberts
dear friend,
it was a huge surprise to see your brother, thomas d. roberts turn up here a month back. but it was tears of joy and
not surprise. it's certain that there is no other person from that side of the ocean that i would be so pleased to see -
that is of course, unless i saw you. i have a child-like longing {hiraeth} for you still - although i have not written to you
in years.
thomas recognized me straight away - from my voice apparently. i only had about three hours' time with him whilst
he was here for a few days, but i hope to have much more time with him before he returns. i look forward to taking
him to those places where we used to play and work back in the day; places where we had so much fun as children.
it was good to hear about daniel and your two sisters, and of course, about your dear old elderly mother and yourself.
although you are now well, you have suffered great loss and have been in pits of despair, but you are still alive and
prospering. give everybody my very best regards- especially your highly-respected mother. i cannot go into detail
about everything that goes through my mind – a wealth of fond memories, but i do not have the words to describe
them.
if i have not misunderstood what tom said, i understand that dafydd peters and his wife lowry (of the watermill at
rhydsarn) are still alive. if so, please convey my sincerest good wishes to the elderly couple. i have enjoyed many of
lowry's tasty honey-and-treacle sandwiches as a reward for carrying milk down from llechddu farm to the factory in
order to feed their daughter, sarah. tell them that 'dafydd llechdu' sends his regards – the grandson of old lowri
lewis (llechddu). if you have their address please send it on to me before they pass away – they were a very kind-
hearted family.
and robert, wouldn't it be great if you could come over to the old country once more? i really think that you should;
as i understand it, you are now a widower.
i have a wife and four children, the oldest is 24 years old and the youngest 13 - two girls and two boys.
i will not write more this time, but wait until i get a letter back from you.
with my sincerest good wishes,
your faithful friend
david roberts
p.s.
my father died ten years ago

letters.title: Rees Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 2 June 1892
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
3980-3981
Llys Dorfil, Blaenau Ffestiniog
2nd June, 1892
Dear Cousin
Well…I finally received a letter from you - after many years waiting.
I was delighted to meet your brother Thomas and learnt that you were quite well and comfortably off, so we have
reason to be thankful. Things are fairly good for us as a family as well.
Well, what shall I write that will be of interest? You will have heard of my mother's death on January 7th, 1892. (My
father also died in the month of March, but 15 years earlier).
I was pleased to hear that that your mother was strong and healthy. All of the old Llety family have by now 'gone to
rest from their labour', leaving behind only their sons and daughters.
Well, I finished working in the quarry six years ago having worked hard all my life. I am glad to say that I receive £100
as a pension. My eldest son is an engineer working on a ship these past 18 months, not setting foot in this country, but
he will return in October. He will soon be sitting the Chief Engineer exam and now earns £8 per month and his keep
but will be much better off if he passes the exam. My second son is a pharmacist in Bangor and doing well. My third is
in Liverpool preparing for the civil service exam – he will be lucky to pass. My daughter is aged twenty, and is in Dublin.
Well! I have re-married – a widow with five children. Quite a handful don't you think! But I have been lucky. One boy is
a clerk in the bank, another is training to be a pharmacist, and the other three preparing for their future. And we have
a two-and-a-half-year-old daughter together. If such a thing is possible, she is even better than my other daughter.
Ellis has been living in Shelton Mason County, Washington for a few years now.
Meurig is in Abergynlowyn, working as an quarry agent. He has a large family and is quite content.
My sister is a widow and has two daughters living at home. One is in service and the other is a school mistress. The
third is married and living happily. The eldest son has been living in Pennsylvania for years.
Ellen died in America.
Elizabeth lives in Llanfrothen and has a large family.
William lives in Penrhyn and has a family and works in the quarry.
The old Llanfrothen family has almost gone now – very few of the ones whom you knew when you visited Llanfrothen
are still there. Much the same can be said about Ffestiniog, few of your old friends remain. The place has changed out
of all recognition.
I don’t know where your brother Tom is by now – somewhere in South Wales.
Commerce in this country has been pretty poor for a few years now, but we shouldn't complain, but rather, give
thanks, as we get much better than we deserve.
This year we had a very hard winter and the harshest spring in years.
I am hurrying now so that I can catch the post. Best regards to you, your mother, your daughter and all my
acquaintances there. Also, I would appreciate receiving your next letter a bit sooner than the last time.
R.W Roberts and family are well and live quite close to us in a good house which he owns outright. His old mother
looks well too.
Remember that your few acquaintances that are left here, will be asking about you.
Kind regards
Your cousin
Rees Roberts

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 16 January 1893
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1901-1903
Bangor, Pa.
16nd January, 1893
My Dear Cousin
Your letter arrived along with your dear mother's Remembrance Card and a picture of the Temple from(?) Hugh T(?)
Roberts, my wife's uncle. Many thanks.
Your mother had had a long life on this earth and saw many difficult times on her journey through this world. I hope
that she has gone to rest in the arms of the Great Saviour. She spoke to Him often in this world, so when the Call
came, there was nothing to be done other than enter his Everlasting Peace.
I am glad to hear that you have buried her next to your father (although there is nothing unique in that) but again,
there is some subconscious feeling that the family is again reunited in the same patch of earth. Such feelings are
expressed very early on in the Old Testament. I can only thank you as a family for putting your mother's body to lie
next to your father's.
Is there a general cemetary there? If so, what is it called? Just in case I can come visit any time – or one of my family
members. It would be a good feeling to visit that place where my dear relatives are resting, or give others instructions
to find the place.
Robert M. Parry lives quite close to me. He got married some time back and now has two young children; the eldest is
a son he got a daughter this morning ( 13th Jan, 1893). They are doing well.
I have not heard from Wales since the start of last summer. My mother is well but is becoming frail.
That old gentleman Griffith Robert Ellis (Dolwyddelan) who used to work in Gloddfa Ganol quarry when you were
there was buried here last autumn. Edward Foulkes is here and has a large family so too Howell Roberts Rowlands (son
of Dafydd Rowlands the blacksmith), you may also recall William Pritchard (Dolgarregddu) – brother of JCO Richard).
His son, John, died here in the madhouse a while back. William Williams (Wil Stabal Mellt we used to call him in Wales)
and the other lads here send you their best regards.
As I write this, my wife is writing a letter to Harlech to her cousin; we have not heard from them in a long time.
When is your brother Thomas returning? I would like to know so that we can arrange to meet. I intend to go to New
York to meet him so that he is not inconvenienced and loses his ..?... on returning.
We are all well as a family and send you our warmest regards
Your Cousin
Evan W Roberts
