letters.title: Robert Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 21 July 1896
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2682-2685
6 New Market Square, Blaenau Ffestiniog
21st July, 1896
Mr Robert Roberts
Dear Cousin
After a long delay, I am at last putting pen to paper to answer your letter which I received at the start of May. I am
sorry that I did not write sooner following the death of our cousin Rees Roberts.
I miss him because he was my only relative on your father's side who still lived in this area. Professionally, he was in a
situation where he could have been of considerable assistance to me - but he did not see fit to do more than the
minimum. He worked as a quarry supervisor for old Holland for 20 years. We all have stories to tell about unjust
supervisors don't we, but he wasn't one of those. He had a quite a good reputation amongst the workers generally.
He was put out to pasture a few years ago, but continued as a pensioner; they say that he got £100 a year in pension
from them. He had gathered quite a fortune by putting money aside during his working career but he spent a lot of it
on his eldest son - trying to make a doctor out of him, but to no avail. Similarly, he spent a lot on his daughter, but
again to no avail. She is currently cleaning floors and black-leading! {black-leading was polishing cast iron fireplaces
and hearths} His third son, Rees is trying to become a pharmacist, but he too has failed two recent exams.
Daniel, his youngest son is an apprentice mariner. He has another year before he completes his training and sits the
Mate's exam and later a Captain's exam. If a boy or girl excels at their studies, there is plenty of room for them at the
top - but many more people have to slot into the lower tiers.
I see that I have somewhat left my intended topic. Here's my excuse, I went to see Rees's wife to ask what had
happened during his illness and she promised …?... But I will let that promise pass and I will you give you all the details
of Rees's death.
He was suffering from ….?...tula which had started three years before, but he had dismissed it and did not go to get
medication and things went from bad to worse. He was getting out of bed, but it was clear that something had gripped
his constitution and taken its toll on his spirit and on his complexion. The end came quite quickly – he was in bed less
than a week.
It was at that time that he received your letter. He was unable to read it and said that it should be passed on to me. I
am ashamed that none of the children answered that letter. He had a Private funeral with just a few family members
present. He was buried in Bethesda cemetery, in the same grave as his son Gruffydd.
He died without having made a will. I fear that his children will have to be dependent on the wife's compassion, but
she is one of the wisest, most careful and quietest women. She had a good education and taken advantage of every
opportunity. She was born October 24th, 1842 - so she is 54 years old this year. She was born in Betws-y-Coed. Her
family are from the Eglwysbach area of Denbighshire. A cousin of hers emigrated to the Salt Lake - a girl who was
reared as an orphan, 40 years ago – was she perhaps your first wife? I cannot remember names – her father was called
Roger and he came from Flintshire. He was English on his father's side. I cannot remember what else she said – my
memory is failing (it was never good).
I began this letter a month ago but let it ride, but here goes again, I will try to continue. But I feel a bit reluctant to re-
start as I have been so remiss about writing.
I was sad to hear that you had been injured and were feeling weak and worried as a result of the injuries that you
sustained in your fall. I hope that you are better by now and feeling as good as ever. In the Bible, Job says "Man's days
are full of sorrows".
I am not going to enter into any discussion about the teachings of the Saints in the Salt Lake as I do not have a good
thing to say about them or false religions. I am surprised that you followed such a foolish teaching but I do not doubt
that you moved to a country where you are much better off materially rather than if you had stayed here.
I received several newspapers from Thomas and am grateful to him for them. In one of them, I read about your giving
a report after returning from your mission to some of the Southern States.

I would be very glad if the children of my Uncle John and Uncle Daniel could me send me their photographs. I have
some recollection about how Elizabeth and William Daniel Roberts looked, but I can only recall Catherine, from my
Uncle Daniels's children.
God willing, I will send you a photograph of us as a family. My youngest daughter has gone to college in Swansea for
two years, God willing. Her name is Mary Ceridwen Roberts (aged 18, birthday 27th June); she won a Queen's
Scholarship (First Class) of £100. The other two have each had two years college. My second daughter has now been
given charge of a school here earning a salary of £85 a year. Elizabeth Alice has not yet been given charge of a school –
she is an Assistant and gets £60 a year. I worked hard to give them a good education, hoping that they would benefit
from it, so long as they also are of good character.
I am still working hard and generally fit and well, but I am starting to feel my age with my limbs not being as flexible as
they used to be. I would like to rest, but that does not look likely.
I read in the last newspaper that you had a successful eisteddfod in Denver, Colorado. Apparently, the Great Salt Lake
Choir excelled. Well done Saints! But it is not true that nothing good came from Nazareth.
I also understand that you have got a second wife – an Irish woman. She may make you a good wife – being a Papist
converted into a Mormon. I hope that she is a wise and virtuous woman – they are Celts and of the same blood as the
old Welsh. I would like to address her in English tongue "I wish you a happy and a long life to live together and rear a
lot of children whom will fight their own battles in this sinful world with ease and success. I hope my cousin in law Mrs
Roberts will pardon me from these untidy lines addressing her." Pardon my disorder, I would like to be able to write
better English, but words fail me as I have little practice speaking English.
I would like to see you all and your country too, but it is too late and old age has crept up on us.
Your old acquaintances have long gone from Blaenau, newcomers fill the district these days. There are so many
changes in the town and in the quarries, which have hollowed out these mountains. Business is booming for slate but
wages remain low, despite all efforts. Supply is greater than demand and so we can only hope that the demand
increases to kill the supply. That is the only way things will get better for us.
I guess that I should end it here lest I burden you by going on and on. If you wish to write to me, I will reply. I love
getting some family news every now and then.
I cannot remember anything special to add. I am sure that you have heard that Hugh Gwilym has died.
I and my family are well and send you all our best regards - Tom and his wife, Dan and his wife and children.
The walking stick which Tom brought back to you was grown in my garden; I hope that you enjoy walking with it in
your hand.
I have had to re-start this letter two or three times. I have just put it to one side. I began it in May but did not finish it
until September! Please, please, excuse my failings, dear cousin and do not follow my example of laziness and delay.
We had a nice summer but it has been raining this last month.
I am, your cousin
Robert Roberts

letters.title: Robert Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 18 May 1897
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2682-2685
6 Market Square, Blaenau Ffestiniog
18th May, 1897
Mr R.D. Roberts
Dear Cousin
After a long delay, here I am trying to acknowledge receipt of the photographs which show such a large portion of my
family. I was delighted to see my aunt and her husband in the photo - looking so good. I think that she has put on
some weight since leaving Wales. Also, her husband looks a really nice gentleman and they look very happy and
contended. Great! I hope that they have every success and blessing. I can remember one particular occasion, when
she was a maid at the Hafod; she stole a bag of red gooseberries and brought it to us children at Tan Lan. So much has
changed in almost fifty years! I hope that she has a long and happy life to the end of her days.
Next comes my cousin W.D. Roberts. Seeing the photo of him really reminded me of his father. Doesn't he look just
like him? He has lovely looking young children.
Elizabeth (Mr & Mrs Shippley) – I assume that her husband is an Englishman (at least his name suggests that to me). I
am delighted to see them too and their children.
I see that I am mistaken, Robert E. Roberts and aunt was the one I last received {???}. Robert is a boy. Weren't there
five children that set off from Rhyd? I am proud of them all. There is nobody here from my father's side but now I can
turn to my album, and I will be there, in their midst. About the other side of my family - well, I might just as well not
hear from any one of them! It would be very boring for you if I listed everything that has happened. I won't start as I
would have to tell you the whole story. Pardon my expressing such bad feelings about my close family.

pointless to list the changes. One of your acquaintances has died – Robert Owen bach (Bethania). He had been an
official at the quarry in Rhiw for 20 years, but had been retired a few years ago and gone to live in Porthmadog. It was
said that he left a sum of £20,000 in his will. Owen Rowlands and Hugh Lewis died years ago - both of these men also
had amassed quite a large sum of money. Few workers have been able to rise above their status in life like this.
S.D. Roberts sent me several copies of The Salt Lake Tribune and I got a lot of enjoyment from reading them. The old
Dome gets a very good share of paying taxes {???}. This makes me think that he must be doing good business. Good
for him!

appreciated.
I can only remember Catherine and Eliza. I seem to recall that one son died crossing the Missouri?
I and my family really appreciate getting your photographs. Tell Aunt Mary and children that I am very grateful for
their kindness too. I intend to have my own family photo taken, and I will send a copy on to you in the Mormon Land.
I can only hope that this letter finds you all well and I end by sending best regards to you all. "My best love to your
Missus and baby" {in English}. I would be grateful to hear from you at your earliest convenience.
Yours until death
Your Cousin
Robert Roberts

letters.title: Robert Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 25 December 1899
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2853-2856
Glyn Tegwel, 6 The Square, Blaenau Ffestiniog
25th December, 1899
Dear Cousin
I got your letter on November 6th and was very pleased to receive it. It gives a good account of all the family, not just
news about the death of old Aunt Mary. I hope that she was warmly welcomed to the Happiness of her Lord.
I got a letter from her about 25 years ago and she asked me for a "long Welsh letter", but I lost her address, so I did
not get back to her. I hope that her children all are well. Give them my condolences.
I am re-reading your letter. David the son of your old friend David Roberts was badly hurt as one of the pulleys in the
quarry mill caught him as he was trying to replace the strap on a moving pulley. He broke his arm, sending his shoulder
out of position and received a huge wound to his head. Thankfully, he is improving and starting to go out.
I understand that you have heard from Evan that my mother died about eighteen months ago. Of all bereavements
nothing is as bad as losing your mother. You probably have already received quite a full account from Evan since he is
a member of The Leaders of the Third Party {???}. It would take me too much time and space to go through what
happened, so if you have been given any account which you would like an explanation about, please write me a note
and I promise to reply in detail about the circumstances.
Somebody that you knew very well died last week – Robin Dafydd James (aged 80).
I have received several papers and books from S.D. Roberts. Tell him that I am very grateful for them.
I must say that I am surprised that your son is a Mormon missionary. It is a pity that you misunderstand and misuse the
holy Scripture. I accept that the olden times have …?... but you are confident that when predicting for another 30
years {???}
I am glad to hear that you and your wife are having more children. They will doubtless be of great comfort to you
when you are 90 years old. I am quite different; I often think that this may be the last that you hear from me. When I
return to the area where I used to live there are no family members left. Rees (son of Rees Roberts) sometimes visits
me - his wife and daughter live just a few yards away from me.
I have been given the address of Ellis Roberts and enclose it with this letter.
If you can, send my best regards to the children of Uncle John and Uncle Daniel.
I would dearly love to see you just one more time but "Goodbye" as I have almost reached 'three score years and ten'
and if I have strength, I may reach 80 years "Our days may come to seventy years, or eighty, if our strength
endures"{Psalm 90}.
We had a lovely summer and we have still not had any frost or snow.
I would be very grateful to hear from you. Make your wife write a letter in English - my daughters can compose a reply.
Can your sons speak Welsh or are they monoglot English speakers? Is there any wish in Utah to see the Old Language
be kept alive?
I must finish by wishing you all a happy new year. Accept our warmest regards as all family.
I remain your faithful cousin
Robert Roberts

letters.title: Ellis Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 26 May 1900
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
500011-500015
2708 Cedar x8ect???
Seattle
Washington
May 26th 1900
Dear Cousin
I got your letter a while back and I am now going to try to reply. But before I start, I have to admit that you are far
better at remembering things than I am. You can remember back forty years as if it were yesterday. I was only young
when you set off and I can only recall yourself, Daniel and Thomas, I cannot for the life of me, recall the girls.
I too have lost both of my parents, my brother Rees and my sisters Ellen and Gwen. I still have two brothers living and
two sisters – Meyrick, William, Mary and Elizabeth.
My father died aged 70 and my mother lived to be 85. My sister Ellin died in America – in Wisconsin. I don't know how
old she was. My sister Gwen died aged 27 years and recently, Rees died aged 63.
Rees had three wives. From his first wife, he got a son, whom he brought him up to be a doctor – but he died aged 27
in America. His second wife gave him four sons and a daughter, but two of the boys died leaving him with only sons
and one daughter living. The girl is married and lives in Corwen. One of his sons is a druggist and the other a sailor
(now in South Africa). The third wife is still alive and has one daughter.
Mary was married twice, but is now a widow. She had two daughters and a son from both husbands.
I do not know how many children Meyrick has – but it is about 12.
My brother William has 5 or 6 children
My sister Eliza is a widow and has three daughters and two sons living –
but has buried quite a few.
That's about all about the family. I am an exception in the family in that I
have not wanted to get married thus far and it is unlikely that, considering
my situation, I will decide to do so. I have not had much luck since I got
here a little more than 12 years ago. I had £1,500 when I arrived but I
spent every penny. I don’t have much to show for it - I have 120 acres of
land, but it is of no use other than to have to pay taxes for! I am going to
try to sell it this summer if I can. Also, I have two houses in this town and I
get a little income from them every month.
I would be glad if my circumstances allowed me to come there to see you
but I am certain that I would not be able to recognise any of you! I am
including my photo with this letter so that you can see what your American
cousin looks like.
I am now drawing this letter to a close and send you my best regards.
Your cousin
Ellis Roberts

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:

Bangor, Northampton, Pa.
24th December, 1906
Well, cousin Robert D. Roberts
I got your letter at the end of the week. I was very sorry to hear that you both had been "imprisoned" in such
circumstances. Whatever, I hope that you will both return to your normal good health very soon.
I am sorry that the doctors failed you so badly - carelessness when handling the knife! I fear that they had a poor
understanding of their work and that you will again have to seek medical advice. Anyway, I hope that next time they
will be more successful and that you will make a full, speedy recovery – both you and your wife, so that you can again
enjoy good health together for many years and see your children grow up to be men and women of good character.
I see that your families have established themselves in that part of the country. I hope that through everything that
you all – young and old, sons and daughters ..?... through faith, will see the Hills of Canaan so that you can forget your
worldly grief and see Jesus as He is, excelling in everything and everybody can socialise with him – and not through any
prophet or priest, but solely by having faith in His name. All communication with Him will be quiet and through the
Spirit - of which the world knows nothing. That sweet community, between the spirit of God in Heaven and through
His dear Son. There will be nobody that stands between us and Him. The pleasure will be a personal one, between us
and God, in His Son. I trust that you, in your illness, get some consolation from this.
As you can see, I have started replying to your letter the very day that I received it, but I was called away before I could
finish it. Three weeks have passed before I continue.
Dear cousin, I hope that you are keeping your spirits high despite your illness and that you get a speedy recovery next
summer – both you and your wife.
The weather here is very changeable. Wet and damp some days, then turning very cold, like today. We had a
snowstorm, then rain and again we had snow today with perhaps a lot more snow tomorrow. The poor weather has
been responsible for much sickness here. Changeable, wet, damp and cold.
There are several things in your last letter that I wish to comment upon, but I will do so fully in my next letter.
You asked about slates. I see that you can remember that roofing slates come in various classes 1st, 2nd and 3rd class.
The 3rd class are quite cheap and I would not recommend you to buy these - they aren't worth shipping so far. "No.1
slate is the best of all. Our number 1 in this valley will compare good with Old Country slate. They are good in every
way" {in English}. I am not afraid to say so but remember that there are different prices for the different sizes.
{Table showing some size and price – illegible}
By tonight I will have made inquiries about prices as well as the cost of shipping.
Well, this letter is beginning to drag on.
Several people here are inquiring about you. Hywel, the son of Dafydd Rolant (the blacksmith) has just buried his wife.
He often inquires and sends you all his regards.
Old 'Sutafiel the Mail' as we used to call him used to work with your father in Gloddfa Ganol {BFf slate mine}, very
often asks about you and sends you his regards. He is now old, frail and quite lonely.
I am glad to say that we as a family are all well and send you all our best regards and hope that God gives you every
blessing.
Regards from your cousin
Evan W. Roberts
P.S. {different handwriting}
Evan has been ill in bed since Monday

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts and Laura to Robert D. Roberts - 11 April 1907
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1342-1345
22 South Main St, Bangor, Pa.
April 11th 1907
Mr R.D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and family
I see from your letter that I received at the start of this week that you have again met with a bereavement. I was very
sorry to hear that; it leaves you with your children orphaned. I am praying that that you will be supported to meet the
bitter things that come against us, wave after wave.
When bitter things come upon us it is good to remember that the Father of the Adopted and the Judge has promised
to look after us in our hour of need. Our three Great Archbishops will help us out in our distress. I hope that you have
come to know Him before now as the Brother and Friend of all sinners who implore Him through faith to receive His
Grace. It is good for us to receive every help from godly brothers and friends in our time of tribulation but we must ,
each one of us, on our own, have faith in Jesus Christ, and then we will receive comfort and solace in our own hearts.
With respect to various faiths, they are good in their place, as far as they go, but they cannot keep us nor can ministers
or bishops open the doors to Paradise for us nor get atonement for us for our sins. We must ask for this ourselves.
Nobody is forgiven at the request of another. Sinner come into the dust and plead for it in the name of Jesus Christ
who accepts us out of the grace of His heart. So we turn to Him in our hour of need and He will be found to be there
waiting for us.
I see that I have gone slightly off-track. I understand that you are going to have more surgery. Well, Robert, I see that
you are again to go through difficult times. It is my hope and prayer that you get a full recovery for a few more years –
for the sake of your young children.
Next, I hope that your brothers Thomas and Daniel are close by so that they can help care for you and that your
families are all close.
The family here are all well and talk about you very often. They send you their warmest regards and send their
sympathy to their uncle in his bereavement and also wish him a full recovery.
Accept our sincerest regards – both of us, me and my wife.
I wish you the very best always and hope that you succeed in all meanings of the word.
I am as usual
Your sincere cousin
Evan W. Roberts
{added in different handwriting}

Excuse the poor handwriting and the paper.

Bangor, Pa.
2nd Sept, 1907
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Relatives
I always read your letters with the greatest pleasure. Just so this time. I was delighted to read that you are better. I
feel grateful for your photograph but I have to say that it looks nothing like I remember when you were in Ffestiniog.
Time changes our appearance and takes its toll on us all. I am glad to hear that your brother Thomas and his son have
gone to enjoy themselves in California. I hope that they had a brilliant time there.
The //… are awaiting a girl for Daniel Hughes(?) of Pengwern(?) she is a widow with children.
What next!
I and my wife have been to Wisconsin. …?... We were away for a month. The reason why we went is that our our
minister's wife died at the end of May and on behalf of the church, we went there to her old home before putting her
to rest there.
There are many Welshmen in that part of the world and they have done well there. Everyone looked happy. That state
is excellent for farming and a good country. It is beautiful there as you travel from Buffalo to Chicago especially.
Most of the time was spent in Chicago. A huge huge city. Really it is like a world of its own and there is beautiful
country all around.
Commerce is progressing well in these areas. Everybody is in work and wages are good. This town (Bangor) is growing
rapidly. There are about 7,000 inhabitants. When I arrived, there was no more than about a dozen families living here.
This has happened in just 40 years since I arrived.
You can see how time flies! We too will have sped past the limits of our time very shortly.
The most important thing is that we have prepared for our next journey which awaits us all. Oh let us hope to inherit
the Truth!
There was a Sunday School meeting yesterday(September 1st ) and the son of Pierce Dafydd (Tanygrisiau) spoke of
Baptism and Jesus in the desert. We had a very good time and everybody took it very seriously. We got a taste of the
old truths as we discussed this over and over.
Well, I must draw this to a close. I trust that these lines find you all well and that you receive all the worldly blessings
that we do not deserve.
So I end with my sincerest regards
Yours faithfully, your cousin
Evan W Roberts
P.S.
We are very grateful for the photo - it is excellent.

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 1 November 1907
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
321-326
Bangor, Pa.
1st November, 1907
Mr R.D. Roberts
Dear Cousin
I am not certain that it is my turn to write, but I will do so anyway since I cannot find your last letter. I have looked
everywhere - but anyway, I will write.
I hope that you are by now in better health than when I last heard from you.
In part of May and June, my wife and I visited Wisconsin state, about 1,200 miles away. We went following the death
of our minister's wife. Rather than leave him and his young daughter to travel all that way on their own, we went
along with him. We were away from home for a month and had a very good time. My wife was keen for us to go on
from there to see you as a family, but we realised that it would take us all summer, and even then, we probably would
not get to see everyone.
The places that we visited were beautiful. Everyone looked comfortably off there. The Welsh have progressed to take
up important positions in the area. Listening to them speak, I think that they are generally of independent means and I
feel good to this day when think about them. I believe that that is how it might be in your area as well. I hope so.
Nothing would give me more pleasure than to think that some of you had become legins?? or that some of the old
family had become millionaires in this new country! It would not surprise me; it is people like us who go on to make
fortunes here. Only one thing gets in the way of us, the Llety family of Llanfrothen, from becoming rich and that is that
we are too honest and speak the truth when discussing business opportunities. In my opinion and in my experience,
this type of person will never become very rich.
How are things regarding commerce, employment and wages in your area? Is it still good there? Farmers are
dependent on next years' crops. Is commerce, employment and are wages good in the area?
There is good demand for slates and for milled stone here. This area has become an important quarrying district and
the area has grown significantly. We dispatch thousands of tons every month. Prices are increasing every month in this
valley - over $60,000 in May. Within two miles …?... their prices are similar; other things have gone well too since we
arrived here 40 years ago. There was nothing here then. But what is next?
I must draw this letter to a close as it is getting too long – but I find that I get pleasure from chatting away to you like
this. I hope that you too feel the same as you read it.
My mind often wanders towards my time with you. I remember you when you were young and living in Llwyn-y-Gell -
a very long time ago. Now I received your photo and Oh! you are an old man of 70! I find it hard to believe, I just
cannot get my mind around all the changes and new circumstances. It just wants things to stay as they were but
reason tells me I must move on and accept the changed circumstances.
Despite receiving your photo (and it is a very good photo) in my mind, I will still see you as you were in the Old Country
– a young man. That's what you will always be for me. And the rest of the family the same – namely Thomas and
Daniel and your two sisters. My memory will still stay there and enjoy the old pleasures. But if I was ever to see you
again of course my mind would have to accept all the changes that have taken place - for you and all your family. I
have a good recollection of all three families in the Old Country, but time sure has changed things.
Well Robert, my dear cousin, please accept my dearest, warmest regards.
Yours
Evan W Roberts

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 20 July 1908
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1702-1704
Bangor, Pa.
20th July, 1908
Mr R.D. Roberts and Family
Dear Cousin
Your letter arrived along with the newspapers (which are published weekly or monthly) which contained the article by
the son of Uncle John Roberts (formerly of Llety, Llanfrothen).
I was delighted to read that you had all been blessed to such a degree and done so well and are now to be comfortably
off.
About the ..?... and family, my wife and I were talking about the fact that it might be better for us get a ticket to come
there to visit you as a family. But you are most likely all quite far apart, so that it would be difficult for us to see
everybody.
I am glad that you are so happy in your current circumstances. We send you our best regards and wish that God guides
you.
I go on to answer your question regarding the slate industry here. This country now compares well with the Old
Country as far as the slate business goes. Our monthly payroll in this (Bangor) valley is $100,000 per month …?...
in Slatington and communities, without considering West Bangor itself. And there is also Virginia, Vermont and Maine
– those places produce huge amounts of slate. I think that we produce more slates than the Old Country at the
moment. Another thing, we are gaining a foothold in the old country as well, and export a lot to England, Scotland,
Ireland and Wales. They send thousands of tons from here to Wales every year. The slate industry is now important in
the States and increasing all the time. The population of this town grows all the time; when I first came here (a little
over 40 years ago) there were no more than two dozen families in the town, but today it is close to 7,000 and the
surrounding villages add to that. The population has increased a lot along with the slate industry.
I must draw this to a close – it is getting too long.
However, I feel that it is only fair that I tell you something about my circumstances. I am not what you would call poor
– I have a little put aside. I am not rich by any means but, by the grace of Heaven above, I hope that we have enough
to carry us through this life, so that I will not have to depend on others. These days, I feel that I am getting on – I was
65 last February. Daniel is a bit older than me if I recall correctly.
Edward Foulkes and Howell (son of Blacksmith Dafydd Rowland) send you their regards. Joseph Griffith ("Joe
Dolgarregddu") was here recently and asked about you and sends his regards. He is now a very old man. His wife is the
daughter of William Roberts (shoemaker).
The weather has been very hot this year and it affects my healthy more than in the past. Well, accept my sincerest
wishes.
I remain, your cousin
E.W. Roberts

102 Bellevue Ave. north
Seattle
July 22, 1908
Dear Cousin
I heard from your brother Thomas and he said that you wanted a programme for the big fair that is being held here. I
am afraid that there is no such thing as a single programme, just daily timetables; that is just a daily programme.
It is likely that you will be here when the Eisteddfod is to be held, namely August 27-28. It looks as if there will be more
Welsh here then than ever before on the shores of Puget Sound. Many compositions have already been received and
there will be choirs attending from all over the place. There are signs for a very successful eisteddfod - let's hope that
it turns out that way.
The weather in this part of the country is now very favourable and many thousands visit the Fair every day - I have
kept records from the first day. It is certainly worthwhile to make a sacrifice in order to see what they have assembled
there. Truly excellent.
If there is anything that I can do for you, then I will do it at once if I can.
Best regards
Ellis Roberts

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established

letters.suppliedText:
491-501
Logan City
August 15th, 1908(??)
Mr David D. Roberts - the son of my old and faithful friend David Roberts of Blaenau Ffestiniog
I received your wise and courteous letter giving me information about the Ffestiniog district and its inhabitants and
asking about some of the Welsh who had emigrated to Utah.
Travelling to Utah in those days was quite a dangerous ordeal – there is a thousand miles between the Mississippi and
Salt Lake City. The travellers set off from the Mississippi near Omaha and crossed the Plains and the Rocky Mountains
whilst being ravaged by wild animals and savage Indians who believed that the White Man had no right to set foot on
their land. The spied on us migrants, waiting for any opportunity to steal our animals and kill us. We had to be on the
lookout day and night with guns at the ready …. and up to a year??? …. 1863 when soldiers settled in Salt Lake City and
controlled the Indians and there was fierce fighting between the soldiers and the Indians in the northern part of the
Valley. They more or less eliminated the whole tribe, before this, they were dangerous and out of control – stealing
and threatening to come down to kill the inhabitants. Day and night, we had to carry arms when went into the fields or
forests in case they jumped us without warning. The inhabitants had to fight them for various parts of the province
before 1863. Since then, a change has taken place and the Indians have become more docile and begun to live like the
White Man and build houses and schools.
Sometime towards the end of 1857, arrangements began for the holding of an eisteddfod in Salt Lake City on January
18th, 1858. The main competition was to compose six englyn {forms of Welsh poetry} – I can't remember what the
other competitions were. People travelled 100 miles on foot or by wagon. There was, at the time, no money around
and everybody had to carry their own food and bedding or rely on the charity of those they met along the way – just
like hobos. From this we can see that love for the old Welsh traditions still burned in their breasts. There was
disagreement and violence between the Government and the Saints and there was no eisteddfod or gathering of the
Welsh until 1895 when another eisteddfod was held in Salt Lake City for two days and also in Logan for two days. This
was a very successful eisteddfod. Another eisteddfod is to be held in Salt Lake City on 1st 2nd and 3rd of October of next
year. It is likely that a large crowd will gather in Salt Lake City. A Cymanfa of Saints will be held on the 4th, 5th and 6th
and a fair of everything that is grown locally – all sorts of fruit, trees, animals of all sort. The winners in all categories
will go forward to compete for the main prize. In Malad City, Idaho, the Welsh from all over the Malad Valley come
together to hold a one a one-day eisteddfod annually.
Regarding religion:
The Christian world is full of religions and this is increasing year by year, with various reformers forming groups and
beliefs to worship according to their own interpretation or fancies. They all aim to lead their followers away from evil.
This is good, but by reading the "old" Bible we read that religion in the time of Jesus Christ and the Apostles,
???Sadiwsas Faresis??? and others, and forms of religion, but this was not acceptable to the Saviour of the World.
They had formed new forms of worship. They did not Tithe and they encouraged people to do good deeds thinking
that they were following the teachings and the commandments set down by Moses. They said that Moses and the
prophets were enough for them - in their blindness and in their blind belief in the laws of Moses they rejected the
inheritor who was given authority by God to perform the sacraments of His house. I was talking to a Catholic once and
he said that read that their authority came from Peter. Of course, Peter and the Apostles …??... death of world
religions or end of different religions.... collect in the city of Nice if I remember correctly.
…???…going around following different religions … that would bring religious peace and an end to murder and stoning
by forming beliefs that would be acceptable to all the world's people. Constantine the Great was emperor at the time
and according to his command, a huge gathering of people was called. His father was a heathen but his mother was a
Christian. According to the story, he did not follow any religion but he must have felt compassion for the Christians
because of his mother. After the church officials were done away with, there was nobody left with authority and the
ability to defend the Church. They were like a land subjugated by its enemies with nothing to do but watch on as its
enemies did as they saw fit, and all through the influence of Constantine, calling themselves Christians.
Today, on which foundation do the Latter Day Saints stand?
On the basis of revelations that Father and Son revealed to man in these Latter Days. Joseph Smith was a 14-15 year-

old boy at a time when there was a religious revival in his local community. He went into the woods to pray and to ask
the Lord which one of all these religions was the True Religion. And the Father and Son appeared…
Regarding the religion of the Saints in Utah:
The basis for the religion of the Latter Day Saints is a direct statement from God that the Father and Son appeared in
our days to speak with man and in order to train him in the proper way of life they sent angels several times to
prepare his mind to accept various the keys of various ordinances of the Kingdom – just as in the time of Jesus Christ
and the Apostles. The Angel John the Baptist came and placed his right hand on the head of Joseph Smith and his left
hand on the head of Christ. …?... and presented the Aaronic Priesthood to them. Peter, James and John presented the
priesthood of Melchizedek. Moses came and presented keys to collect the saints together. Elijah brought the keys to
turn the hearts of the Fathers towards the children and the children towards the fathers. His way was to build temples
and to celebrate ordinations in the Temple and present blessings to the deserving. They were authorised to call men
to different occupations in the Church- Teacher, Priest, Elder, Three-score-and-ten, Archbishop, Patriarch, and
Prophets; all the church members just as in the time of Jesus Christ and the Apostles. They have been instructed to set
out before the world that which they have been given and the evidence which they know. All who obey with open
hearts and come forward to be baptised and who present themselves to the Holy Spirit will get evidence for
themselves to allow them to decide whether it is God or Man that they are going to obey.
Now, where is it the fraud in this promise - which is just as it was in the time of the Apostles? Everyone will get
evidence. When Jesus asked the Disciples who do they say…??... to Peter he answers "Well who do you say that I am?"
Peter answers. Jesus answers. God bless you Simon, son of Jonah because it is not flesh and bone that you have seen
but my Father who is in Heaven. It is not possible for our flesh to give information or evidence about the truth of the
gospel of Christ; this comes directly from God.
If the leader of the Church gets a revelation then the members are entitled to know if it comes from God or from Man.
The Saints are not in the dark if they live according to their professed beliefs. We can read Revelations Ch.14 Vs.6 and
also Daniel Ch.2 Vs.44-45 from which we see that God in Heaven will do something different to anything on earth in
the days of the Kings themselves. The world generally believes that there will be no Revelation or prophesy after this.

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established

22 Main St., Bangor, Pa.
3rd April, 1909
Mr Robert D Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
Here I am writing you a short note, hoping that it finds you fit and well, as we are, to a degree. I am partly recovered,
but not totally, but I hope that, as the weather improves, then so shall my health improve.
This winter has been very changeable sometimes wet, cold and damp. The weather has caused a lot of illness here;
much illness and many deaths among the young as well as the old; no difference between them– when the Call comes,
they have to go. It is important to be ready when the Call comes.
I have nothing much to add. Commerce has not been very good here this past year or so, but we hope for better times
as spring comes. That's what everybody says.
We as Calvinistic Methodists are repairing our chapel. I think that it is going to look pretty good when finished. We will
re-open around the start of June. At that time, we expect to have ministers to lead our prayers that God gives us
Eternal Life.
I enclose my photograph - you complained that I had not done so.
Well, accept our sincere regards.

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 24 May 1910
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1442-1444
Bangor, Pa.
24th May, 1910
Mr Robert D Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
I received your letter on the 23rd. Thank you very much for your kind invitation to come visit you. I would be delighted
to see you all; I very often think about you. However, we have already made all the arrangements to visit the Old
Country. We will be setting off from New York on Saturday the 28th. We will be on our way by the time that you
receive this letter.
The main reason for my trip is to follow my doctor's instructions as I have not been too well for quite some time. I am
though, feeling better now, otherwise I would not think of going. My wife will of course accompany me.
If we have a few more years, we may well come out there to see you, but our time is running out. If we are spared a
few more years, we will make every effort to come to see you.
Things are quite busy here now and it is difficult to get this letter written. Old friends are popping in as I try to write.
There are three or four women chatting to my wife in the other room as I write.
I must repeat words that you wrote in one of your letters a few years ago, that I am truly fortunate to have a life-
partner who is a good wife and has looked after me over the years and is a truly religious person and a quiet woman.
Accept our kindest regards as a family.
Your Cousin
Evan W Roberts
P.S.
I really hope that you are fully recovered and that your family are all well and enjoying all life's blessings.

letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1762-1764
Bangor, Pa.
12th May, 1910
Mr Robert D Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
After far too long a delay I answer your letter. I hope that you will excuse me. I have been quite poorly in my health
this past 18 months but now feel better.
It has been a long fight in my mind these past few months whether to come there and visit you family members or go
to the Old Country to visit. Now, I have made my mind up. My wife and I will be going to the Old Country setting off on
the 28th of May if everything goes right.
The children have all grown into men and women who can look after themselves and so I feel compelled to visit the
old haunts one more time before I leave this world.
Last summer my wife and I were down in Maryland visiting Joseph Griffith (the Del as we'd call him) and his wife – the
daughter of William Roberts the shoemaker who used to live in Four-Crosses. Humphrey Lloyd and his brother Ed all
send their regards.
On returning, we heard that your son was in Washington D.C. with the government. I am sorry that I did not know this
before now. It is not far from here to Washington – I would have gone there to see him.
The son of Joseph Griffith I believe is a foreman in one of the newspaper offices there.
My wife got a letter from your nephew William Morgan recently along with a photograph of her and her mother and
also brother and she was pleased to receive it; she has shown it to lots of people.
Next, a man from Seattle called on his way to the Old Country. He had met you in Salt Lake City and had met your
brother and his son in Seattle as I understood. He was not well though; I hope that he is now better and that you too
are now healthy.
With kindest regards to you all as family.
Your Cousin
Evan W Roberts
P.S.
I hope to visit old Brondanw {Ramoth} cemetery in Llanfrothen and will place flowers on the graves of those resting
there.

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts and Laura to Robert D. Roberts - 22 November 1910
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1162-1165
22 Main St., Bangor, Pa.
22nd November 1910
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
Here I am sending you a few words after our return from the Old Country, having spent four months there. To be
honest, I have never spent a more pleasant few months in my life. I experienced the utmost hospitality and my health
was much better than I had anticipated before I set off.
There have been huge changes there since we left. From the bog at Glan-y-Pwll, all the way across, they have built and
there is now one large town. They have all the travelling facilities that you would expect and you can go from there to
anywhere very easily. The old quarries have really grown; the more they work, the more wealth they discover. The
slate has been developed and it is clear that there are sufficient resources for centuries to come.
The faces there have changed; there were few of our acquaintances remaining, having been taken to their Eternal
Rest. I visited about twelve cemeteries to see where old friends had been laid to rest.
I visited the old Brondanw {Ramoth} cemetery in Llanfrothen, and saw my father and brother's grave. The gravestone
is in good condition and did not require any work done to it. My Gelli grandmother and grandfather are also there, as
is my Uncle Edward and his wife, Uncle Robert and his wife, and their son and daughter – Gwen (& husband) and
William.
At my father and brother's grave I felt how strange it was to see a man of 64 standing beside the grave of his father
and brother, and shedding tears, which fell on a tiny patch of ground which was their grave.
I met all my cousins from both sides. Mary and Elizabeth (daughters of Erw Fawr) have grown old and frail. Their
brother Meurig Roberts is still well and lives in Towyn, Merionethshire with his sister, Mary. It is a pleasant place – lots
of visitors in the summer.
The name of my Gelli grandfather's father was Robert Roberts. I did not find out exactly where he came from, but it
was somewhere around Clynnog. That's where the old family came from.
We visited Harlech, Beaumaris and Dolgellau and then went on to Leeds in Yorkshire, England. This took us more than
five weeks.
Then we returned to Ffestiniog and afterwards we went via Llanrwst to Penmaenmawr, Llanfairfechan, Bangor,
Caernarfon and Lanberis. We did not climb Snowdon as it was too wet. After a week in Llanberis we returned to the
old town of Caernarfon for a day and from there on to Penygroes and Llanllyfni for four days, before returning to
Ffestiniog.
By now it had almost become time to head home. We visited Dolwyddelan, Trawsfynydd, Penrhyndeydraeth and
Llanfrothen - but none of the old family remain.
We set off on October 7th (?) on the Moritania and arrived in New York on the 7th and got home at 7pm after travelling
all day. Our youngest son, second daughter and two granddaughters were waiting for us. They were all well and
everything had gone well and there was no bad news to report. We were grateful to the Father of all Goodness for his
utmost care for us as a family on all our travels.
We had bad weather on the voyage home – everyone was sea-sick for more than half of the voyage; I have never seen
as many people being ill. Everybody felt relieved and happy by the time we arrived in New York and had been met by
our families.
In Harlech, we stayed with the sister of your first wife; she's called Mrs Humphreys. She is 80 years old but still very
smart-looking. Her oldest daughter lives with her and they are very contented. We had a great time there with all the
old relatives.
Well, I will finish now as I have no more news. Everybody sent you their best regards.

I am as always,
Your Cousin
Evan W. Roberts
P.S.
I have one small favour to ask. Bryfdir asks if you have any poetry that you could send him. If you send them to me, I
will forward them.
Dear Cousin
Here is a photo of my cousin Jane and me that I took in a bit of a rush just before setting off. You can see how well she
looks. She is 13 years older than me. We were delighted to meet once again. She said that she had lived with my
parents for a few years when she was young.
She has one daughter at home with her who is a seamstress and her mother helps out as needed. I will try to get a
better photo for you.
We must make some economies now I'm afraid – but if I had the means, I would like to go on travelling.
Best regards
Laura Roberts

Bangor, Pa.
3rd October, 1911
Mr Robert D Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
I am taking a few moments to write you a short note, hoping that you are well, as we ourselves are, to quite a degree,
at the moment thanks to Heavenly Providence.
Firstly, as you know, your son D.R. Roberts came here to visit us. We were delighted to see him and enjoyed his
company for about ten days. Time just flew – we didn't have half enough time with him.
We heard a lot of news about the family in Utah and surrounds. We were very happy to hear of your successes and to
hear that you also partook of the spiritual and eternal aspects of life.
I am surprised that you have not made more of an effort to retain the Welsh language in your religious circle.
I must say again that we enjoyed their company immensely whilst they were here with us. I felt bad that our daughter
Margaret was not home so that they could see us all. But she did not return home until after they had left. I have sent
them a photo of her (to Washington).
We really hope that we can see you here before your son and family return back there. Perhaps you will visit him in
Washington and, from there, come on to visit us. We will eagerly await this.
I am not going to give you any Bangor news as I am sure that he will have told you all about that.
Before I finish, remember us to Thomas and family, Daniel and family, Ann and family, and Jane and family, and also
the family of your late sister Elizabeth. We wish you all well.
It is likely that you have received the photo of the 'old crew', I hope that you will be able to remember everybody. Old
William Williams (the 'mail stable' we'd call him in the Old Country - and we do here as well) who used to work with
you when you set off. He is now 84 years old and, as the photo shows, still quite well. All the crew send you kindest
regards.
I will finish by hoping that these lines find you enjoying full health.
We as a family come together in wishing you all the best.
I remain
Your cousin
Evan W Roberts
{in different handwriting}
Your son and his family are very nice people. They look just like my family – by which I mean his mother's side of the
family.
I am your cousin's wife
Laura

22nd Main St, Bangor, Pa.
15th April, 1913
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
Thank you for your kind letter expressing sympathy to us as a family in our bereavement.
I don't know what to say other than we are reasonably well these days. Our son William's wife has started to improve
and we are very thankful for that.
We miss my wife terribly; she was a caring wife and mother. A better wife, mother or Christian was never put to rest.
I am enclosing this Memorial Card along with the letter. My son Clarence sent a dozen of the cards to David R. Roberts
a while back but has not received an acknowledgement. He thought that he knew better than us how to distribute
these cards amongst the family. Anyway, I am sending this directly to you.
Accept our very best regards,
Your Cousin
E.W. Roberts

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 19 December 1913
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1802-1806
22nd Main St, Bangor, Pa.
19th December, 1913
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
I have delayed writing much longer than I had intended to. Although I have intended to reply to your very kind letter
every day, I just could not settle down to do so.
Things have changed dramatically here for us. Mrs Roberts left us a year ago today – exactly a year ago today was her
last day here on earth. She finished her worldly days at half past midnight, with her husband, sons daughters and
grand-children around her bed as she drew her last breath.
I feel very lonely despite having all the children around me. But I must say that they have been very good to me.
It is likely that you have heard of the bereavement in Harlech last summer near Dolgellau. He and his family used to
come on holiday to Wales every year from Leeds. Perhaps you remember that near Dolgellau there is a steep hill,
down into town. The car lost control and she was thrown out and injured. She died within a day at a local hotel. She
was buried in a family grave in Harlech. She was a good woman who raised a good family all of whom who grew into
good men and women. I and my wife visited them and spent a week there. They were well-off, in a good business
there.
Things are looking pretty bad around here. Several of the quarries have shut and others work a three-day week. Many
are unemployed.
I do not know what to make of this Democratic government – things look pretty bad! The large towns complain
bitterly that nothing is happening. Everything is being shipped into the country from the old countries and millions of
dollars will have left the country very soon if things continue as they are. Perhaps things may improve, but at the
moment, things are looking bad.
Where is Jab?(Job?)? We have not heard from him since he left for Washington. Are they alive and well? Give them
our regards, also Thomas & family, Daniel & family, your two sisters, Ann and Elizabeth. I hope that you are all, as
families, well and enjoying life fully and making preparations to enjoy the next life in the presence of the Saints and
Jesus Christ in Heaven.
Our views on these things differ, but the important thing is that we depend upon Jesus Christ as our only Saviour . He
is the Truth who will pay for our sins. He is our Archbishop who has ascended to Heaven to plead on our behalf. It is
not any man-made organisation that will bring sinners into Heaven but Jesus Christ, who died, rose the third day and
ascended to Heaven. It is not Mormonism, nor the Papacy of the Church of Rome, nor John Wesley, nor John Calvin,
nor any other man, however good he might be, only communion with faith in God in His son Jesus Christ. This is the
only basis for hope of our Eternal Life in His Son.
I am not going to say any more. It is not things that men believe that will keep others, it is necessary for everyone to
argue their own case in the name of Jesus Christ. Also he is the Truth for our sins. Neither Pope nor Bishop will keep
us, man himself must bend down and plead for forgiveness in the name of Jesus Christ.
He is the head of the church and nobody else will do.
Happy New Year to you all
Your Cousin
E.W. Roberts

letters.title: Evan W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 2 January 1913
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1612-1616
Bangor, Pa.
2nd January, 1913
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
At the start of a new year I need to write you a few words to inform you of our loss - namely the death of my beloved
wife, on December 19th0 after five days of illness. She died quietly, releasing herself into the arms of Jesus, with faith
that she would have a better future. She was buried on the 23rd. I, and all the children, were by her bedside as she
drew her last breath. She recognised us all up until an hour before the end. I can easily say a better wife waws never
laid to rest than her.
She has gone to her reward and left us behind for a while to grieve. Our sadness is huge.
I believe that she suffered a stroke on the Saturday 14th December as we were going to bed around midnight. She was
well before that and enjoyed herself and ate a good supper and put the dishes away as usual and was as happy as any
of us. At around 11 o'clock she complained of a headache. "Well," my eldest daughter said and prepared some spirits
of camphor and alcohol for her and she was then much better. My daughter added "You had better go to bed. It is
close to midnight. I will come and help you undress" "No, No. I will manage myself" she replied." I said "You go first
and I will wait until you have gone and I will put out the light". So, she went to bed. We went to our bedroom door and
asked "Are you ready?" and she replied that she wanted a damp cloth to put on her forehead. I asked her if she was
better and she replied that she was better but asked for a warm cloth for her forehead. She went to bed and I brought
the warm cloth and put it on her forehead. As I was putting it there, she had a stroke. I thought that she had died
there and then – even before I had called the girls. But we called for a doctor and he arrived within a few minutes and
stayed until 4a.m. On the Sabbath she improved and became quite coherent and recognised us all by the afternoon.
She was again better on Monday and Tuesday, and began to talk more and to recognise us all. But by Wednesday she
was obviously not as well and was clearly weakening. She was the same on Thursday but still ate a little and
recognised us all. At half past midnight on the 19th her spirit flew up to God who gave her Eternal Peace.
I hope that you will inform the Rev. William Morgan and family of this, as I cannot find their address. Our son Clarence
will write to David D. Roberts in the next few days so I will not go into detail.
I ask you to accept our kindest regards as a family.
Here I am, in quite a bad mental state,
Your Cousin
E.W. Roberts

letters.title: Ellis Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 17 March 1914
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2291-2293
Brynsaethon, Penrhyndeudraeth
17th March, 1914
Mr Roberts
Dear Cousin
Thank you for your letter. We had mis-placed your address or I would have written to you earlier, to inform you that I
had left America, a while back - I did not stay very long after having lost my old friend M.J. Williams. It is not likely that
I will return, except, perhaps, to attend the large San Francisco exhibition to celebrate the opening of the Panama
Canal.
I will try to answer your questions as well as I can. First of all, questions about family matters.
My brother Rees died aged 63 and left his third wife widowed; by now she too has followed him. He had one child
from his first wife, and he brought him up to be a doctor, but he died in America over 20 years ago. From the second
wife, he had five children, three of whom are still living. One keeps a drug store in Menai bridge, another is a ship's
captain, then there is a daughter who has married a preacher and lives in Corwen, another daughter, from the third
wife, has graduated as B.A. and now works in South Wales with the Insurance Act and has a good salary.
Mary lives in Towyn and is widowed, having lost two husbands; one child from first husband lives in Ffestiniog. Both
the son and husband were killed in the setts works in Penmaenmawr. He was in America for a short while. She had
two daughters with the last husband, one lives with their mother in Towyn, one is a teacher and another is a cook.
They keep a lodging house.
Bryfdir (the poet) is the son of Mary. He has won about two dozen eisteddfodic chairs.
Ellin died in America over 40 years ago. She was married and her husband has now joined her.
Eliza, had lots of children - six of whom are still living. She is the least successful of all of us. Her husband died around
the same time as my brother Rees.
Meurig has lots of children – seven sons and one daughter (living) and two who passed away. They all had a good
education. The eldest is a quarry supervisor in Corwen, one is in South Africa (and quite poorly at the moment), one is
a farmer, another a carpenter, another a doctor, another a banker and one is the secretary of an education board. The
daughter is married to a newspaper reporter.
William died aged 61. He had several children, five of whom are still alive. One has been to South Africa for a while
and two has been to America. Two are married and one son and two daughters living at home with them.
My sister Gwen died quite young. Her husband was killed in the quarry, shortly after her death. They had three
children. One son is a quarry supervisor (in Llanbedr near Harlech), another is a minister in Manchester. The daughter
is married and lives very close to us. Her husband has gone to South Africa. I think that they are comfortably off.
I don't have any more family information for you. They have all moved away from Llanfrothen, except for one of Eliza's
daughters. It is now strangers that live everywhere apart from Ynysfor- where the same family live (now into the third
generation there).
The old Llety is no more – it fell into ruin many years ago.
Griffith Griffiths now lives in Erw Fawr, the son of Bwlch Llindir (Croesor), his brother used to live in Carreg Alldrem but
he has since died, but family still live there.
The old Factory is empty as well as the Pandy. Strangers live in Gelli and in Parc. One of Aunt Gwen's family now lives
in Cae Glas (my mother's old home).
Best regards to you all as family
Ellis Roberts

letters.title: Robert D. Roberts? to D.D. Roberts - 19 October 1914
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.notes: The addressee is described as a son of David Roberts in Wales and is not automatically identified with David D. Roberts (The Judge), son of Robert D. Roberts.
letters.suppliedText:
500051-500052
People's Coal Company
One Block North of Logan Depot
Corner 1st North and 6th West St
19th October 1914
Mr. D.D. Roberts – son of my dear friend David Roberts who has left this worldly realm
Mr Roberts, as you see, I have not totally forgotten you! Quite a while has passed since you have heard from me, but
from this you will see that I am still in the Land of the Living!
I am enjoying quite good health and have food and clothing to fulfil my worldly needs. How are the people of
Ffestiniog doing? Are things continuing with their good deeds and are they successful in worldly matters. How has the
War affected the country?
Can you tell me your father's date and place of birth and also when he died? Is your mother still alive? Who are her
family? I hope that this does not inconvenience you.
I am sending you the Revelation that was given to Joseph Smith in May 1843. In the year 1844, he was murdered by a
murdering mob who disgraced themselves with this treacherous act. Do with is as you see fit; if you think that it is
worthy of your attention, you may want to translate it {into Welsh} and send it to the newspaper. If so, remember to
send me a copy of the paper. But remember, if you do not think that this would be wise, then I will agree with you. It is
likely that he did not recount his Revelation with the purpose of publication, but during the present War, some might
want to keep a written copy, lest it be lost. One of my neighbours took it to the newspaper and here is a copy. Do with
it as you see fit. If convenient, show it to Bryfdir.

letters.title: E.W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 10 April 1915
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1252-1253
Bangor, Pa.
10th April, 1915
Robert D Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
Today I am sending the rest of the hazel trees by Adams Express. That means that they will arrive more quickly and
safer. I think that they have been well-packed in a strong box.
I did not pay Adams Express but chose "Pay at other end".
I paid $1 to a farmer who lives close to me to dig them up and bring them down here. They were raised in the foothills
of the Blue Mountains. The reason why I asked the farmer to raise them from his own farm is that I only go out very
rarely these days. I hadn't been out for four weeks until this last week. My son William is now working and so he did
not have the time to go looking for them either.
I hope that they will reach you safely.
I finish by wishing you all well.
Your Cousin
E W Roberts
P.S. Let me know when they arrive. All that I paid was the $1 for the Dutchman.
Your Cousin
E.W. Roberts

letter-076 e.w. roberts to robert d. roberts - 10 april 1915 e.w. roberts robert d. roberts 10 april 1915   pdf page 103 1252-1253
bangor, pa.
10th april, 1915
robert d roberts
dear cousin and family
today i am sending the rest of the hazel trees by adams express. that means that they will arrive more quickly and
safer. i think that they have been well-packed in a strong box.
i did not pay adams express but chose "pay at other end".
i paid $1 to a farmer who lives close to me to dig them up and bring them down here. they were raised in the foothills
of the blue mountains. the reason why i asked the farmer to raise them from his own farm is that i only go out very
rarely these days. i hadn't been out for four weeks until this last week. my son william is now working and so he did
not have the time to go looking for them either.
i hope that they will reach you safely.
i finish by wishing you all well.
your cousin
e w roberts
p.s. let me know when they arrive. all that i paid was the $1 for the dutchman.
your cousin
e.w. roberts

letters.title: E.W. Roberts to Robert D. Roberts - 11 February 1915
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
1255-1256
Bangor, Pa.
11th February, 1915
Mr Robert D. Roberts
Dear Cousin and Family
I received the two letters from you and a large bundle of newspapers. The reason that I have not replied sooner is that
I have not been well. I have not written more than two letters in the whole of the last year.
Last spring, I had a bad spell and I was in bed for about four weeks and I have still not recovered fully. I feel weak and
cannot eat very much – I have no taste for food. I don't mind missing mealtimes. I have recently had more of an
appetite, but still not enough for me to gather my strength back.
Some of our family news now. Everybody, apart from me, are well. Commerce is poor – most small businesses have
only been working three days a week since the middle of last summer. Recently they stopped working in all the big
quarries and only some of the smaller ones still produce slates. It appears that we are going to have a hard time until
we change the government in Washington. Wilson & Brayn (??) have run us to the wall. The Democratic Party cannot
run anything here. They need a lot more schooling. There were never as many people unemployed as there are now.
New York Stant (??) Steel has thousands dependent on charity.
Despite this, there is a religious fervour in our midst and God is being hailed. In Bangor, hundreds have become
members of the churches. There is a big General Revival - amongst all races in our town and Balle(??) Sunday has been
a means to save thousands. He is doing good and a great service to our church as I understand; I hope that his health
keeps up so that he can keep on doing good and serve our Heavenly Father to bring thousands to the Saviour of Souls.
I believe sincerely that he is being used by God to save sinners and to draw them towards Christ our Saviour. All
success to him I say! My prayer is that they should not stop doing good.
Some news about our church now. We have been without a minister for three years now. We tried several men, but
failed, but by now we have attracted one from the Old Country and he is just as excellent an orator in both languages.
We pray that he will be a means for us as a church to attract more people to the Great Saviour, who gave His life for us
and who was resurrected on the third day and who went to Heaven to plead on our behalf. "We thank Him for
remembering the dust of the earth."
I finish by hoping that you will pardon me for having taken so long to reply.
In your letters, there were a few things that I had intended to comment on, but I will just finish by sending you, and all
the family, my best regards.
Your Cousin
E.W. Roberts

letters.title: M.G. Roberts to Mr. Roberts - 4 March 1915
letters.language: English supplied translation/transcription; underlying letter language not established
letters.suppliedText:
2972-2973
Brynsaethon, Penrhyndeudraeth
March 4th 1915
Mr Roberts
I have often thought that I should write to you, but have delayed doing so I'm afraid.
I am sorry to have to inform you that Uncle Ellis has died. He had not been well all summer and died November 29th.
He was buried at Ramoth, Llanfrothen in the same grave as his mother and father.
He died as a result of bladder cancer.
He leaves a big gap behind - he was always so cheerful and pleasant.
The newspapers that you sent arrived safely – thank you. Uncle would have ben very glad to have read them.
We see that you live in a very rich and beautifuyl city.
Kind regards
M.G. Roberts
